1:5.headline: "Made them holy" here means he summoned them
1:5.body: The verb usually means to make holy. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say Job was inviting his children to come to him, while Ramban says he had them purify themselves before his offerings.

sources.quote: הָיָה שׁוֹלֵחַ וּמְקַדְּשָׁם, כְּלוֹמַר: מְזַמְּנָם וְקוֹרְאָם
sources.says: Rashi says Job would send for them and 'sanctify' them, meaning he invited and called them.

sources.quote: ויקדשם. ענין הזמנה כמו התקדשו למחר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means inviting, as in 'prepare yourselves for tomorrow' in Numbers.

sources.quote: קדשם מאשה וכבסו שמלותם
sources.says: Ramban says Job had them keep apart from their wives and wash their clothes, to be ready for the offerings.

1:5.headline: "Blessed God" is a polite way of saying cursed
1:5.body: The word literally says the children may have blessed God. Rashi and Ibn Ezra say the writer used the opposite word so as not to write a curse against God, and the Targum translates it as angering God.

sources.quote: וּבֵרְכוּ. לְשׁוֹן כִּנּוּי כְּלַפֵּי מַעְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is a polite substitute word, used about speech against God.

sources.quote: וברכו - לשון כינוי, ובהפך כמו: ברך נבות אלהים ומלך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a substitute meaning the opposite, as in the false charge that Naboth 'blessed' God and the king.

sources.quote: וְאַרְגִיזוּ קֳדָם יְיָ בְּרַעְיָנֵהוֹן
sources.says: The Targum translates it 'and they angered the Lord in their thoughts'.

1:6.headline: "The day" may be the day the world is judged
1:6.body: ויהי היום can simply mean "one day". Rashi and the Targum say it was Rosh Hashanah, the day of judgment, and Ibn Ezra gives both readings.

sources.quote: אוֹתוֹ יוֹם שֶׁהָיָה רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה
sources.says: Rashi says it was Rosh Hashanah, when God told the Satan to bring the merits and faults of all creatures.

sources.quote: וַהֲוָה בְיוֹמָא דְדִינָא בְּרֵישׁ שַׁתָּא
sources.says: The Targum translates 'it was on the day of judgment, at the start of the year'.

sources.quote: או יהיה פירושו: ויהי היום שאירע בו כך וכך, כמו: ויהי היום ויעבור אלישע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra offers Rosh Hashanah, or Job's own day of judgment, or simply the day these things happened, as in a story about Elisha.

1:6.headline: Standing before God: to argue a case, or to serve
1:6.body: להתיצב means to take a stand. Rashi says it is how one stands in court, so the angels came to argue, while Maimonides says it shows they stand ready under God's command.

sources.quote: לָרִיב עִמּוֹ, שֶׁאֵין לְהִתְיַצֵּב אֶלָּא עַל־דִּין
sources.says: Rashi says they came to contend, since this kind of standing is only used for judgment.

sources.quote: היא שהם נמצאים ככפופים לציוויו במה שהוא רוצה
sources.says: Maimonides says the phrase means they are subject to God's command, and notes the Satan is not said to take this stand the first time.

1:6.headline: Who the Satan is, and why he has that name
1:6.body: Metzudat Zion calls him an accusing angel, and Ralbag says the name means one who turns things off the path God intends. Ibn Ezra reports Saadia Gaon's view that he was a jealous man, and rejects it.

sources.quote: השטן. מלאך מקטרג
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the Satan is an accusing angel.

sources.quote: וקראו שטן להיותו מטה מן הדרך המכוון
sources.says: Ralbag says it is called Satan because it turns aside from the path God intended.

sources.quote: הגאון רב סעדיה אמר: כי השטן בן אדם היה מקנא באיוב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that Saadia Gaon thought the Satan was a man who envied Job, then argues that the Satan is an angel.

1:10.headline: Job's herds spread out, or broke nature's rules
1:10.body: פרץ means to burst out. Ibn Ezra reads it as the herds growing many, while Rashi brings the Sages' reading that Job's flocks broke the world's fence, with goats killing wolves.

sources.quote: פרץ - רבה, כמו: ופרצת ימה וקדמה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'increased', as in God's promise to Jacob that he would spread out west and east.

sources.quote: פָּרַץ גְּדֵרוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, שֶׁהָעִזִּים הוֹרְגִים הַזְּאֵבִים
sources.says: Rashi gives the plain sense 'grew strong', then the Sages' reading that the flocks broke the order of the world, so that goats killed wolves.

sources.quote: כאלו לא יכילם מקום נגדר כי מלאו פני תבל
sources.says: Metzudat David says the herds were so many that no fenced place could hold them.

1:14.headline: Grazing right beside the plow, a taste of paradise
1:14.body: על ידיהם means beside them, as Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David explain. Rashi brings the Sages' reading that the donkeys grazed at once on grain sprouting from the furrow just plowed, a taste of the world to come.

sources.quote: ידיהם - מקומם, כמו: ויד תהיה לך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word means their place.

sources.quote: על ידיהם. אצלם בסמוך להם
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means next to them.

sources.quote: שֶׁהִטְעִימָם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא
sources.says: Rashi says it is not a word for place, and brings the Sages' teaching that God gave them a taste of the world to come, as the donkeys grazed straight from the new furrow.

1:15.headline: The Targum names the raiders: Lilith, queen of Zemargad
1:15.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra read שבא as the kingdom or army of Sheba camping against Job's herds. The Aramaic Targum instead says Lilith, queen of Zemargad, fell on them suddenly.

sources.quote: נִתְנַפְּלָה וְחָנְתָה מַלְכוּת שְׁבָא עֲלֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the kingdom of Sheba fell on them and camped against them.

sources.quote: ותפל שבא - מחנה שבא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means the army camp of Sheba.

sources.quote: וּנְפָלַת בִתְכֵּיף לִילִית מַלְכָּת זְמַרְגַד
sources.says: The Targum translates 'Lilith, queen of Zemargad, fell suddenly'.

1:16.headline: "Fire of God" may just mean a huge fire
1:16.body: Metzudat Zion says the Bible adds God's name to something to show it is very great, as with "cedars of God", so this is a mighty fire. The Targum reads it as fire sent from before God.

sources.quote: דרך המקרא שרוצה להגדיל דבר מה סומכו למלת השם וכן ארזי אל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says Scripture attaches God's name to a thing to show its greatness, as in 'cedars of God' in Psalms.

sources.quote: אֶשְׁתָּא מִן קֳדָם יְיָ נְפָלַת מִן שְׁמַיָא
sources.says: The Targum translates 'a fire from before the Lord fell from the sky'.

1:19.headline: The same word meant servants a moment ago
1:19.body: In verses 15 to 17 הנערים meant Job's servants, but here it means his children. Rashi says it names the sons and the daughters go without saying, while Ramban says the word itself takes in the daughters.

sources.quote: וְאֶת־הַנְּעָרִים. מְשָׁרְתֶיךָ, הַשּׁוֹמְרִים אוֹתָם
sources.says: Rashi says that in verse 15 the word means your servants who guarded the herds.

sources.quote: עַל הַנְּעָרִים. בָּנִים, אֲבָל אֵין צָרִיךְ לְהַזְכִּיר הַבָּנוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says here it means the sons, and there was no need to mention the daughters.

sources.quote: במלה הזאת יכלול גם הבנות, כי בבית היו כלם
sources.says: Ramban says this word includes the daughters too, since they were all in the house.

1:20.headline: Did Job cut his hair or tear it out?
1:20.body: ויגז usually means he sheared, and the Targum says he cut his hair. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say he tore it out, and Rashi points to Psalms 71, where the same root means drawing out.

sources.quote: וַיָּגָז. תָּלַשׁ, כְּמוֹ ״גָּזִּי נִזְרֵךְ״
sources.says: Rashi says it means he pulled out his hair, citing Jeremiah and the verse in Psalms 'you drew me from my mother's womb'.

sources.quote: ויגז. ותלש כמו קרחי וגזי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means he tore out his hair, as in Micah.

sources.quote: וְסַפַּר יַת רֵישֵׁיהּ
sources.says: The Targum translates 'and he cut the hair of his head'.

1:21.headline: His mother's womb, or the earth he came from
1:21.body: Job says he left his mother's womb naked and will go back "there", yet no one returns to the womb. Rashi and Ibn Ezra offer that the mother is the earth, and Ramban reads "there" as the earth's belly, the grave.

sources.quote: הָאֲדָמָה אֲשֶׁר לוּקַחְתִּי מִשָּׁם
sources.says: Rashi says 'my mother' may be the earth from which man was taken, or his actual mother.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: כי מבטן אמי - היא הארץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a view that the womb here is the earth.

sources.quote: רמז על בטן האדמה כי הוא המקום המעותד לאדם להיות נכנס בתוכו והוא לו כבטן אמו
sources.says: Ramban says 'there' hints at the belly of the earth, where every person goes, which is like a mother's womb to him.

1:22.headline: Not prayer, but something tasteless
1:22.body: Written without vowels, תפלה looks like the word for prayer. Here it comes from תפל, food without salt: Job said nothing senseless against God.

sources.quote: תפלה - כמו תפל. והעניין לא יצא מפיו דבור, שאין לו טעם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like תפל, tasteless: no senseless word left Job's mouth.

sources.quote: דבר שאינו בטעם, כמו היאכל תפל מבלי מלח
sources.says: Ramban says it means something without sense, as in Job's later line about eating bland food without salt.

sources.quote: לֹא שׁוּם שֶׁמֶץ וְתִפְלוּת נָתַן עַל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says Job did not attach any hint of foolishness to God.

10:1.headline: Sick of living, or cut off while still alive
10:1.body: This word appears only here in the Tanach. Rashi reads it as Job's soul quarrelling with being alive, while Metzudat Zion and the Targum read it as "cut off".

sources.quote: נַפְשִׁי מִתְקוֹטֶטֶת עַל שֶׁאֲנִי חַי
sources.says: Rashi says Job's soul quarrels with the fact that he is alive, and ties the word to a verse in Ezekiel about loathing yourself.

sources.quote: נקטה. נכרתה כמו אשר יקוט כסלו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means "cut off", like a similar word in Bildad's speech in chapter 8.

sources.quote: אִתְגְזַרַת נַפְשִׁי בְּחַיָי
sources.says: The Targum translates it with an Aramaic word for being cut off.

10:1.headline: Let the complaint pour out, or load it on himself
10:1.body: עזב usually means "let go", so Job lets his complaint pour out. Metzudat Zion reads it as taking up a load, as in the law of helping with a donkey's burden, and Ibn Ezra mentions that view but keeps the plain sense.

sources.quote: אעזבה. ענין טעינת משא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means carrying a load, as in the verse about a donkey's burden.

sources.quote: ולזה אטען על עצמי משא ספור תלאותי
sources.says: Metzudat David says Job loads on himself the burden of telling his troubles.

sources.quote: יש אומר: שהוא מן עזוב תעזוב עמו. והקרוב אלי: שהוא כמשמעו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra notes that some tie it to the donkey verse, but he prefers the plain meaning, "leave".

10:2.headline: Do not condemn me, or do not make me sin
10:2.body: The verb can mean to declare someone guilty or to make him guilty. The Targum reads "do not condemn me", while Malbim reads "do not make me wicked": if God already knows what Job will do, Job says, his sins are forced on him.

sources.quote: לָא תְחַיְבִנַנִי
sources.says: The Targum translates it "do not find me guilty".

sources.quote: תרשיעני תעשה שאהיה רשע
sources.says: Malbim explains the word as "make me be wicked".

sources.quote: אל תרשיעני היינו אל תעשה אותי שארשיע, כי רשעי מחוייבת ע"י ידיעתך הקדומה
sources.says: Malbim says Job argues that God's knowing the future in advance forces him to sin.

10:8.headline: Your hands shaped me, or your hands gave me pain
10:8.body: This form appears only twice in the Tanach. Rashi and Ralbag read it as shaping, like casting a form, while Metzudat Zion reads it as sorrow, and Ramban reports a view that it names the body's nerves.

sources.quote: עִצְּבוּנִי. עֲשָׂאוּנִי, עֶצֶב דְּפוּס
sources.says: Rashi says it means "made me", from a word for a mold.

sources.quote: עצבוני. ציירוני כטעם עצביהם כסף וזהב
sources.says: Ralbag says it means "shaped me", like idols, which are shaped figures.

sources.quote: עצבוני. מלשון עצבון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from עצבון, sorrow.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים כי החוטים הבאים מן המוח וחוט השדרה נקראו עצבים בלשון הקודש
sources.says: Ramban reports a view that the cords running from the brain and spine are called עצבים in Hebrew.

10:8.headline: Hands that made me, or hands that crushed me
10:8.body: ויעשוני looks like "they made me", and Ramban reads it that way. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it as "they pressed me down", the sense the verb has in Zephaniah 3:19.

sources.quote: ידיך עשוני ותקנו אותי אברים סביב להיות גופי תקיף וחזק
sources.says: Ramban reads it as God's hands making Job and fitting his limbs so his body would be strong.

sources.quote: ויעשוני. ענין כתישה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means crushing, as in Zephaniah.

sources.quote: גם ויעשוני - כמו הנני עושה את כל מעניך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads it as in Zephaniah, where God deals harshly with Israel's oppressors.

10:12.headline: God's guards, God's command, or God's care
10:12.body: פקודה can mean a guard, an order, or a visit of care. Rashi reads guards, Ibn Ezra a command, Ramban God's constant care, and the Talmud the moment of conception, when the soul is given.

sources.quote: פְּקֻדַּת מִשְׁמַרְתְּךָ, שֶׁמִּנִּיתָ לִי שׁוֹמְרִים
sources.says: Rashi says it means the guard God posted, the watchmen he appointed over Job.

sources.quote: ופקודתך - היא הפועלת והוא כמו צוויך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means God's command.

sources.quote: שאתה צריך לפקוד הבריות ולספק צרכם
sources.says: Ramban says God must keep attending to his creatures and supplying their needs, as when God remembered Sarah.

sources.quote: אֶלָּא מִשְּׁעַת פְּקִידָה. אָמַר רַבִּי: דָּבָר זֶה לִמְּדַנִי אַנְטוֹנִינוּס, וּמִקְרָא מְסַיְּיעוֹ
sources.says: The Talmud says the soul enters at conception, and Rabbi Yehudah haNasi finds support in this verse.

10:15.headline: Not "see my misery" but "I keep seeing my misery"
10:15.body: וראה looks like a plea to God: "see my misery". Rashi and Ralbag say it is not a command at all: Job is full of shame and keeps seeing his own misery.

sources.quote: אֵין זֶה צִוּוּי, אֶלָּא שֵׁם דָּבָר
sources.says: Rashi says it is not a command but a noun-like form: Job sees his misery all the time.

sources.quote: וראה. מקור והרצון בזה הנני שבע קלון ורואה עניי תמיד
sources.says: Ralbag says it is a verbal noun: I am full of shame and always see my misery.

10:16.headline: God shows wonders on Job, or judges him too finely
10:16.body: תתפלא comes from פלא, a wonder. Ibn Ezra reads it as God showing his wonders on Job, Rashi as judging him with exactness, and Malbim as God acting surprised at what Job does.

sources.quote: תתפלא בי - תראה פלאיך בי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means God shows his wonders on Job.

sources.quote: לְדַקְדֵּק וּלְהַפְלִיא בַּמִּשְׁפָּט
sources.says: Rashi says it means to be exacting and strict in judgment, like the word used for making a special vow.

sources.quote: ההתפעל מורה על הפעולה המדומה, תעשה א"ע כמתפלא
sources.says: Malbim says the verb form shows a pretended action: God acts as if he were amazed.

10:17.headline: Job's sores serve as God's witnesses against him
10:17.body: עדיך means "your witnesses", and Ibn Ezra and Ramban say the witnesses are Job's sores, which seem to prove he sinned. Ralbag notes that in Aramaic a scab is called עדיתא, while Metzudat David says the witnesses are Job's friends.

sources.quote: עדיך - הם הנגעים שיעידו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the witnesses are the sores, which testify.

sources.quote: הנגעים המעידים שאני רשע תחדש לבקרים
sources.says: Ramban says God renews each morning the sores that testify Job is wicked.

sources.quote: נגעיך ולו דמיון מה בלשון ארמי כי הספחת נקראת עדיתא
sources.says: Ralbag says it means "your sores", and notes that in Aramaic a scab is called עדיתא.

sources.quote: ועל רעיו יאמר אשר ירשיעו אותו
sources.says: Metzudat David says the witnesses are Job's friends, who condemn him.

10:20.headline: "Fleeting" or "stop": two readings of Job's plea
10:20.body: Some read חדל as "fleeting", as if it were חלד, a word for a lifetime, with letters swapped. Ramban reads it plainly as "stop": my days are few, so leave me alone.

sources.quote: פותרין אותו מלשון אדעה מה חדל אני, והפכוהו מן יושבי חלד
sources.says: Ramban reports that some read it as "how fleeting I am", taking it as a swapped form of חלד.

sources.quote: ולדעתי הוא מל' ויחדלו לבנות העיר
sources.says: Ramban himself reads it as "stop", as in "they stopped building the city".

10:22.headline: A land of darkness, or of flickering, flying light
10:22.body: Rashi reads עפתה as darkness, while Ralbag reads it as light. Ramban says the Targum saw sparks that seem to fly after dawn, and a midrash says the wicked there fly like birds, with no ground to stand on.

sources.quote: עֵיפָתָה. שֵׁם דָּבָר, חֲשֵׁיכָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is a noun meaning darkness, as in Amos 4:13.

sources.quote: עיפתה. אורה
sources.says: Ralbag says it means light.

sources.quote: והם אמרו נתרי האור הזורחים אחרי עמוד השחר ועושים תימורים, והם כאילו עפים לעיני האדם
sources.says: Ramban explains the Targum as sparks of light after dawn that seem to fly before the eye.

sources.quote: שהרשעים בה כעוף, מפני שאין בה אויר, ואין בה ארצות
sources.says: The midrash reads the word as flying: in that land the wicked hang like birds, with no ground.

10:22.headline: No order in that land, or no Torah study there
10:22.body: Rashi reads סדרים as the ordered life of people, and Ibn Ezra as the ordered rows of stars. The Talmud reads it as the order of Torah study and prayer: where that exists, light breaks out of the darkness.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֵין שָׁם סִדְרֵי אָדָם
sources.says: Rashi says there is no human order there, no settled life.

sources.quote: סדרים - הם מערכות הכוכבים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word means the arrangements of the stars.

sources.quote: הָא יֵשׁ סְדָרִים — תּוֹפִיעַ מֵאוֹפֶל
sources.says: The Talmud says the world survives on the prayer said with Torah study, and reads the verse: where there are sedarim, light shines out of the gloom.

12:2.headline: "You are the people": the crowd, or the only ones who count
12:2.body: Job tells his friends אתם עם, "you are the people". Metzudat David hears "you are many against me alone", while Ramban hears mock praise: you are the choicest people, and everyone else is cattle in your eyes.

sources.quote: האמת כי אתם הרבים ולמולי תחשבו לעם כי נשארתי לבדי
sources.says: Metzudat David says the friends are many and count as a whole people against Job, who is alone.

sources.quote: כלומר מבחר האנשים הראויים להקרא עם הדור, כי שאר האנשים בהמה המה להם
sources.says: Ramban says Job calls them the pick of mankind, the only ones worth calling a people, as if everyone else were beasts.

sources.quote: בְּקוּשְׁטָא אֲרוּם אַתּוּן חַבְרַיָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it "truly, you are the company".

12:2.headline: Wisdom will die with you, or dies in your hands
12:2.body: On the surface Job says wisdom will die when his friends die, since they own all of it. Malbim says the line is built to be read two ways: wisdom, a living thing, dies the moment it is in their hands.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁתָּמוּתוּ, תָּמוּת עִמָּכֶם כָּל חָכְמָה
sources.says: Rashi says that when they die, all wisdom will die with them.

sources.quote: וכיון ג"כ להליץ עליהם במאמר בעל שתי פנים, כאלו החכמה אשר היא חיה ורבת פעלים תמות בהיותה עמהם
sources.says: Malbim says Job mocks them with a two-faced line: wisdom, which is alive and active, dies when it is with them.

sources.quote: עמכם בעבור כסילותכם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says wisdom dies with them because of their foolishness.

12:4.headline: A joke to his friend, or a joke to any thinking mind
12:4.body: לרעהו usually means "to his friend", and Ramban reads it that way: Job has become a joke to his friends. Metzudat Zion and Malbim read it from רעיון, a thought, as in Psalms 139:2: the idea is laughable to anyone who thinks it through.

sources.quote: שחוק איש לרעהו מכם אהיה עתה
sources.says: Ramban says Job has become a laughingstock, one friend to another.

sources.quote: לרעהו. מלשון רעיון ומחשבה כמו בנת לרעי מרחוק
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from רעיון, thought, as in Psalms 139:2.

sources.quote: לרעהו. לרעיוניו, כמו בנת לרעי מרחוק
sources.says: Malbim says it means "to his thoughts".

12:5.headline: A torch of contempt, or contempt for the one struck by disaster
12:5.body: Ramban reads לפיד as a torch: shame flares up suddenly for the one who felt safe. Ibn Ezra splits it into ל and פיד, disaster, and the Talmud reads it as Noah's warnings, hard as torches, which the generation of the flood despised.

sources.quote: לפיד בוז, הנכון בעיני שהוא מלשון הקולות ואת הלפידים, ופירושו כי בזיון בוער יבא פתאום
sources.says: Ramban says it means a torch, as in "the thunder and the torches": burning shame comes suddenly.

sources.quote: לפיד בוז - הלמ"ד נופל והוא מן: אם בפידו להם שוע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the ל is a prefix and the root is פיד, disaster.

sources.quote: וְאָמַר לָהֶם דְּבָרִים שֶׁהֵם קָשִׁים כְּלַפִּידִים, וְהָיוּ בּוֹזִים אוֹתוֹ
sources.says: Rava says Noah told the generation of the flood words as harsh as torches, and they despised him.

12:6.headline: A god carried in the hand, or God who hands them peace
12:6.body: Ibn Ezra and Ralbag read the line as idol-worshippers, who carry their god in their hand or make it with their hands. Rashi reads אלוה as God, who brings peace into the hands of those who anger him.

sources.quote: לאשר הביא אלוה בידו - עובדי כו"ם שיעשה אלוהו בידו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means idol-worshippers who make their god with their own hand.

sources.quote: ר"ל לעובדי כו"ם שיביאו הכו"ם בידיה' וישתחוו להם
sources.says: Ralbag says it means idol-worshippers who carry their idols in their hands and bow to them.

sources.quote: לְכָל אֲשֶׁר הֵבִיא לוֹ הַצּוּר הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּיָדוֹ
sources.says: Rashi reads it as God, the Rock, bringing peace into their hand.

12:12.headline: The very old are called ישיש: those who have lasted
12:12.body: Metzudat Zion says a very old man is called ישיש from יש, "there is", because his existence has lasted many days. The Talmud adds that scholars grow wiser as they age.

sources.quote: הזקן הרבה יקרא ישיש והוא מלשון יש כי עמדה בו הישות ימים דבים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says a very old man is called ישיש, from יש, because his being has lasted many days.

sources.quote: תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּזְקִינִין, חָכְמָה נִתּוֹסֶפֶת בָּהֶם
sources.says: The Talmud says that Torah scholars gain wisdom the older they get, citing this verse.

12:16.headline: Who leads people astray: the Satan, or God himself?
12:16.body: Job says the one who errs and the one who misleads both belong to God. Rashi says the misleader is the Satan, while Malbim says God himself turns a person off the path.

sources.quote: וּמַשְׁגֶּה. שָׂטָן הַמַּשְׁגֵּהוּ
sources.says: Rashi says the misleader is the Satan, who leads a person astray.

sources.quote: ומשגה, ר"ל וה' הוא משגה אותו מני דרך
sources.says: Malbim says it is God who leads him off the road.

sources.quote: או שישגה אחרים והם לא ידעו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it may mean a person who misleads others without their knowing.

12:17.headline: Counselors led off in folly, or carried off as plunder
12:17.body: שולל is rare. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as foolishness, so God leads the wise into folly, while Ralbag hears שלל, plunder: God carries off each counselor like spoils.

sources.quote: שׁוֹלָל. שֵׁם דָּבָר הוּא שְׁטוּת
sources.says: Rashi says it is a noun meaning foolishness.

sources.quote: שולל. ענין שטות כמו אשתוללו אבירי לב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means foolishness, as in Psalms 76:6.

sources.quote: ר"ל שהוא מוליך שלל כל אחד מהיועצים כאשר ירצה
sources.says: Ralbag says God leads each counselor away as plunder, as he wishes.

12:19.headline: Priests, or simply high officials
12:19.body: כהנים usually means priests. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it here as officials, as when David's sons are called כהנים, while Malbim keeps priests: religious leaders who rein in the crowd.

sources.quote: כֹּהֲנִים. שָׂרִים, כְּמוֹ ״כֹּהֵן מִדְיָן״
sources.says: Rashi says it means officials, as in "the priest of Midian".

sources.quote: כהנים. שרים כמו ובני דוד כהנים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means officials, as in "David's sons were כהנים".

sources.quote: ע"י כהני הדת אשר ישימו רסן בפני ההמון
sources.says: Malbim reads it as priests of religion, who hold back the crowd.

12:20.headline: God silences the faithful, or the fine speakers
12:20.body: Rashi reads נאמנים as the faithful, like Abraham, who trusted God yet later stumbled in speech. Metzudat Zion reads it from נאם, to speak, so it means skilled speakers.

sources.quote: אַף לְנֶאֱמָנִים, כִּי פְּעָמִים שְׂפָתָיו נִבְלָלִים לְדַבֵּר סָרָה, כְּגוֹן אַבְרָהָם
sources.says: Rashi says even the faithful sometimes speak wrongly, like Abraham.

sources.quote: הוא מלשון וינאמו נאום (ירמיה כג) שהוא ענין דבור
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from נאם, speech, so it means eloquent speakers.

sources.quote: הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר בְּיִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב, שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם בִּקְשׁוּ לְגַלּוֹת מִסְטוֹרִין שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: The midrash says the verse is about Isaac and Jacob, whose speech God took when they tried to reveal his secrets.

12:21.headline: The belt of the strong, or the banks that hold a river
12:21.body: מזיח appears only here. Rashi reads it as a belt that God loosens on the strong, while Malbim reads it as the banks that belt a river in and keep the water from bursting out.

sources.quote: וַחֲגוֹר הַחֲזָקִים מְרַפֶּה, וּמְפַתֵּחַ חֲגוֹרָם לְהָתִישׁ כֹּחָם
sources.says: Rashi says God loosens the belt of the strong to sap their strength.

sources.quote: ואחרים פירשו, חוזק התקיפים מרפה ומחליש, מלשון אין מזח עוד
sources.says: Ramban reports others who read it as the strength of the mighty, which God weakens.

sources.quote: והומלץ על גדותי הנהרות ואפיקי מים החוגרים בעד המים בל יפרצו גבולם
sources.says: Malbim says the word is used for river banks, which belt the water so it does not break out.

12:23.headline: God makes nations great, or leads them astray
12:23.body: Some read משגיא from שגה, to mislead, as when God lured Egypt to the sea by leaving their idol Baal Zephon standing. Rashi rejects this because of the dot on the letter, and reads it as "makes great": their success is what ruins them.

sources.ref: Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Vayehi Beshalach 2:5
sources.quote: בִּשְׁבִיל לְפַתּוֹת לִבָּן שֶׁלַּמִּצְרִיִּים, עָלָיו הוּא אוֹמֵר
sources.says: The Mekhilta says Baal Zephon was left standing to lure the Egyptians, and applies this verse to it.

sources.quote: וְזֶה הַלָּשׁוֹן אֵינוֹ עִקָּר; דְּאִם כֵּן הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר בְּצַד יָמִין ׳מַשְׁגִּיא׳
sources.says: Rashi says the "mislead" reading is wrong, since then the letter would be ש with the dot on the right.

sources.quote: אֲבָל זֶה עִקָּר ׳מַגְדִּיל׳, לְשׁוֹן ״שַׂגִּיא כֹחַ״
sources.says: Rashi says the true meaning is "makes great".

13:4.headline: Doctors of nothing, or doctors for an incurable wound?
13:4.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion hear אל, "not", in אלל: the friends heal with nothing, and idols are called אלילים for the same reason. The Talmud, which Rashi cites, reads אלל as a part of the neck that no doctor can heal.

sources.quote: כָּל אֱלִיל שֶׁבַּמִּקְרָא לְשׁוֹן אַל
sources.says: Rashi says every אליל in Scripture means "not", and brings the rabbis' reading: a neck sinew that cannot be healed, called אלל.

sources.quote: אלל. אל ולא ולכן יקראו עבודת כוכבים אלילים בעבור זה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אלל means "not", and that is why idols are called אלילים.

sources.quote: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר מַרְטְקָא – הַיְינוּ דְּלָאו בַּר רְפוּאָה הוּא
sources.says: The Talmud says that if אלל is the part called מרטקא, the verse fits, since that cannot be healed.

13:11.headline: שאתו: God's majesty, or the flame of His fire?
13:11.body: Rashi and Ralbag read שאתו from נשא, to lift: God's height and majesty will frighten you. Rashi also brings a reading that Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra share: the flare of His fire.

sources.quote: גָּבְהוֹ וְאֵימָתוֹ תְּבַעֵת אֶתְכֶם. וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים: שְׂאֵתוֹ שְׂרֵפַת אֵשׁוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says שאתו is God's height and awe, and some say it is the burning of His fire.

sources.quote: שאתו. התנשאותו ורוממותו
sources.says: Ralbag says שאתו means His being lifted up and exalted.

sources.quote: שאתו. להב אשו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שאתו is the flame of His fire.

sources.quote: הלא שאתו - אשו כמו: והמשאת החלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שאתו is His fire, or else it means His exaltation.

13:15.headline: Written "I will not hope", read "I will hope for Him"
13:15.body: The word is written לא, "not", but read לו, "for Him". The Mishnah uses the verse to say Job served God out of love, and the Talmud asks which spelling decides it.

sources.quote: לֹא עָבַד אִיּוֹב אֶת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶלָּא מֵאַהֲבָה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״הֵן יִקְטְלֵנִי לוֹ אֲיַחֵל״. וַעֲדַיִין הַדָּבָר שָׁקוּל: לוֹ אֲנִי מְצַפֶּה, אוֹ אֵינִי מְצַפֶּה
sources.says: The Mishnah says Job served God only out of love, from this verse, but admits it is unclear whether it means "I hope for Him" or "I do not hope".

sources.quote: אִי בְּלָמֶד אָלֶף כְּתִיב — ״לֹא״ הוּא, אִי בְּלָמֶד וָיו כְּתִיב — ״לוֹ״ הוּא
sources.says: The Talmud asks: if it is written with א it means "not", and if with ו it means "for Him".

sources.quote: אֵינִי נִפְרָד מִמֶּנּוּ, וְתָמִיד לוֹ אֲיַיחֵל
sources.says: Rashi reads it as "for Him": even if God kills him, Job will not leave Him and will always hope to Him.

13:17.headline: Spelled like "my sister", but it means "what I declare"
13:17.body: This word appears only here. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion take it from חוה, to tell, as in Job 32:10 and Psalms 19:3, with an א in place of a ה.

sources.quote: ואחותי - האל"ף מקום ה"א והוא מן: אחוה דעי אף אני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the א stands in place of a ה, and the word comes from אחוה דעי, "I will tell my opinion".

sources.quote: ואחותי. אמרי כמו יחוה דעת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ואחותי means my words, as in יחוה דעת in Psalms 19:3.

sources.quote: ואחותי. והגדתי
sources.says: Ralbag says ואחותי means my telling.

13:26.headline: מררות: acts of rebellion, or bitter decrees?
13:26.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it from מרי, rebellion: God writes down every time Job defied Him. Ralbag hears מר, bitter: God writes harsh decrees against him.

sources.quote: סַרְבָנִיּוֹת אֲשֶׁר מָרִיתִי פִּיךָ אַתָּה כּוֹתֵב
sources.says: Rashi says God writes down the times Job defied His word, and not his good deeds.

sources.quote: מרורות - מן מרי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מרורות comes from מרי, rebellion.

sources.quote: את' גוזר עלי גזירות קשות ומרות
sources.says: Ralbag says it means God decrees harsh and bitter decrees against him.

13:27.headline: בסד: wooden stocks, or plaster that shows every step?
13:27.body: Rashi links סד to the Aramaic סדנא: a heavy block of wood that locks a prisoner's feet. Ibn Ezra links it to סיד, plaster, which would show every step Job takes.

sources.quote: עֵץ גָּדוֹל שֶׁנּוֹתְנִין בּוֹ רַגְלֵי הָאֲסוּרִים
sources.says: Rashi says סד is a big piece of wood that holds prisoners' feet, from the Aramaic סדנא.

sources.quote: בסד - כמו: ושדת אותם בסיד שיראו בו כל ארחותי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares סיד, plaster, so that all Job's paths would show in it, and brings Rav Hai, who says it is a fetter.

13:27.headline: God traces Job's footsteps, or carves the stocks to his feet
13:27.body: Rashi reads תתחקה as tracing: God follows every step Job takes. Ralbag and Metzudat David read it as carving: the stocks are cut so tight around his feet that they hurt.

sources.quote: אַתָּה עַצְמְךָ מִתְחַקֶּה עַל פְּסִיעוֹתַי
sources.says: Rashi says God Himself traces Job's footsteps.

sources.quote: כי תחקוק נקבי עצי הסד מצומצמים לפי מדת שרשי רגלי
sources.says: Metzudat David says God carves the holes of the stocks tight to the size of Job's feet.

sources.quote: כאילו נחקק על שרשי רגליו
sources.says: Ralbag says the stocks are as if carved to the shape of his feet.

14:5.headline: A fixed limit on life, or God's laws that guard it
14:5.body: Job says God set a person's חק, a limit he cannot pass. A midrash reads חק as God's laws: whoever keeps them, harm will not pass over him.

sources.quote: ושמת לו חקים וגבולים לא יוכל לעוברם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God set limits and borders on a person's life that he cannot cross.

sources.quote: אִם עֲשִׂיתֶם אֶת חֻקַּי, אֵין הַשָּׂטָן נוֹגֵעַ בָּכֶם
sources.says: The midrash has God tell Israel that if they keep his laws, the Satan cannot touch them.

14:6.headline: Let him rest, or let him enjoy his short life
14:6.body: חדל usually means "stop", and Rashi reads it as resting from pain. Ibn Ezra also reads it like חלד, a lifetime, which has the same letters in another order: let him enjoy the little life he has.

sources.quote: וְיֶחְדַּל לוֹ מִמַּכְאוֹב
sources.says: Rashi says it means let him have a rest from pain.

sources.quote: ויחדל - ישמח בחלדו, כמו: כל יושבי חלד, או ויחדל מהתרעם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra offers two readings: let him enjoy his lifetime, like the word חלד, or let him stop complaining.

sources.quote: ויחדל. וישלים חדלו וזמנו
sources.says: Ralbag says it means let him finish his span of time.

14:6.headline: Until he wants his end, or until he finishes his term
14:6.body: ירצה usually means "he wants", and Rashi reads it that way: the old man wants his last day like a worker wants quitting time. Ibn Ezra and Ramban read it as "complete", like the land completing its rest years in Leviticus 26.

sources.quote: עַד יִרְצֶה בְּזִקְנוּתוֹ וְתַשּׁוּת כֹּחוֹ אֶת יוֹם מוֹתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says that in old age and weakness a person will want the day of his death.

sources.quote: עד ירצה - ישלים, כמו: והרצה את שבתותיה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means "complete", as the land makes up its missed sabbath years.

sources.quote: ירצה, מלשון והרצת את שבתותיה
sources.says: Ramban ties it to the same verse about the land's sabbath years.

14:9.headline: Not a harvest but a fresh branch
14:9.body: קציר usually means harvest. Here Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it as a new shoot growing from the cut stump, as in Psalms 80:12.

sources.quote: וְעָשָׂה קָצִיר. הִיא יוֹנֶקֶת, כְּמוֹ ״תְּשַׁלַּח קְצִירֶיהָ עַד יָם״
sources.says: Rashi says it means a young shoot, as in "it sent out its branches to the sea".

sources.quote: קציר. ענף כמו תשלח קציריה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a branch.

sources.quote: קציר - סעיף, כמו: תשלח קציריה עד ים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means a bough, citing the same verse in Psalms.

14:10.headline: A man does not just weaken, he is cut down
14:10.body: ויחלש looks like "grows weak". Ramban and Ralbag read it as "is cut down", as when Joshua cut down Amalek: unlike a tree, a dead man does not grow back.

sources.quote: והנראה יותר כי החלישות בלשון הקדש ענין שבר וכריתה, וכן ויחלוש יהושע
sources.says: Ramban says the word means breaking and cutting down, as when Joshua defeated Amalek.

sources.quote: ויחלש. ויכרת כמו ויחלוש יהושע את עמלק
sources.says: Ralbag says it means cut off, and that a man, unlike a tree, does not sprout again.

14:11.headline: The Targum hears the Red Sea and the Jordan
14:11.body: Job compares death to a sea that drains away and a river that dries up. The Targum names them: the Red Sea and the Jordan, which drew back for Israel and then flowed back.

sources.quote: אֲזַלוּ מוֹי מִן יַמָא דְסוּף וַהֲדַרוּ לְבֵית כְּנִשְׁתְּהוֹן
sources.says: The Targum says the waters left the Red Sea and returned to their gathering place.

sources.quote: וְיוּרְדְנָא אִתְנְגִיב וְיִתְיַבֵּשׁ קֳדָם אֲרוֹנָא
sources.says: It says the Jordan dried up before the Ark.

14:12.headline: Until there are no heavens, or until the heavens wear out
14:12.body: בלתי usually means "without" or "except". Metzudat Zion reads it from בלה, to wear out: the dead will not rise until the sky itself wears out, which means never.

sources.quote: בלתי. ענינו כמו בלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means "wear out".

sources.quote: עד יבלו ויופסדו השמים
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means until the heavens wear out and are ruined, that is, forever.

14:12.headline: Who will never wake? The Targum says: the wicked
14:12.body: Job seems to say the dead never wake from their sleep, and Metzudat David reads it that way. The Targum adds one word: it is the wicked who will not wake.

sources.quote: ר״ל עד עולם לא יקיצו המתים ולא יעורו מן השינה
sources.says: Metzudat David says the dead will never wake from their sleep.

sources.quote: לָא יִתְעַרוּן רַשִׁיעַיָא
sources.says: The Targum says the wicked will not wake.

14:14.headline: Job's "change": dying, or being remade like a butterfly
14:14.body: חליפה means a change. Ibn Ezra reads it as Job's death, his passing away, while Malbim reads it as being exchanged for a new form, like a worm that wraps itself up and comes out with wings.

sources.quote: חליפתי - מיתתי מן והאלילים כליל יחלוף או הליכתי כמו חלף הלך לו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means my death, or my going away.

sources.quote: כמו הפורחים שהיו תחלה רימה ותולעה ויתעטפו במעטפה ואח"כ יתחדשו להיות בעלי כנף
sources.says: Malbim compares it to flying creatures that start as worms, wrap themselves in a casing, and come out with wings.

sources.quote: עַד דְיֵתֵי חִלוּפֵי חַיָי
sources.says: The Targum renders it "until the change of my life comes".

14:16.headline: Not "guard" but "wait": God does not wait to punish
14:16.body: שמר usually means "guard" or "keep". Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as "wait", as when Jacob waited to see Joseph's dream come true: Job says God does not wait before punishing him.

sources.quote: אֵינְךָ מַמְתִּין עַל חַטָּאתִי מִלְּהִפָּרַע
sources.says: Rashi says it means you do not wait before punishing my sin, as in "his father kept the matter".

sources.quote: תשמור. תמתין כמו ואביו שמר את הדבר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means "wait", as in Genesis 37:11.

sources.quote: ובלשון חכמינו ז"ל אל יאמר אדם לחבירו שמר לי על פתח עבודה זרה פלונית
sources.says: Ramban adds that the sages use the word this way, for waiting for someone at a certain spot.

14:18.headline: A falling mountain, a giant mountain, or Lot
14:18.body: Some read נופל as "falling", others as "giant", from the נפילים of Genesis 6. A midrash reads the falling mountain as Lot and the rock that moves as Abraham.

sources.quote: הר נופל - יש אומרים: שהוא מן הנפילים. ויש אומרים: נופל ויבול
sources.says: Ibn Ezra gives both readings: from the נפילים, the giants, or simply "falling".

sources.quote: ואולם הר נופל יבול, פירשו בו גדול, מלשון והנפילים היו בארץ
sources.says: Ramban reports that some read it as "great", from the giants in Genesis 6.

sources.quote: וְאוּלָם הַר נוֹפֵל, זֶה לוֹט, שֶׁנָּפַל מֵהָר, וְצוּר, זֶה אַבְרָהָם
sources.says: The midrash reads the falling mountain as Lot, who fell, and the rock as Abraham, who moved away.

14:19.headline: Self-sown growth, or a sweeping flood
14:19.body: This form appears only here. Metzudat Zion reads it as plants that sprout on their own from fallen grain, while Ralbag suggests the letters are swapped from סחף, a sweeping rain.

sources.quote: ספיחיה. הם הגדילים מהגרעינין הנופלים מאליהם בעת הקציר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says these are plants that grow from grain that fell by itself at harvest.

sources.quote: או יהיה ספיחי' הפוך כמו מטר סוחף
sources.says: Ralbag suggests the word may have its letters reversed, from "sweeping rain".

sources.quote: כי האבנים הם ספיחים של הארץ
sources.says: Malbim says stones are the earth's own growth, which water turns back into soil.

14:22.headline: Does the dead man's flesh hurt, or just rot?
14:22.body: יכאב means "it hurts", and the Talmud and Rashi take it literally: worms hurt the dead like a needle in living flesh. Ibn Ezra reads it as rotting, like a field ruined with stones.

sources.quote: קָשָׁה רִימָּה לַמֵּת כְּמַחַט בַּבָּשָׂר הַחַי
sources.says: The Talmud says worms are as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh.

sources.quote: קָשָׁה רִמָּה לַמֵּת כְּמַחַט בַּבָּשָׂר הֶחָי
sources.says: Rashi quotes the same teaching from the Talmud.

sources.quote: ענינו ימס וירקב וישחת כמו: וכל החלקה הטובה תכאיבו באבנים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means the flesh melts and rots, as in 2 Kings 3:19.

15:8.headline: Did Job draw wisdom down, or keep it from everyone else?
15:8.body: גרע usually means "take away", but Rashi reads it the other way, as wisdom drawn down to Job from above. Ralbag reads it as keeping wisdom from everyone else, so that Job has all of it.

sources.quote: וְתִגְרַע. וְתַרְבֶּה מִלְמַעְלָה לְמַטָּה לָרֶדֶת עָלֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi reads ותגרע as drawing more wisdom down from above onto Job.

sources.quote: ותמנע לך החכמה עד שתהיה כולה לך ואין לזרים אתך
sources.says: Ralbag reads it as withholding wisdom from others until Job holds it all.

sources.quote: ורבים פירשו ותגרע כמו תרבה עליך חכמה
sources.says: Ramban notes that many explained ותגרע as "you increase wisdom for yourself".

15:11.headline: A gentle word from God, or a sin kept hidden
15:11.body: Rashi reads לאט as "gently": God spoke kindly to Job for many years. Ibn Ezra and the Metzudot read it as "in secret": Job keeps something hidden inside him.

sources.quote: וּדְבָרוֹ הַטּוֹב אֲשֶׁר לָאַט עִמָּךְ בְּלַאט וְנַחַת
sources.says: Rashi says God's good word dealt with Job gently and calmly.

sources.quote: לאט - דבר בלאט עמך, כמו בסתר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says לאט means in secret.

sources.quote: לאט. ענין ההסתר והטמון כמו לאט את פניו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says לאט means hiding, as when David covered his face.

15:12.headline: Two letters swapped: your eyes wink
15:12.body: ירזמון appears only here. Rashi says it is ירמזון, "they wink", with two letters swapped, just as שמלה and שלמה both mean a garment.

sources.quote: יִרְזְמוּן. כְּמוֹ יִרְמְזוּן, כְּמוֹ שִׂמְלָה שַׂלְמָה
sources.says: Rashi says ירזמון is ירמזון with letters swapped, like שמלה and שלמה.

sources.quote: ירזמון עיניך - אין לו חבר והפוך בלשון קדמונינו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner in the Bible and appears reversed in the sages' language.

sources.quote: ירזמון. הוא הפוך מן ירמזון והוא מל׳ רמיזה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is ירמזון reversed and means hinting.

15:15.headline: Even the heavens do not shine in His eyes
15:15.body: זכו usually means "pure" or "innocent". Rashi says that every use of זך means brightness: even the stars do not shine before God.

sources.quote: זַכּוּ. יִצְהָרוּ. כָּל לְשׁוֹן זַךְ הוּא צֹהַר
sources.says: Rashi says זכו means they shine, since every זך means brightness.

sources.quote: וְשָׁמַיִם. צְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says the heavens here are the host of heaven.

sources.quote: עם כי זכים ובהירים המה הנה בעיניו לא יזכו
sources.says: Metzudat David says the heavenly host is clear and bright, yet not bright in God's eyes.

15:18.headline: Wise men who confessed: Judah and Reuben
15:18.body: Rashi reads יגידו, "they tell", as "they confess", pointing to Judah over Tamar and Reuben over Bilhah. One version of the Targum also turns the verse toward repentance.

sources.quote: אֲשֶׁר חֲכָמִים יַגִּידוּ. וְיִתְוַדּוּ פִּשְׁעָם
sources.says: Rashi says the wise men tell by confessing their sins.

sources.quote: יְהוּדָה הוֹדָה וְלֹא בוֹשׁ בְּמַעֲשֵׂה תָמָר
sources.says: Rashi says Judah confessed and was not ashamed in the matter of Tamar.

sources.quote: דְשִׁבְטוֹי דְיַעֲקֹב חַכִּימַיָא יְתוּבוּן
sources.says: A second Targum version says the wise tribes of Jacob will repent.

15:24.headline: A one-time word: a ball, a battle, or a fire
15:24.body: Metzudat Zion reads this one-time word as a ball tossed from hand to hand, and Ralbag as a king ready for battle. Rashi says he found no parallel, then swaps ר for ד to get a king doomed to burn, Sennacherib.

sources.quote: כְּמֶלֶךְ עָתִיד לַכִּידוֹר. לֹא מָצָאתִי דִּמְיוֹנוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says he found no other word like it.

sources.quote: אַף כָּאן לַכִּידוֹר – כְּמוֹ לַכִּידוֹד, כְּאוֹתוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁהוּא עָתִיד לִיקוֹד בָּאֵשׁ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנֹּם; וְהוּא סַנְחֵרִיב
sources.says: Rashi reads it as כידוד, sparks, and says it means the king who will burn in Gehinnom, Sennacherib.

sources.quote: לכידור. עשוי הוא לשחוק בו לזרקו מיד ליד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is a ball for playing, thrown from hand to hand.

sources.quote: כמו המלך שעתיד לכידור ומזומן למלחמה
sources.says: Ralbag says it describes a king ready for battle.

15:27.headline: Fat folded so thick it looks like a mouth
15:27.body: פימה appears only here. Rashi and Ralbag read it from פה, "mouth": the man's fat folds over his loins and looks like lips.

sources.quote: עָשָׂה פֶה עַל חֲלָצַיִם, שֶׁחֶלְבּוֹ וְעֹבִי שׁוּמָנוֹ כָּפוּל עַל כְּסָלָיו, וְנִרְאִין כְּמִין פֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says the fat doubled over his loins looks like a mouth.

sources.quote: פימה עלי כסל. שעשה פיות על כסליו מרוב השומן
sources.says: Ralbag says he made mouths on his loins from so much fat.

15:29.headline: What was set aside for them, or their completion
15:29.body: Rashi and Ramban split this one-time word into two, מן להם, "what was set aside for them". Ibn Ezra and Ralbag read it as "their completion", like כנלתך in Isaiah 33:1.

sources.quote: מִנְלָם. מַתַּת תַּאֲוָתָם וְזִמּוּן מַחֲשַׁבְתָּם, וְהוּא כִּשְׁתֵּי תֵיבוֹת: מִן לָהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says מנלם is two words, מן להם, meaning what they wanted and planned.

sources.quote: מנלם, כמו שתי מלות מן להם, כמו וימן להם המלך
sources.says: Ramban also reads it as two words, as in "the king allotted them".

sources.quote: מנלם. שלמות' כעניין כנלות' לבגוד יבגדו בך
sources.says: Ralbag says מנלם means their completeness, as in Isaiah 33:1.

15:33.headline: Not violence: a vine shedding its unripe grapes
15:33.body: חמס usually means violence, but Ibn Ezra and the Metzudot read it here as "strip off" or "scatter", as in Lamentations 2:6. Malbim cites Rabbi Yonah that the word means this in Arabic.

sources.quote: יחמס - כמו ויחמוס כגן סכו נחמסו עקביך ועניינו יתפזר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares Lamentations 2:6 and says the word means to scatter.

sources.quote: יחמוס. יסור כמו נחמסו עקביך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means to remove.

sources.quote: פי' ר' יונה שהוא הסרת הדבר ממקומו בלשון ערבי
sources.says: Malbim cites Rabbi Yonah that in Arabic it means removing a thing from its place.

16:7.headline: Made desolate, or struck silent?
16:7.body: השמות usually means "you laid waste". Rashi reads it as silence: Job's company is stunned into quiet. Ramban reads it as astonishment.

sources.quote: הֲשִׁמּוֹתָ. לְשׁוֹן שְׁתִיקָה
sources.says: Rashi says השמות means silence.

sources.quote: השמות. מל׳ שממה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says השמות comes from desolation.

sources.quote: השמות כענין מתמה, כמו כאשר שממו עליך רבים
sources.says: Ramban says השמות means astonishment, as in Isaiah 52:14.

16:8.headline: Wrinkled me, or tied me up?
16:8.body: This rare verb has two readings. Ralbag hears קמטים, wrinkles: Job's wrinkles are witnesses to his wasting. Ramban hears the Aramaic for being bound, as the sages use it.

sources.quote: ותקמטני. מענין קמטים כי הם עדות כל הכחישות
sources.says: Ralbag says the word comes from wrinkles, which testify to thinness.

sources.quote: הנלכד ונקשר בחבלו נקרא בלשון ארמי קמוט
sources.says: Ramban says one caught and tied with a rope is called קמוט in Aramaic.

16:8.headline: My leanness, or my liar, rises to testify
16:8.body: כחש usually means a lie. Ramban and Metzudat Zion read it here as leanness: Job's thin body speaks against him. The Targum keeps the sense of lying: a false witness rises against him.

sources.quote: כחשי כמו רזוני, וכן ובשרי כחש משמן
sources.says: Ramban says כחשי means my thinness, as in Psalms 109:24.

sources.quote: וַאֲקִים לְאַסְהָדָא עֲלַי כַּדְבוּבִי
sources.says: The Targum translates: my liar rose to testify against me.

16:10.headline: They fill up against me, meaning they gather
16:10.body: יתמלאון looks like "they fill". Rashi says filling here means gathering, as in Jeremiah 12:6 and Isaiah 31:4. His friends crowd together against him.

sources.quote: וְאֵינוֹ מִשְׁתַּנֶּה מִלְּשׁוֹנוֹ, כִּי כָל ׳מִלּוּי׳ – ׳נֶאֱסָף׳ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says the word keeps its sense, because all filling is a gathering.

sources.quote: יתמלאון. יתקבצון כמו מלא רועים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means they gather, as in Isaiah 31:4.

16:11.headline: Two identical words: the first is God, the second is not
16:11.body: The verse says אל אל: "God hands me over to the wicked". The letters are the same, but the first is God's name and the second means "to". Scribal law treats the first as holy and the second as plain.

sources.quote: יסגירני אל אל עויל (איוב ט״ז:י״א) הראשון קודש והשני חול
sources.says: Tractate Soferim says that in this verse the first אל is holy and the second is not.

16:12.headline: A target is named for watching, from the Aramaic
16:12.body: מטרה means a target for arrows. Metzudat Zion says it comes from watching: the Aramaic for משמרת, a watch, is מטרת. Archers watch the mark to hit it.

sources.quote: כי משמרת תרגומו מטרת ויקרא כן ע״ש שהמורים שומרים להפיל בו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the target is so named because archers watch it, and משמרת is מטרת in Aramaic.

16:13.headline: The sages took Job's spilled gall literally
16:13.body: Job says his gall is poured on the ground. Ramban reports that the sages read this literally: his kidneys were split and his gall spilled, and it was a miracle he lived.

sources.quote: ורז"ל אמרו כי כן היה שנכרתו כליותיו ונשפכה המרה אשר בכיס הכבד, והוא אצלם מעשה נס כי יחיה
sources.says: Ramban says the sages held this really happened, and that his living was a miracle.

16:15.headline: גלד, found only here, is a scab or skin
16:15.body: Rashi says גלד is the dry crust over a wound, a word the Mishnah also uses. Ibn Ezra says it simply means skin, and that the word is Arabic.

sources.quote: גִּלְדִּי. מַכָּה יְבֵשָׁה וְהַעֲלָאַת גֶּלֶד
sources.says: Rashi says גלד is a dried wound with a crust over it.

sources.quote: עלי גלדי - עורי והוא מלשון קדר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says גלדי means my skin, and the word is Arabic.

16:15.headline: Not his horn but his shine
16:15.body: קרן usually means a horn. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as radiance, like the shining skin of Moses' face (Exodus 34:35). Job has buried his glow in the dust.

sources.quote: קַרְנִי. זִיוִי
sources.says: Rashi says קרני means my radiance.

sources.quote: קרני. ענין זוהר כמו קרן עור פני משה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means brightness, like the shining of Moses' face.

16:16.headline: His face from weeping: wrinkled, muddy, or red?
16:16.body: This rare doubled verb gets three readings. Rashi says wrinkled, as in the Mishnah. Ralbag says smeared with mud, חמר. Ibn Ezra says reddened, from the Arabic.

sources.quote: חֳמַרְמְרוּ. נִקְמְטוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it means wrinkled.

sources.quote: חמרמרו. נמלאו חמר ולכלוך
sources.says: Ralbag says it means filled with mud and dirt.

sources.quote: חמרמרו - בלשון קדר התאדמו ברוב החום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that in Arabic it means turned red from great heat.

16:17.headline: Is there such a thing as a dirty prayer?
16:17.body: Job says his prayer is pure. A sage asks: is any prayer impure? He answers that a man with stolen goods in his hands is not answered. Job had no theft, so his prayer was clean.

sources.quote: וְכִי יֵשׁ תְּפִלָּה עֲכוּרָה, אֶלָּא כָּל מִי שֶׁיָּדָיו מְלֻכְלָכוֹת בְּגָזֵל הוּא קוֹרֵא לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְאֵינוֹ עוֹנֶה אוֹתוֹ
sources.says: Rabbi Yehoshua HaKohen asks if there is a murky prayer, and says one whose hands are soiled by robbery calls to God and is not answered.

16:19.headline: Job names his witness twice, once in Aramaic
16:19.body: עדי is Hebrew for "my witness". The next word, שהדי, appears only here and is the Aramaic word for the same thing.

sources.quote: ושהדי. כמו וסהדי בסמ״ך והוא עד בלשון ארמי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שהדי is like סהדי with a ס, the Aramaic word for witness.

sources.quote: היינו עד היינו סהד
sources.says: Sekhel Tov says עד and סהד are the same thing.

17:1.headline: A word found only here, read as נדעכו with a ז
17:1.body: Ibn Ezra says נזעכו has no twin in Scripture, so only the context explains it. Rashi reads it as נדעכו from Job 6:17, with ז in place of ד: my days have been cut short.

sources.quote: נזעכו - מהענין יתפרש שאין לו חבר במקרא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says נזעכו has no other example in Scripture and is explained from the context.

sources.quote: נִזְעָכוּ. נִקְפְּצוּ, כְּמוֹ ״נִדְעָכוּ״
sources.says: Rashi says נזעכו means cut short, like נדעכו in Job 6:17.

sources.quote: נזעכו. נכרתו
sources.says: Ralbag says נזעכו means cut off.

17:5.headline: רעים: friends, or thoughts?
17:5.body: Rashi reads רעים as friends: each one flatters his friend. Ralbag reads it as thoughts, as in Psalms 139:2, "you understand my thought (רעי)".

sources.quote: יַגִּיד כָּל אֶחָד מֵהֶם אֶת רֵעוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says each of them speaks smoothly to his friend.

sources.quote: רעים. מחשבות ורעיונים כטעם בנת לרעי
sources.says: Ralbag says רעים means thoughts, as in בנת לרעי.

17:6.headline: תפת: a drum, the pit of Gehinnom, or a lord?
17:6.body: Rashi reads תפת as תף, a drum. Metzudat Zion reads it as Gehinnom, named so because whoever is seduced (מתפתה) by his desire falls there, and Ralbag reads it as a ruler, like the officials called תפתאי in Daniel.

sources.quote: וְתֹפֶת. כְּמוֹ ״תֹּף״
sources.says: Rashi says תפת is like תף, a drum.

sources.quote: ע״ש שכל המתפתה ביצרו נופל בה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says Gehinnom is called תפת because everyone seduced by his inclination falls into it.

sources.quote: ותפת. אדון כענין תפתאי האמור בדניאל
sources.says: Ralbag says תפת means a lord, like תפתאי in Daniel.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: כי התי"ו האחרון נוסף והוא כמו תוף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads it as the place of Tofet, and brings others who say the last ת is extra and it means a drum.

17:11.headline: Ibn Ezra hears an Arabic word for tying in זמתי
17:11.body: Metzudat Zion reads זמתי as my plans, as in Deuteronomy 19:19. Ibn Ezra adds that in Arabic the word means something that ties, so a plan is thought tied together.

sources.quote: זמותי. מחשבותי כמו כאשר זמם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says זמותי means my thoughts, as in כאשר זמם.

sources.quote: זמותי - מחשבותי ובלשון קדר, דבר שיקשור וזהו קשר המחשבה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says זמותי means my thoughts, and in Arabic it is something that ties, the tying of thought.

17:16.headline: בדי שאול: my limbs, or the branches of the grave?
17:16.body: Rashi reads בדי as body parts: the limbs that will go down to the grave. Ibn Ezra reads it as branches, as if the grave were a tree, and Ralbag reads it as the grave's deepest corners.

sources.quote: אוֹתָם אֵבָרִים שֶׁסּוֹפָן לֵירֵד שְׁאוֹל
sources.says: Rashi says בדי are the limbs that will end up going down to the grave.

sources.quote: בדי שאול - כמו סעיפי שאול על דרך משל, כאילו השאול עץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בדי שאול means the branches of the grave, as a figure, as if it were a tree.

sources.quote: והרצון בו לירכתי שאול
sources.says: Ralbag says it means the far depths of the grave.

18:2.headline: Ends to your words, or a great many words
18:2.body: Bildad asks how long Job will put קנצי on his words. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as "ends", from קץ. Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner anywhere and means "a great many".

sources.quote: (מענה בלדד):קִנְצֵי. סוֹף
sources.says: Rashi says קנצי means an end.

sources.quote: קנצי. הוא מלשון קץ וסוף
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from קץ, an end.

sources.quote: והנכון שאין לו דומה ועניינו רוב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no match elsewhere and means a large amount.

18:3.headline: Not "hidden" but "stopped up", like a blocked well
18:3.body: Bildad asks why Job treats the friends as נטמינו. Rashi says it does not mean "hidden", since that would need two nuns. It means stopped up, like the wells the Philistines blocked: closed to good sense.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ מְפָרְשִׁים לְשׁוֹן טְמִינָה, וְטָעוּת הוּא בְּיָדָם
sources.says: Rashi says those who read it as "hiding" are mistaken, and ties it to the Aramaic for the wells the Philistines stopped up.

sources.quote: נטמינו. מלשון אטימות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means being sealed shut.

sources.quote: נטמינו, מלשון טמונין פלישתאי
sources.says: Ramban ties it to the Aramaic for the Philistines stopping up the wells.

18:4.headline: Will a rock move for Job, or will God?
18:4.body: Bildad asks whether a צור, a rock, will move from its place for Job's sake. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read צור as God, the Maker. Ramban reads it as real rocks, the roots of the mountains: the world will not change its order for Job.

sources.quote: וְיֶעְתַּק צוּר. הַיּוֹצֵר
sources.says: Rashi says the צור here is the Maker.

sources.quote: צור. היוצר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion also says צור means the Maker.

sources.quote: ויעתקו הצורים, שהם מוסדות הרים
sources.says: Ramban reads it as the rocks that are the foundations of the mountains.

18:5.headline: The light of the wicked goes dark, or jumps away
18:5.body: Ralbag reads ידעך as "grows dark". Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as "leaps from its place": the good fortune of the wicked jumps away from them.

sources.quote: ידעך. יחשך
sources.says: Ralbag says ידעך means grows dark.

sources.quote: אוֹר רְשָׁעִים יִדְעָךְ. יִקְפֹּץ מִמְּקוֹמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the light of the wicked jumps from its place.

sources.quote: ידעך. יקפץ וינתר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means leaps and springs away.

18:9.headline: Thirsty men, a robber, or stones: readers disagree
18:9.body: Metzudat Zion and Ramban read צמים as צמאים, "thirsty ones", who thirst for the wicked man's blood. Ralbag reads it as a violent robber. Ibn Ezra reports others who read it from the Arabic for stones.

sources.quote: צמים. כמו צמאים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says צמים is like צמאים, thirsty ones.

sources.quote: יחזיק על עצמו הצמאים לשתות דמו
sources.says: Ramban says the man brings on himself those who thirst to drink his blood.

sources.quote: צמים. פריץ
sources.says: Ralbag says צמים means a violent robber.

sources.quote: ואחרים אומרים: בלשון קדר אבנים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that others read it from the Arabic word for stones.

18:11.headline: Terrors, spelled with two letters swapped
18:11.body: Metzudat Zion says בלהות is the word בהלות, "terrors", with two letters switched. Rashi says these terrors are demons.

sources.quote: בלהות. הוא הפוך מן בהלות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בלהות is בהלות turned around.

sources.quote: בַּלָּהוֹת. שֵׁדִים
sources.says: Rashi says the בלהות are demons.

18:12.headline: Trouble waits at his side, or for his wife
18:12.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read לצלעו, "for his side", as his wife, since the first woman was built from a rib. Ibn Ezra reads it plainly as a side, like the side of the Tabernacle.

sources.quote: לְצַלְעוֹ. אִשְׁתּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says לצלעו means his wife.

sources.quote: לצלעו. לאשתו ע״ש שנאמר ויבן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means his wife, because God built the rib into a woman.

sources.quote: לצלעו - כמו: ולצלע המשכן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares it to the side of the Tabernacle.

18:13.headline: The "firstborn of death" is death's chief
18:13.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read בכור here as a chief, so the phrase means the prince of death. Rashi points to Psalms, where God says "I will make him firstborn". Ibn Ezra adds another reading: death comes early.

sources.quote: בְּכוֹר מָוֶת. שַׂר הַמָּוֶת
sources.says: Rashi says the firstborn of death is the prince of death.

sources.quote: בכור. ענין שר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בכור here means a chief.

sources.quote: חוזק או ראשית והעניין שיבכר המות בבאו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means strength or being first, so death comes early.

18:13.headline: Death eats his branches: his limbs or his children
18:13.body: A בד is a branch. Metzudat Zion says the word is borrowed here for the limbs of the body. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read "his branches" as his children.

sources.quote: והוא מושאל על האברים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word for branches is borrowed for the body's limbs.

sources.quote: וְיֹאכַל כָּל שְׁאָר בַּדָּיו – בָּנָיו וּבְנוֹתָיו
sources.says: Rashi says his branches are his sons and daughters.

sources.quote: יאכל בדיו - הם בניו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says his branches are his sons.

18:14.headline: Torn from his tent, or from his wife
18:14.body: Rashi reads "his tent" as his wife, who trusted in him. Metzudat Zion says the sages read "tent" this way elsewhere too. Ramban rejects this and reads it as a real home where the man no longer lives safely.

sources.quote: יִנָּתֵק מֵאָהֳלוֹ. מֵאִשְׁתּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says torn from his tent means torn from his wife.

sources.quote: מאהלו. זו אשתו וכעין זה ארז״ל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says his tent is his wife, as the sages also said elsewhere.

sources.quote: ינתק מאהלו מבטחו, שלא ישב באהלו לבטח
sources.says: Ramban says it means he will no longer live safely in his tent.

sources.quote: ותוליכהו לקבר, ואז תשכון היא באהל שאיננו לו, אלמנה וגלמודה. ואיננו נכון
sources.says: Ramban sets out Rashi's reading about the wife and says it is not right.

18:20.headline: Looks like "hair", but Rashi says it cannot be
18:20.body: The word looks like שֵׂעָר, hair. Rashi says the stress and vowels rule that out, and admits he has heard no explanation. Metzudat Zion and Ralbag read it as סער, a storm, spelled with a samekh.

sources.quote: לֹא יִתָּכֵן לִהְיוֹת מִגִּזְרַת שֵׂעָר, שֶׁאֵין טַעַם שֵׂעָר בְּשִׁי״ן אֶלָּא בְּעַיִן, וְאֵינוֹ נֶהְפָּךְ לְקָמַץ בְּאַתְנַחְתָּא וְסוֹף פָּסוּק. לֹא שָׁמַעְתִּי
sources.says: Rashi says the word cannot come from hair because of its stress and vowels, and that he has not heard an explanation.

sources.quote: שער. כמו סער בסמ״ך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is like סער, storm, with a samekh.

sources.quote: שער. סערה: ביאור
sources.says: Ralbag says the word means a storm.

19:3.headline: Ten times: an exact count, or just "many"?
19:3.body: Rashi and Saadia count the speeches so far and find exactly ten. Ibn Ezra says ten is a round number meaning "many", as in "ten women" in Leviticus 26:26.

sources.quote: עֶשֶׂר פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת יֵשׁ עַד כָּאן
sources.says: Rashi says there have been ten speeches up to this point.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני: שהוא כמו ואפו עשר נשים בעבור היות חשבון עשרה סך חשבון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra brings Saadia's count of ten speeches, but prefers to read ten as a round number, like "ten women".

19:12.headline: Did God's troops pave a road, or hedge it with thorns?
19:12.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read ויסלו from מסלה, a paved road: the troubles marched to Job on a beaten path. Ibn Ezra reads it from סלון, a thorn, as in Ezekiel 28:24.

sources.quote: וַיָּסֹלּוּ. לְשׁוֹן ״מְסִלָּה״
sources.says: Rashi says ויסלו comes from מסלה, a road.

sources.quote: ויסלו. מל׳ מסילה ודרך כבושה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ויסלו comes from a paved, trodden road.

sources.quote: ויסולו - מן סלון ממאיר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ויסולו comes from סלון ממאיר, a pricking thorn.

19:13.headline: Rashi hears אכזר, "cruel", in אך זרו
19:13.body: The two words אך זרו, "only strangers", sound like one word, אכזר, "cruel". Rashi reads them that way, as in Job 30:21, so the people who knew Job have turned cruel.

sources.quote: אַךְ זָרוּ. לְשׁוֹן ״אַכְזָר״
sources.says: Rashi says אך זרו is the language of אכזר, cruel, as in Job 30:21.

19:17.headline: Job's children are dead, so who are "the children of my womb"?
19:17.body: Job's children died in chapter 1. Rashi says these are the people Job raised like sons, and Ralbag says Job pleads for children to come, or may have had new ones by now.

sources.quote: לְאוֹתָם שֶׁגִּדַּלְתִּי בְּבֵיתִי, כְּאִלּוּ הֵם בָּנַי
sources.says: Rashi says the children of my womb are those Job raised in his house as if they were his sons.

sources.quote: ואיפשר שהיו לו עתה בנים כי לא ידענו הזמן
sources.says: Ralbag says Job pleads with his wife to have children by her, or perhaps he had children again, since we do not know how much time passed.

19:18.headline: עוילים: little boys, or wicked men?
19:18.body: Metzudat Zion reads עוילים as young boys, from עול ימים, an infant, in Isaiah 65:20. Ralbag reads it from עול, injustice: wicked men despise me. Ibn Ezra gives both.

sources.quote: עוילים. נערים וכן ישלחו כצאן עויליהם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says עוילים means young boys, from עול ימים.

sources.quote: עויליה. אנשי עול וחמס
sources.says: Ralbag says עוילים are men of injustice and violence.

sources.quote: עוילים - נערים, או רשעים בעלי עול
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says עוילים are boys, or wicked people.

19:24.headline: The lead is not a pen; it fills the carved letters
19:24.body: A pen of lead could not cut stone, Rashi says, since lead is soft. So the letters are cut with iron, then lead is run into them to make them dark and lasting.

sources.quote: וְלֹא יִתָּכֵן לְפָרֵשׁ עֵט שֶׁל עוֹפֶרֶת, שֶׁהֲרֵי רַךְ הוּא אֵצֶל הָאֶבֶן
sources.says: Rashi says it cannot mean a pen of lead, since lead is soft next to stone.

sources.quote: מַעֲבִירִין אֶת הָעוֹפֶרֶת עֲלֵיהֶם, לָתֵת לָאוֹתִיּוֹת מַרְאֵה שַׁחֲרוּרִית
sources.says: Rashi says lead is passed over the carved letters to make them look black.

sources.quote: ויותך עופרת בחללי החקיקות למען יהיה הכתב ניכר ומתקיים
sources.says: Metzudat David says lead is melted into the carved hollows so the writing is clear and lasting.

19:25.headline: Job's redeemer: God, or a person who will speak for him?
19:25.body: Rashi and Metzudat David say the redeemer is God, who lives forever. Ibn Ezra reads it as a person who will speak up for Job, whether alive today or born in a later time.

sources.quote: גּוֹאֲלִי חַי – לִיפָּרַע, וְהוּא יִתְקַיֵּם וְיַעֲמֹד
sources.says: Rashi says Job's redeemer lives to repay, and will endure.

sources.quote: כי הן אני ידעתי שה׳ הגואל נפשי
sources.says: Metzudat David says the redeemer of Job's soul is God, who lives forever.

sources.quote: והתאויתי שאדע שגואלי שדיבר בשבילי, טוב הוא היום בחיים, או יהיה אחרון שיולד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Job wished to know whether his redeemer, who spoke for him, is alive today or will be born later.

19:26.headline: "From my flesh I see God": what does Job see?
19:26.body: Rashi says אלוה here means judgment: in his own flesh Job sees God's punishments. Metzudat David says Job knows God better than his own flesh, and the Midrash gives the words to Abraham: through his circumcision God appeared to him.

sources.quote: אֱלוֹהַּ. לְשׁוֹן מִשְׁפָּט וְיִסּוּרִין
sources.says: Rashi says אלוה here means judgment and suffering.

sources.quote: עם כי הייתי רואה אלוה ומשיג אותו בדבר האפשר יותר ממה שאני רואה ומשיג בשרי
sources.says: Metzudat David says Job perceived God, as far as possible, more than he perceived his own flesh.

sources.quote: אִילוּלֵי שֶׁעָשִׂיתִי כֵן מֵהֵיכָן הָיָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נִגְלָה עָלַי
sources.says: The Midrash has Abraham say that had he not circumcised himself, God would not have appeared to him.

19:29.headline: שדון packs "that there is judgment" into one word
19:29.body: The word is written שדין and read שדון. Rashi, the Midrash and Metzudat Zion split it into ש, "that", and דין, "judgment": know that there is judgment in the world.

sources.quote: שַׁדִּין כְּתִיב – כְּמוֹ שֶׁיֵּשׁ דִּין בָּעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says it is written שדין, meaning that there is judgment in the world, citing Tanchuma.

sources.quote: שַׁדִּין כְּתִיב, שֶׁיֵּשׁ דִּין בָּעוֹלָם
sources.says: The Midrash says it is written שדין, that there is judgment in the world.

sources.quote: שדון. אשר דון השי״ן היא במקום אשר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the ש stands for אשר, "that", and דון comes from דין, judgment.

2:1.headline: Which day? The Targum calls it the great day of judgment
2:1.body: The verse just says "the day". The Targum makes it the great day of judgment, a day of forgiving sins. Metzudat David says it was the day set for those who speak for and against people.

sources.quote: וַהֲוָה יוֹם דִינָא רַבָּא יוֹם שְׁבוֹק סָרְחָנַיָא
sources.says: The Targum translates: it was the great day of judgment, the day of forgiving sins.

sources.quote: היום המוכן לשיבואו בו מלמדי הזכות והחובה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it was the day set for those who argue for merit and for guilt to come.

2:1.headline: This time the Satan also comes "to stand before" God
2:1.body: In chapter 1 only the angels come להתיצב, "to stand before" God. Here the same word is added for the Satan too. Maimonides says the word means standing ready under God's command.

sources.quote: הרי בפעם הראשונה לא אמר בו "להתיצב", ואילו בשנייה אמר
sources.says: Maimonides points out that the first time the word is not said of the Satan, and the second time it is.

sources.quote: היא שהם נמצאים ככפופים לציוויו במה שהוא רוצה
sources.says: Maimonides says the phrase means they stand subject to God's command in whatever He wants.

2:3.headline: God says "you incited me", but God cannot be pushed
2:3.body: ותסיתני means "you incited me against him". Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David say this is the Torah speaking in human terms. Nobody can really sway God.

sources.quote: ותסיתני - דברה תורה כלשון בני אדם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the Torah speaks here in the language of people.

sources.quote: דבר בלשון בני אדם ור״ל קטרגת עליו להשחיתו בחנם
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is human language and means the Satan accused Job to destroy him for no reason.

sources.quote: כָּל לְשׁוֹן הֲסָתָה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן הַמְשָׁכָה
sources.says: Rashi says inciting always means drawing a person toward one's own plan.

2:4.headline: "Skin for skin" really means a limb for a limb
2:4.body: The Satan says עור בעד עור, "skin for skin". Rashi and the Targum read skin as a limb: a man throws up his arm to save his head. So he will give up all his wealth to save his life.

sources.quote: אֵבֶר בִּפְנֵי אֵבֶר. כֵּן דֶּרֶךְ בְּנֵי אָדָם
sources.says: Rashi says it means a limb in place of a limb, which is how people act.

sources.quote: אֵבְרָא אַמְטוֹל אֵבְרָא
sources.says: The Targum translates: a limb for the sake of a limb.

sources.quote: עור בעד עור - גוף בעד גוף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says skin here means body: a body for a body.

2:6.headline: Guard his נפש: his life, or his soul?
2:6.body: Rashi reads נפשו as Job's life: do not let it leave him. Maimonides reads it as the part of a person that lasts after death, which the Satan can never rule.

sources.quote: אַךְ אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ שְׁמֹר. שֶׁלֹּא תֵצֵא
sources.says: Rashi says guard his life, so that it does not leave him.

sources.quote: ושהוא חל על הדבר הנשאר מן האדם לאחר המוות, והוא מה שאין לשטן שלטון עליו
sources.says: Maimonides says נפש can mean what remains of a person after death, and the Satan has no power over it.

2:8.headline: A word found only here, explained from the Mishnah
2:8.body: להתגרד, "to scrape himself", appears nowhere else in the Bible. Rashi says it is spelled with ד and matches the Mishnah's word for scraping. With ר instead, the word would mean dragging.

sources.quote: בְּדָלֶ״ת כָּתוּב, וּלְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה הִיא
sources.says: Rashi says the word is written with ד and is the language of the Mishnah.

sources.quote: אֲבָל גּוֹרֵר בְּרֵי״שׁ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן סְחִיבָה
sources.says: Rashi says that with ר the word only means dragging.

sources.quote: להתגרד - להתחכך, ואין לו אח במקרא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means to rub oneself and has no partner in Scripture.

2:8.headline: Why sit in ashes: mourning, or to cool the sores?
2:8.body: Metzudat David says Job sat in the ashes to cool the heat of his boils. Ibn Ezra says it was a mourning custom, and asks for proof that the boils were hot.

sources.quote: בתוך האפר. לקרר חמימות השחין
sources.says: Metzudat David says he sat in the ashes to cool the heat of the boils.

sources.quote: בתוך האפר - כדרך אבילות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says sitting in ashes was the way of mourners.

sources.quote: צריך להביא ראיה שהיה השחין חם ולח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says whoever claims it was for cooling must prove the boils were hot and wet.

2:9.headline: The Targum gives Job's wife a name: Dinah
2:9.body: The verse only says "his wife". The Targum names her דינה, Dinah.

sources.quote: וַאֲמַרֵת לֵיהּ דִינָה אִתְּתֵיהּ
sources.says: The Targum translates: Dinah his wife said to him.

2:9.headline: "Bless God and die" is a polite way to say curse
2:9.body: ברך means "bless", but here it stands for its opposite. Metzudat Zion calls it a polite substitute used when speaking about God. Job's wife is telling him to curse God.

sources.quote: ברך. לשון כנוי כלפי מעלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ברך is a substitute word used about God.

sources.quote: לא חטא בשפתיו לברך את ה׳ כאשר הסיתתו אשתו
sources.says: Metzudat David says Job did not sin by cursing God as his wife urged.

sources.quote: ברך נבות אלהים ומלך, ברך אלהים ומות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites this phrase, with the false charge against Naboth, as places where ברך means reviling God.

2:10.headline: He did not sin "with his lips", but what about his heart?
2:10.body: The verse says Job did not sin בשפתיו, "with his lips". Rashi and the Targum read this as a hint that he sinned in his heart or thoughts. Ibn Ezra says it hints that he will sin with his lips later.

sources.quote: בִּשְׂפָתָיו. אֲבָל בְּלִבּוֹ חָטָא
sources.says: Rashi says Job did not sin with his lips, but he sinned in his heart.

sources.quote: בְּרַם בְּרַעְיָנֵיהּ הִרְהֵר בְּמִלִין
sources.says: The Targum adds that in his thoughts he mused on words.

sources.quote: להורות כי עוד יחטא בשפתיו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the phrase shows that he will yet sin with his lips.

20:2.headline: Thoughts are called שעפים, branches growing from the heart
20:2.body: Metzudat Zion says שעפי means my thoughts, as in Job 4:13. Ramban explains why: thoughts spread from the heart the way branches, סעיפים, spread from a tree.

sources.quote: שעפי. מחשבותי כמו בשעפים מחזיונות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שעפי means my thoughts.

sources.quote: שעיפים המחשבות שהם ללב כענפים לאילן, מלשון בסעיפיה פוריה
sources.says: Ramban says thoughts are called שעיפים because they are to the heart what branches are to a tree.

20:2.headline: חושי: my silence, my senses, or my haste?
20:2.body: Rashi reads it as silence, as in "a time to keep silent", while Metzudat Zion reads it as feeling and sense. Ibn Ezra reads it as haste: Zophar hurries to answer.

sources.quote: חוּשִׁי. שְׁתִיקוּתִי, כְּמוֹ ״עֵת לַחֲשׁוֹת״
sources.says: Rashi says חושי means my silence, as in Ecclesiastes 3:7.

sources.quote: חושי. מל׳ חוש והרגשה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from sense and feeling.

sources.quote: לכן שעפי חושי בי - מהירותי להשיבך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means my haste to answer you.

20:7.headline: Gone like his dung, or gone at a single turn?
20:7.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read גלל as dung: the wicked man vanishes like his own waste. Ramban reads it from rolling over: he barely turns before he is destroyed for good.

sources.quote: כְּגֶלְלוֹ. גָּלָל שֶׁל רְעִי
sources.says: Rashi says גלל here is dung.

sources.quote: כגללו. הצואה כמו גללי האדם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means excrement, as in Ezekiel 4:12.

sources.quote: כאשר יתגלגל ויסוב מעט יאבד לנצח
sources.says: Ramban says it means that as soon as he rolls and turns a little, he is lost forever.

20:11.headline: His bones full of youth, or of hidden things?
20:11.body: Rashi reads עלומו as the strength of youth, and Metzudat David as the sins of youth. Ralbag also reads it as עלום, hidden: his bones are full of what he secretly stole.

sources.quote: עַצְמוֹתָיו מָלְאוּ עֲלוּמָיו. כֹּחַ נַעֲרוּתָיו
sources.says: Rashi says עלומיו is the strength of his youth.

sources.quote: לפי שעצמותיו נמלאו מחטאות נעוריו
sources.says: Metzudat David says his bones are full of the sins of his youth.

sources.quote: לפי שהוא מלא עצמותיו מהדברים העלומים והמכוסים אשר גנב וגזל
sources.says: Ralbag offers that his bones are full of hidden, covered things that he stole and robbed.

20:16.headline: The snake's head, or its poison?
20:16.body: Metzudat David reads ראש as the snake's head, where its venom sits. Ralbag and Ibn Ezra read it as poison, as in the pair ראש ולענה, poison and wormwood.

sources.quote: יימר לנפשו כאלו יינק ומצץ ארס נחש שהוא בפיו שבראש
sources.says: Metzudat David says he sucks the venom from the snake's mouth, which is in its head.

sources.quote: ראש פתנים. מעניין ראש ולענ' ופתני' הם נחשי'
sources.says: Ralbag says ראש here is like ראש ולענה, poison, and פתנים are snakes.

sources.quote: כעניין: שרש פורה ראש ולענה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares Deuteronomy 29:17, a root bearing poison and wormwood.

20:20.headline: A belly never at rest, or children with no peace?
20:20.body: Rashi says the robber's belly is never quiet: it keeps telling him to rob and bring more. Ramban reads בטן as his children, who come from the belly: none of them will know peace.

sources.quote: בִּטְנוֹ אוֹמֵר לוֹ תָּמִיד: גְּזוֹל וְהָבֵא לְמַלְּאֵנִי
sources.says: Rashi says his belly always tells him to rob and bring food to fill it.

sources.quote: הבנים יקראו יוצאי בטן
sources.says: Ramban says children are called those who come out of the belly.

20:21.headline: Nothing left for the poor, or no scholars at his table?
20:21.body: Rashi first says the man left nothing of his food for the poor. The Talmud reads שריד as Torah scholars, as in Joel 3:5: whoever does not share his wealth with scholars sees no blessing.

sources.quote: לֹא שִׁיֵּר מִמַּאֲכָלוֹ לְחַלֵּק לַעֲנִיִּים
sources.says: Rashi says he left none of his food to give to the poor, and also cites the sages' reading.

sources.quote: אֵין ״שָׂרִיד״ אֶלָּא תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים
sources.says: The Talmud says שריד here means Torah scholars, citing Joel 3:5.

20:22.headline: When he has enough, or when his measure is full?
20:22.body: Rashi reads שפק as "enough", like the Aramaic for "when the camels had drunk enough". The Talmud reads it as a measure: God does not punish a person until his measure of sin is full.

sources.quote: סִפְקוֹ. לְשׁוֹן דַּי, כְּדִמְתַרְגְּמִינָן: ״כַּד סְפִיקוּ גַמְלַיָּא״
sources.says: Rashi says ספקו means enough, as the Aramaic translation uses the word.

sources.quote: אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נִפְרָע מִן הָאָדָם עַד שֶׁתִּתְמַלֵּא סְאָתוֹ
sources.says: The Talmud cites this verse to say God does not punish a person until his measure is full.

20:23.headline: בלחומו: in God's war, in the man's flesh, or his food?
20:23.body: Rashi reads it from מלחמה: God rains fire on him in His war, as on Sodom. Ralbag reads it as "in his flesh", and Ramban prefers "in his food", from לחם, bread.

sources.quote: בִּלְחוּמוֹ. בְּזַעַף מִלְחַמְתּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means in the fury of His war.

sources.quote: בלחומו. בבשרו
sources.says: Ralbag says it means in his flesh.

sources.quote: והנכון כי בלחומו, במאכלו
sources.says: Ramban says the right reading is in his food.

20:25.headline: Drawn from its sheath, or out of the wicked man's body?
20:25.body: Metzudat Zion says גוה means a body, used here for the sword's sheath, which holds the blade as a body holds a soul. Ralbag allows both: the sheath, or the wicked man's own body.
