sources.quote: מגוה. ענין גוף כמו גוית שאול (שמואל א ל״א:י״ב) והושאל על תיק החרב שהיא כמו הגוף להנפש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says גוה means body, borrowed for the sheath, which is to the sword as the body is to the soul.

sources.quote: מגוה. מהתיק אשר לה או ירצה בזה מגוף הרשע
sources.says: Ralbag says it means from its sheath, or from the body of the wicked man.

20:26.headline: Darkness here is the element of fire, says Maimonides
20:26.body: Metzudat David reads חשך as the darkness of troubles stored up for the wicked. Maimonides says חשך in Genesis 1 is the element of fire, which gives no light, and cites this verse as proof.

sources.quote: כל מיני חשכת הצרות טמונים ושמורים
sources.says: Metzudat David says all kinds of dark troubles are stored up for him.

sources.quote: הוא יסוד האש, אל תחשוב אחרת
sources.says: Maimonides says darkness is the element of fire, and brings this verse as one proof.

20:26.headline: Evil befalls the survivor, or he is shattered?
20:26.body: Rashi reads ירע as "evil will come" to whoever survives in his tent, and cites a midrash that this is Lot's wife. Metzudat Zion reads it from רעע, to shatter, as in Psalms 2:9.

sources.quote: אֲפִלּוּ לוֹט הַנִּמְלָט מֵהֶם בָּאָה רָעָה לְאָהֳלוֹ; זוֹ אִשְׁתּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says even Lot, who escaped Sodom, had evil come to his tent: his wife.

sources.quote: ירע. ישבר וירוצץ כמו תרועם בשבט ברזל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ירע means will be broken and crushed, as in Psalms 2:9.

21:10.headline: The same word the sages use for purging pots
21:10.body: Job says the bull of the wicked breeds and לא יגעל. Rashi says this root always means to throw something out: the seed is not cast back out. He compares the Mishnah's word for purging pots in boiling water.

sources.quote: כָּל לְשׁוֹן הַגְעָלָה – פְּלִיטָה הוּא; וְכֵן בִּלְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה: מַגְעִילָן בְּרוֹתְחִין
sources.says: Rashi says this root always means expelling, as in the Mishnah's purging of pots in boiling water.

sources.quote: יגעיל. ענין השלכה אל החוץ
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means throwing something outward.

sources.quote: יגעיל - מלשון רבותינו ז"ל: מגעילן ברותחין
sources.says: Ibn Ezra ties it to the sages' phrase for purging vessels in boiling water.

21:12.headline: A musical instrument, or just a word for merry-making
21:12.body: Metzudat Zion says עוגב is the name of a musical instrument. Rashi says it only means laughter and fun, from עגבות, lustful play. He adds, "so I have heard".

sources.quote: עוגב. שם כלי זמר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says עוגב is the name of a musical instrument.

sources.quote: עוּגָב אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן שְׂחוֹק, עַל שֵׁם הָעֲגָבוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says עוגב only means laughter, named for עגבות, and that this is what he heard.

21:13.headline: They go down to the grave in a moment, or in calm
21:13.body: Ralbag reads ברגע as "in a moment": the wicked die quickly, without long pain. Ramban reports readers who take it from מרגוע, rest: they go down calmly. He says the Aramaic translation gives both readings.

sources.quote: ובזמן קצר מאד ימותו
sources.says: Ralbag says they die in a very short time.

sources.quote: והמפרשים הוציאו ברגע מן וזאת המרגוע
sources.says: Ramban reports that commentators read ברגע from מרגוע, rest.

sources.quote: ובעל התרגום תרגם את שתיהן
sources.says: Ramban says the Aramaic translation renders both readings.

21:17.headline: God hands out pains, or a measured share
21:17.body: Metzudat Zion reads חבלים as pains, like a woman in labor. Rashi reads it as the share the wicked deserve. Ibn Ezra prefers the share: it is the opposite of "my portion has fallen in pleasant places" in Psalms.

sources.quote: חבלים. צירים ומכאובים כמו חבלי יולדה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חבלים are pains, like the pains of a woman giving birth.

sources.quote: חֲבָלִים. גּוֹרָל הָרָאוּי לָהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says חבלים is the lot the wicked deserve.

sources.quote: הפך: חבלים נפלו לי בנעימים. ויש אומרים: מן חבלי יולדה והראשון נכון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the opposite of the pleasant portion in Psalms, and prefers this over the reading of birth pains.

21:19.headline: God stores up his sin, his loot, or his pain
21:19.body: Job asks if God saves a wicked man's אונו for his sons. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read אונו as his wickedness. Metzudat Zion and Ralbag read it as what he took by force, and Ramban as his pain, as in the name Ben-Oni.

sources.quote: וְאוֹנוֹ – וְרִשְׁעוֹ יִצְפֹּן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְבָנָיו
sources.says: Rashi says אונו is his wickedness, which God stores up for his sons.

sources.quote: אונו - רשעו כמו מחשבות אונך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אונו is his wickedness.

sources.quote: אונו. ענין הגזל שעשק בכח ואון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the robbery he did by force.

sources.quote: אונו. גזלתו
sources.says: Ralbag says it is what he stole.

sources.quote: אונו, מלשון בן אוני
sources.says: Ramban reads it as pain, from the name Ben-Oni.

21:20.headline: A word Rashi could not match anywhere else
21:20.body: Rashi says כידו means his ruin, but he found no other example in Scripture, and neither did the master before him. He reads it as אידו, "his disaster", with a kaf in place of the alef. Metzudat Zion also offers כידון, a spear.

sources.quote: וְאֵינִי יָכוֹל לִמְצוֹא לוֹ דִּמְיוֹן בַּתּוֹרָה, כִּי אִם לְפִי עִנְיַן הַפָּסוּק נִרְאֶה שֶׁבֶר, וְכֵן הָרַב לֹא מָצָא לוֹ דִּמְיוֹן. (כִּידוֹ. לְשׁוֹן אֵידוֹ, אָלֶ״ף מִתְחַלֵּף בְּכָ״ף
sources.says: Rashi says he found no parallel and reads ruin from the context; he links it to אידו, with alef and kaf swapped.

sources.quote: כידו. ענינו כמו אידו, או הוא מל׳ כידון ורומח
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is like אידו, or comes from כידון, a spear.

sources.quote: כידו - כמו אידו מן העניין ואין לו חבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means like אידו and has no partner elsewhere.

21:23.headline: Two words for "at ease" blended into one
21:23.body: Metzudat Zion says שלאנן joins two words, שלוה, "calm", and שאנן, "at ease". Rashi reads it simply as שאנן, and Ibn Ezra says the lamed is an extra letter.

sources.quote: שלאנן. הוא מלה מורכבת מן שלוה ושאנן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is built from שלוה and שאנן.

sources.quote: שַׁלְאֲנַן. כְּמוֹ ״שַׁאֲנָן״
sources.says: Rashi says it is like שאנן.

sources.quote: שלאנן - הלמ"ד נוסף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the lamed is added.

21:24.headline: His body is stocked like a vat of olives
21:24.body: Rashi ties עטיניו to the Mishnah's word for the vat where olives are piled so their oil gathers, so it means the fat stored in his body. Metzudat Zion says it means breasts, a word borrowed from that vat. Ibn Ezra reads it from Arabic, the place where camels kneel by the water.

sources.quote: אַף כָּאן: חֶלְבּוֹ וְלַחְלוּחוֹ וְשׁוּמָנוֹ נִקְרָא עֲטִינָיו
sources.says: Rashi says that, like olives piled in a vat, his fat and moisture are called עטיניו.

sources.quote: עטיניו. הם השדיים והוא מושאל מדרז״ל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means breasts, borrowed from the sages' word for the olive vat.

sources.quote: עטיניו - בלשון ישמעאל, המקום שיברכו עליו הגמלים על המים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that in Arabic it is the place where camels kneel at the water.

21:32.headline: A stack of grain, or the mound over a grave
21:32.body: A גדיש is a stack of grain sheaves. Ralbag and Ibn Ezra say here it is the mound or dome raised over a grave. Rashi says the man is buried in the fields beside the stacks.

sources.quote: גדיש. הוא כרי מאלומות התבואה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says a גדיש is a pile of grain sheaves.

sources.quote: ונקרא הקבר גדיש להתקבץ עליו עפר ואבנים
sources.says: Ralbag says the grave is called a גדיש because earth and stones pile up on it.

sources.quote: אמר רב האיי ז"ל: שהיא הקובה שעל הקבר כמנהג ארץ ישמעאל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites Rav Hai Gaon: it is the dome over a grave, as built in Arab lands.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁהוּא נִקְבָּר בַּשָּׂדוֹת אֵצֶל הַגְּדִישִׁים
sources.says: Rashi says he is buried in the fields beside the grain stacks.

22:2.headline: Does a man benefit God, or teach him?
22:2.body: The verse uses יסכן twice. Rashi says the first means "benefit", as with Abishag who served King David, and the second means "learn", as with Balaam's donkey; the Targum reads "can a man teach God?"

sources.quote: יִסְכָּן הָרִאשׁוֹן – לְשׁוֹן הֲנָיָה, כְּמוֹ ״וַתְּהִי לוֹ סֹכֶנֶת״
sources.says: Rashi says the first יסכן means benefit, like Abishag who "served" David, and the second means learning.

sources.quote: אֶפְשַׁר דְלֶאֱלָהָא יְאַלֵף גְבַר
sources.says: The Targum translates "can a man teach God?"

sources.quote: והקרוב שהוא כמו יוכיח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra lists "benefit" and "lean on", and thinks it most likely means "rebuke".

22:6.headline: Stripping the naked: they were dressed in rags
22:6.body: You cannot strip clothes off someone already naked. Ramban and Malbim say ערומים here means people with too few or torn clothes, and Metzudat David says they are called naked for how they ended up.

sources.quote: ובגדי ערומים, אשר לא יספיקו בגדיהם להם
sources.says: Ramban says these are people whose clothes are not enough for them, as the Sages read Isaiah walking "naked".

sources.quote: ערומים, ר"ל שבגדיהם קרועים
sources.says: Malbim says it means their clothes were torn.

sources.quote: וקראם ערומים ע״ש סופם
sources.says: Metzudat David says they are called naked because of what they became once stripped.

22:15.headline: The ancient path, or the belief the world always existed
22:15.body: ארח עולם can mean "the old path", the road the wicked took long ago, as Rashi reads it. Ibn Ezra reads it as the view of those who say the world was never created but always was.

sources.quote: הַדֶּרֶךְ הָרִאשׁוֹנִים אֲשֶׁר מֵאָז
sources.says: Rashi says it is the path of the people of long ago.

sources.quote: אורח העולם הם האומרים: כן היה העולם ואיננו חדש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the view of those who say the world always was and is not new.

sources.quote: ארח עולם. דרך הטבע הקיימת מעולם
sources.says: Malbim says it means the way of nature that has always existed.

22:15.headline: מתי here means men, not the dead
22:15.body: מתי looks like מתים, "the dead", but here it means "men". The midrash Sekhel Tov lists this verse among others, and suggests men are called this because their bodies are whole, as in מתום.

sources.quote: ולמה נקראו הגברים מתים, שהן שלמים בגוף
sources.says: Sekhel Tov says מתי means men, and they are called this because their bodies are whole.

sources.quote: אשר דרכו בו אנשי און הם אנשי דור המבול
sources.says: Metzudat David reads the phrase as "men of wickedness", the people of the Flood.

22:16.headline: Cut down early, or wrinkled from Torah study
22:16.body: Rashi reads קמטו as "cut down before their time", and Metzudat Zion as "wrinkled", aged early. The Talmud turns it into praise: scholars who wrinkle themselves over Torah in this world, to whom God reveals secrets in the next.

sources.quote: קֻמְּטוּ וְלֹא עֵת. נִגְזְרוּ בְּלֹא עִתָּם
sources.says: Rashi says they were cut off before their time.

sources.quote: קומטו. נתכווצו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says they shriveled, that is, grew old early.

sources.quote: אֵלּוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁמְּקַמְּטִין עַצְמָן עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
sources.says: Rav Nachman bar Yitzhak says the word is written as a blessing, for scholars who wrinkle themselves over Torah.

22:25.headline: God as your treasure, or God in your troubles
22:25.body: בצריך can mean "your treasures", "your enemies" or "your troubles", and Rashi admits he is puzzled by it. Ibn Ezra reads "your silver", while the Talmud reads "your troubles": whoever brings God's name into his trouble has his living doubled.

sources.quote: אִם שַׁדַּי זֶה קֹדֶשׁ תָּמַהְתִּי עַל פִּתְרוֹנוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says he is puzzled, because read plainly it sounds like God counted among your enemies, so he reads it as wealth.

sources.quote: בצריך - כספך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means your silver, and mentions a view that it means "in your trouble".

sources.quote: כׇּל הַמְשַׁתֵּף שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם בְּצַעֲרוֹ — כּוֹפְלִין לוֹ פַּרְנָסָתוֹ
sources.says: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says whoever joins God's name to his troubles has his living doubled, citing this verse.

22:29.headline: Say "rise up", or say "it was pride"
22:29.body: גוה is a rare form of גאוה, "height" or "pride". Rashi reads a promise: when people are brought low, you will say "rise" and they will. Ibn Ezra reads a verdict: you will say pride brought the wicked down.

sources.quote: גוה. כמו גאה בחלוף אל״ף בוי״ו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is גאה with ו in place of א, meaning greatness.

sources.quote: תֹּאמַר בְּהַבְטָחָה לְהַגְבִּיהוֹ, וְיִגְבַּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says you will promise to lift the lowly, and they will be lifted.

sources.quote: והעניין: כי הגאוה השפילה אותם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the meaning is that pride brought them low.

22:30.headline: Not innocent, an island, or an ounce?
22:30.body: אי is a puzzle. Rashi reads it as "not", as in the name Ichabod, "no glory", so God saves even one who is not innocent; Ramban reads "island"; and a midrash hears אונקיא, "an ounce": Noah held only one ounce, yet was saved.

sources.quote: אֵין נָקִי, כְּמוֹ ״אִי כָבוֹד״
sources.says: Rashi says אי means "not", as in "no glory".

sources.quote: אי נקי. כמו אין נקי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion also reads "one who is not innocent".

sources.quote: אי נקי, ירצה לומר יושבי האי שהוא נקי
sources.says: Ramban reads it as the people of an island that is innocent.

sources.quote: אוּנְקִיָא אַחַת הָיְתָה בְּיַד נֹחַ
sources.says: Rabbi Chanina reads the verse about Noah: he held only one ounce, so why was he saved?

23:2.headline: Is Job's complaint rebellious, or bitter?
23:2.body: Metzudat Zion and Ralbag read מרי as rebellion: Job admits he has complained defiantly. The Targum hears מר, bitter: his words are bitter.

sources.quote: מרי. ענין מרד וסרוב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מרי means rebellion and refusal.

sources.quote: הרצון בו שהמריתי והפלגתי בכעסי להתרעם
sources.says: Ralbag says Job means he rebelled and went too far in his anger and complaint.

sources.quote: מְרִיר מֵימְרִי
sources.says: The Targum translates: my speech is bitter.

23:2.headline: "My hand" here means the blow that struck me
23:2.body: ידי usually means "my hand". The commentators read it as "my wound", because people strike with the hand. Job says his wound is heavier than his groaning shows.

sources.quote: ידי. מכתי ע״ש שהדרך להכות ביד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ידי means my wound, because one strikes with the hand.

sources.quote: והענין שמכתי יותר כבדה מאנחתי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the point is that his wound is heavier than his groaning.

sources.quote: מַכַּת נִגְעִי תַּקִּיפָה יוֹתֵר מֵאַנְחָתִי
sources.says: Rashi says the blow of his illness is stronger than his groaning.

23:6.headline: Rashi hears "force" in a little word that means "only"
23:6.body: אך usually means "only". Rashi reads it as a blow and pressure: God would not press His terror on Job. He also gives a second reading with the usual sense of "only".

sources.quote: לֹא אַךְ. מַכָּה וּכְפִיָּה. לֹא יָשִׂים בִּי אָכְפּוֹ וְאֵימָתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says אך means a blow and force: God would not lay His pressure and terror on Job.

sources.quote: כִּי לֹא יָשִׂים בִּי אַךְ הָרִיב שֶׁל תּוֹכַחַת פְּשָׁעַי
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: God would bring against me only the argument over my sins.

23:8.headline: "In front" and "behind" here mean east and west
23:8.body: קדם means "in front" and אחור means "behind". The commentators read them as east and west. A person faces the sunrise, so the west is behind, the north on the left, the south on the right.

sources.quote: כי יחשב פני האדם אל מול זריחת השמש וא״כ המערב היא מאחור והצפון משמאל והדרום מימין
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says a person is taken to face the sunrise, so west is behind, north is left and south is right.

sources.quote: הוֹאִיל וְהַמִּזְרָח – קִדְמַת עוֹלָם, נִמְצָא הַמַּעֲרָב – אֲחוֹרָיו שֶׁל עוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says the east is the front of the world, so the west is its back.

23:9.headline: Not "I grasp" but "I see"
23:9.body: אחז looks like "grasp". Rashi says it means "I see", from the Aramaic word for seeing. He proves it from the accent: if it meant grasp, the stress would fall on the ח.

sources.quote: אָחַז. תַּרְגּוּם שֶׁל ״אֶרְאֶה״
sources.says: Rashi says אחז is the Aramaic translation of "I will see".

sources.quote: וְאִם לְשׁוֹן אֲחִיזָה הוּא, הָיָה טַעֲמוֹ מִלְּרַע, תַּחַת הַחֵי״ת
sources.says: Rashi says that if it meant grasping, the stress would be on the last syllable, under the ח.

sources.quote: אחז. אראה כמו ואתה תחזה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אחז means I see, like תחזה in Exodus 18.

23:12.headline: חק here is Job's daily bread, not a law
23:12.body: חק usually means a law. Rashi reads it as Job's daily food, as in "my portion of bread" (Proverbs 30:8). Job kept God's words closer than his meals.

sources.quote: יוֹתֵר מֵחֻקֵּי מְזוֹנוֹתַי הָיִיתִי זָרִיז לִצְפֹּן אִמְרֵי פִיו
sources.says: Rashi says Job was more eager to store up God's words than his daily food.

sources.quote: דבר קבוע וצורך קרוי חוק
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says a fixed need is called חק.

23:13.headline: God's נפש here means His will
23:13.body: נפש often means soul or life. Metzudat Zion and Ralbag read it as will: what God wants, He does. Maimonides warns that this does not mean God acts on whim. He wills only what His wisdom requires.

sources.quote: ורצוני כמו אין נפשי אל העם הזה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says נפש here means will, as in Jeremiah 15:1.

sources.quote: ונפשו אותה. ורצונו נכספה
sources.says: Ralbag says it means His will longed for it.

sources.quote: אלא שהוא יתעלה אינו רוצה אלא דברים אפשריים, ולא כל דבר אפשרי אלא מה שחכמתו מחייבת שיהיה כך
sources.says: Maimonides says that God wills only possible things, and only what His wisdom requires.

23:14.headline: Job's חק: the sentence passed on him, or what he needs?
23:14.body: Rashi reads חקי as the sentence God decreed on Job, which God will carry out to the end. Ralbag reads it as what Job needs, as in "my portion of bread".

sources.quote: עַד אֲשֶׁר יַשְׁלִים חֹק גְּזֵרוֹתָיו – פֻּרְעָנִיּוֹת אֲשֶׁר גָּזַר עָלַי
sources.says: Rashi says God will finish the decree of punishments He set on Job.

sources.quote: המצטרך לאדם יקרא חק כאמרו הטריפני לחם חקי
sources.says: Ralbag says what a person needs is called חק, as in "my portion of bread".

24:6.headline: בלילו: his crop, or a field that is not his?
24:6.body: Rashi reads בלילו as "his crop". Ibn Ezra and the Targum hear בלי לו, "not his": the wicked reap a field that belongs to someone else.

sources.quote: בְּלִילוֹ. יְבוּלוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says בלילו means his crop.

sources.quote: בלילו - שאיננו לו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בלילו means a field that is not his.

sources.quote: בְּחַקְלָא מִדְלָא דִלְהוֹן חָצְדִין
sources.says: The Targum translates: they reap in a field that is not theirs.

24:9.headline: Torn from the breast, or robbed of what was left?
24:9.body: Rashi reads משד as "from the breast": the orphan is pulled from nursing. The Targum hears שוד, plunder: they take the little the orphan has left.

sources.quote: יְנִיקַת הַיָּתוֹם, מְקוֹם מוֹצָא מַאֲכָלוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means the orphan's nursing, where his food comes from.

sources.quote: והתרגום אמר: יאנסון מביזת יתום, עשה אותו משוד ושבר
sources.says: Ramban notes that the Targum takes the word from שוד, plunder.

24:13.headline: Rebels against the light: daylight, God, or the Torah?
24:13.body: Ralbag first reads the light as God, then prefers daylight: these people hate the day. Ibn Ezra says the light is God. The Targum says they rebel against the Torah.

sources.quote: במורדי אור - השם שהוא אור המאורות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the light is God, the light of all lights.

sources.quote: ואיפשר שיהיה הרצון הזה אור היום והוא יותר נכון
sources.says: Ralbag says it may mean daylight, and that this is more correct.

sources.quote: הִנוּן הֲוָן בְּמָרְדִין בְּאוֹרַיְתָא
sources.says: The Targum translates: they were among those who rebel against the Torah.

24:15.headline: The adulterer hides his face, but the Hidden One sees
24:15.body: Plainly, the adulterer hides his face. The midrash reads סתר as God, "who sits in secret". Vayikra Rabbah adds that God shapes the child's face like the real father's, so the sin comes out.

sources.quote: וּבַסֵּתֶר יָשִׂים פָּנָיו לַעֲבוֹר עֲבֵירָה
sources.says: Rashi says he turns his face to secrecy to commit the sin.

sources.quote: וסתר פנים ישים כלומר יושב בסתר. עליון פנים ישים
sources.says: Lekach Tov reads the words as the One who sits in secret, the Most High, setting His face against him.

sources.quote: שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב בְּסִתְרוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, זֶה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא צָר כָּל קִטּוֹרִין שֶׁלּוֹ בִּדְמוּתוֹ בִּשְׁבִיל לְפַרְסְמוֹ
sources.says: Vayikra Rabbah says God, who sits in the secret of the world, shapes the child's features like the adulterer's to expose him.

24:16.headline: By day they sealed themselves in, or sealed a mark?
24:16.body: Rashi first reads חתמו as "they shut themselves in" all day. Rava in the Talmud reads it as marking the houses: by day they left perfume with the rich, and at night they sniffed it out and dug in.

sources.quote: וּבַיּוֹם הָיוּ חֲתוּמִים וּמְסֻגָּרִים בְּבָתֵּיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says by day they were sealed and shut in their houses.

sources.quote: וּמַפְקִידִים אֶצְלוֹ אֲפַרְסְמוֹן, וּמַנִּיחִים אוֹתוֹ בְּבֵית גִּנְזֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rava says they deposited balsam with rich men, who put it in their storerooms, so the robbers could find it at night.

sources.quote: בַּיּוֹם הָיוּ עוֹשִׂים סִימָנִים
sources.says: Rashi, citing the sages, says by day they made marks.

24:18.headline: Vineyards, or the ways of the lofty ones?
24:18.body: כרמים means vineyards. Rashi also hears כ־רמים, "like the lofty": the wicked swore not to follow the ways of the righteous. In another reading he takes vineyards as the leaders of the generation.

sources.quote: לֹא יִפְנֶה דֶּרֶךְ הַטּוֹב בְּדַרְכֵי הַצַּדִּיקִים הָרָמִים וְשׁוֹכְנִים בְּרוּמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi reads the word as the lofty righteous who dwell on high.

sources.quote: כְּרָמִים הֵם הַצַּדִּיקִים וּפַרְנְסֵי הַדּוֹר
sources.says: In another reading Rashi says the vineyards are the righteous leaders of the generation.

24:19.headline: חטאו: they sinned, or they were changed?
24:19.body: חטאו usually means "they sinned". Ramban notes the Targum reads it as "they were changed", from the sense of missing the mark: their form changes as they go down to the grave.

sources.quote: פתר "חטאו" שנוי, כי נשתנית צורתם ברדתם שאולה
sources.says: Ramban says the Targum explains חטאו as change, since their form changes as they go down to Sheol.

sources.quote: מלשון אל השערה ולא יחטא
sources.says: Ramban links it to Judges 20:16, slinging at a hair without missing.

24:20.headline: Forgotten by the womb, by a friend, or by mercy?
24:20.body: Rashi reads רחם as the womb, his mother. Ralbag reads it as a loved one. The midrash reads it as mercy: they forgot mercy, so God forgot His mercy for them.

sources.quote: יִשְׁכָּחֵהוּ רֶחֶם. אִמּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says רחם means his mother.

sources.quote: רחם. אוהב תרגום אהב מרחם
sources.says: Ralbag says רחם means a loved one, since the Aramaic for love is מרחם.

sources.quote: הֵן שִׁכְּחוּ רַחֲמַי מִן הַבְּרִיּוֹת, אַף הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שִׁכַּח רַחֲמָיו מֵהֶם
sources.says: The midrash says they forgot mercy toward people, so God forgot His mercy toward them.

24:21.headline: Does he feed the barren woman, or crush her?
24:21.body: רעה usually means to tend or feed. Rashi reads it that way: he pampers a wife made barren on purpose. Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra read it as "breaks", as in Psalms 2:9.

sources.quote: הָעֲקָרָה שֶׁלֹּא תֵלֵד הָיָה רוֹעֶה וּמֵטִיב
sources.says: Rashi says he tended and treated well the wife who would not bear children.

sources.quote: רועה. משבר ומרצץ כמו תרועם בשבט ברזל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רועה means breaks and crushes, as in Psalms 2:9.

sources.quote: רועה עקרה - מן תרועם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says רועה comes from תרועם, to break.

25:2.headline: Rule and fear, or the angels Michael and Gabriel?
25:2.body: Plainly, המשל ופחד means rule and fear belong to God. Rashi reads them as two angels: rule is Michael and fear is Gabriel. Can Job answer even one of them?

sources.quote: הַמְשֵׁל זֶה מִיכָאֵל, וָפַחַד זֶה גַּבְרִיאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says rule is Michael and fear is Gabriel.

sources.quote: כְּלוּם אַתָּה יָכוֹל לְהָשִׁיב אֶת אֶחָד מֵהֶם
sources.says: Rashi has Bildad ask Job whether he could answer even one of them.

sources.quote: המשל. מענין ממשלה ושולטנות
sources.says: Ralbag says המשל simply means rule and power.

26:4.headline: Whose breath came out of you: whose words, or whose soul?
26:4.body: Metzudat Zion reads נשמת as breath, meaning the speech that comes out with it. Ralbag reads it as soul: teaching someone is like making their soul.

sources.quote: מלשון נשימה ונשיבת רוח
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ונשמת comes from breathing and means speech carried out on the breath.

sources.quote: כי מי שילמד חבירו דבר דומה כאלו עושה נפשו
sources.says: Ralbag reads it as "whose soul came from you", since one who teaches another is as if he made his soul.

26:5.headline: Who are the רפאים: the dead, giants, or seeds?
26:5.body: Metzudat Zion says the dead are called רפאים because they grew weak (רפה), and Rashi says it is Gehinnom, which weakens people. The Targum makes them giants, and Ralbag reads them as seeds that lie still like the dead.

sources.quote: כן יקראו המתים ע״ש שנרפו ונחלשו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the dead are called רפאים because they became weak.

sources.quote: גֵּיהִנֹּם הַמְּרַפֶּה אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says הרפאים is Gehinnom, which weakens people.

sources.quote: אֶפְשַׁר דְגִבָּרַיָא דְמִתְמַזְמְזִין
sources.says: The Targum renders הרפאים as giants.

sources.quote: הם גרעיני הזרע וקראם רפאים להיותם קודם הזריעה כמתים
sources.says: Ralbag says they are seeds, called רפאים because before planting they are like the dead.

26:5.headline: יחוללו: hollowed out, or brought into being?
26:5.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion connect יחוללו to חלל, a hollow; Rashi thinks of the seven chambers of Gehinnom. Ralbag reads it as "they are created".

sources.quote: שִׁבְעָה חֲלָלִים שֶׁלּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says יחוללו refers to the seven hollows of Gehinnom.

sources.quote: יחוללו. מל׳ חלל ונבוב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says יחוללו comes from חלל, hollow and empty.

sources.quote: יחוללו. יבראו
sources.says: Ralbag says יחוללו means they are created.

26:7.headline: The Talmud hears Moses' "what are we" in this word
26:7.body: Moses and Aaron said of themselves ונחנו מה, "what are we?". The Talmud finds that מה in בלי מה and says the world stands only because of them.

sources.quote: אֵין הָעוֹלָם מִתְקַיֵּים אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן, כְּתִיב הָכָא: ״וְנַחְנוּ מָה״
sources.says: The Talmud says the world exists only for Moses and Aaron, linking their ונחנו מה to תולה ארץ על בלימה.

26:9.headline: The Talmud reads the odd word פרשז as a hidden phrase
26:9.body: פרשז appears only here. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say it means פרש, "spread", with an extra ז, while the Talmud reads its letters as פירש שדי זיו: God spread the glow of His presence over Moses.

sources.quote: פרשז - אין לו חבר ועניינו: פרש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says פרשז has no other example and means spread.

sources.quote: פרשז. מל׳ פרישה והזי״ן נוספת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says פרשז comes from spreading and the ז is added.

sources.quote: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁפֵּירַשׂ שַׁדַּי מִזִּיו שְׁכִינָתוֹ וַעֲנָנוֹ עָלָיו
sources.says: The Talmud reads פרשז as "the Almighty spread some of the radiance of His presence and His cloud over him".

26:10.headline: To the edge of light, or until light ends?
26:10.body: Ibn Ezra reads תכלית as a place: the border where light ends and darkness begins. Metzudat David reads it as time: the sea keeps its border until light and darkness come to an end.

sources.quote: עד מקום שהוא תכלית האור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads it as the place where light ends, and notes others read it as until light and dark end.

sources.quote: עד אשר תכלה האור עם החושך ר״ל לעולם
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means until light and darkness end, that is, forever.

26:11.headline: Do the sky's pillars shake, or were they once soft?
26:11.body: Metzudat Zion reads ירופפו as trembling. Rashi and the Midrash read it as soft: at creation the heavens wobbled like milk until God's rebuke made them firm.

sources.quote: ירופפו. ירעדו כי עמודיה יתפלצון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ירופפו means they tremble.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁבְּרָאָם וְהִקְרִישָׁם הָיוּ רוֹפְפִים
sources.says: Rashi says that when God made the heavens they were soft until He rebuked them and they became firm.

sources.quote: עַד שֶׁלֹּא תֵּרֵד לְתוֹכוֹ טִפָּה אַחַת שֶׁל מְסוֹ הוּא מְרַפֵּף
sources.says: The Midrash compares the heavens to milk that wobbles until a drop of rennet sets it.

26:12.headline: God split the sea, folded it, or calmed it
26:12.body: Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read רגע as "split". Rashi reads it as wrinkled, the waters drawn into folds at creation, and Ralbag reads it as "made calm".

sources.quote: רגע – עניינו בקע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says רגע means split.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ ״עוֹרִי רָגַע״ (איוב ז:ה), נִקְמַט
sources.says: Rashi says רגע means wrinkled, as in Job 7:5.

sources.quote: נח הים ולא ירוץ על הארץ
sources.says: Ralbag explains that by God's power the sea rests and does not run over the land.

26:12.headline: Who is רהב: Egypt, or the prince of the sea?
26:12.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion say רהב is a name for Egypt, as in Isaiah 30:7. The Talmud tells of the prince of the sea, who refused God's order at creation and was struck down.

sources.quote: מִצְרַיִם קְרוּיִין רְהָבִים
sources.says: Rashi says Egypt is called רהב.

sources.quote: מצרים קרואים כן כמ״ש קראתי לזאת רהב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says Egypt is called רהב, as in Isaiah 30:7.

sources.quote: אָמַר לוֹ לְשַׂר שֶׁל יָם: פְּתַח פִּיךָ וּבְלַע כׇּל מֵימוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם
sources.says: The Talmud says God told the prince of the sea to swallow the world's waters, and when he refused God killed him, citing this verse.

26:13.headline: שפרה: the sky spread like a tent, or made beautiful
26:13.body: The word appears only here. Rashi links it to שפרירו, a royal tent, in Jeremiah 43:10. Metzudat Zion adds that a fine tent gets that name from שפר, beautiful, and Ralbag reads it as beauty.

sources.quote: בִּדְבָרָיו וּבְרוּחַ פִּיו אִיהֵל, כְּמוֹ ״וְנָטָה אֹהֶל שַׁפְרִירוֹ״
sources.says: Rashi says God pitched the heavens like a tent, as in Jeremiah 43:10.

sources.quote: ואוהל היפה נקרא כן מל׳ אמרי שפר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שפרה means a tent, and a beautiful tent is called that from שפר.

sources.quote: היו השמים בזה האופן מהיופי והשלימו
sources.says: Ralbag says the heavens were made in this beauty and perfection.

26:13.headline: God's hand made the serpent tremble, or formed it
26:13.body: Rashi first reads חללה as the shaking and pain (חיל) God brought on Pharaoh, the "fleeing serpent". His second reading, like Metzudat Zion's, is "formed", as in Proverbs 8:25.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן חִיל וְצָרָה
sources.says: Rashi first reads חוללה as trembling and distress.

sources.quote: יִסְּדָה יָדוֹ אֶת לִוְיָתָן, כְּמוֹ ״גְּבָעוֹת חוֹלָלְתִּי״
sources.says: Rashi's second reading is that God's hand founded Leviathan, as in Proverbs 8:25.

sources.quote: חוללה. בראה כמו ותחולל ארץ
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חוללה means created.

26:14.headline: שמץ: a faint whisper, or something shameful?
26:14.body: Metzudat Zion reads שמץ as a tiny bit: we hear only a whisper of God's ways. Rashi gives a second reading from לשמצה, "for shame", in Exodus 32:25, and Ibn Ezra reads it that way.

sources.quote: שמץ. ענין משהו ומעט
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שמץ means a tiny amount.

sources.quote: דָּבָר אַחֵר: שֵׁמֶץ כְּמוֹ ״לְשִׁמְצָה״ (שמות לב:כה), לִגְנוּת
sources.says: Rashi says שמץ means a hint, or else it is like לשמצה, for disgrace.

sources.quote: שמץ דבר - כמו לשמצה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שמץ is like לשמצה.

27:2.headline: Swearing "as God lives" shows Job still loves God
27:2.body: Rashi and the Jerusalem Talmud say no one swears by a king's life unless he loves the king, so this oath shows Job served God out of love. Maimonides notes the form חַי, not חֵי: God's life is not something separate from Him.

sources.quote: אֵין אָדָם נוֹדֵר בְּחַיֵּי הַמֶּלֶךְ אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן אוֹהֵב אֶת הַמֶּלֶךְ
sources.says: Rashi says this is an oath, and from it Rabbi Yehoshua learned Job served God out of love, since no one swears by the king's life unless he loves him.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֵין אָדָם נוֹדֵר בְּחַיָיו שֶׁלְּמֶלֶךְ אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן אוֹהֲבוֹ
sources.says: The Jerusalem Talmud says no one vows by the king's life unless he loves him.

sources.quote: ולכן אומרים חַי ה' ולא אומרים חֵי ה', כי אין חייו דבר שונה מעצמותו
sources.says: Maimonides says we say חַי ה' and not חֵי ה', because God's life is not something other than His essence.

27:7.headline: Here כ does not mean "like"; it means "truly"
27:7.body: Metzudat Zion says the כ in כרשע and כעול marks the real thing, as in Job 24:14. Metzudat David explains that Job hates wickedness so much that wishing it on his enemy is his curse.

sources.quote: כרשע. כעול הכפי״ן באו לאמתת הדבר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the כ in כרשע and כעול come to state the thing as true.

sources.quote: כי כ״כ הדבר רע בעיני עד שתחשב לקללה
sources.says: Metzudat David says wickedness is so bad in Job's eyes that wishing it on his enemy counts as a curse.

27:8.headline: Whose life does God take: the robber's or his victim's?
27:8.body: Rav Huna and Rav Hisda disagree about נפשו. One says the verse speaks of the victim's life, and the other says the robber's own.

sources.quote: חַד אָמַר: נַפְשׁוֹ דְּנִגְזָל, וְחַד אָמַר: נַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁל גַּזְלָן
sources.says: The Talmud brings two views: one says נפשו is the soul of the one robbed, the other says the robber's.

27:20.headline: בלהות: demons, or waves of terror?
27:20.body: Rashi reads בלהות as demons that overtake the wicked man. Metzudat Zion reads it as בהלות, terrors, with the letters swapped, and Ralbag sees them coming one after another like a flood.

sources.quote: בַּלָּהוֹת. שֵׁדִים
sources.says: Rashi says בלהות are demons.

sources.quote: בלהות. בהלות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בלהות means terrors.

sources.quote: תשיגהו בלהה אחרי בלהה בלי הפסק
sources.says: Ralbag says terror after terror overtakes him without stopping.

27:22.headline: Who runs away: the wicked man's partner, or his wealth?
27:22.body: Rashi says his partner in crime runs off when he falls, as the Talmud says Harbonah did to Haman. Ibn Ezra says it is the wicked man's wealth that runs from his hand.

sources.quote: בֶּן עֲצָתוֹ שֶׁהָיָה מְסַיְּעוֹ בַּתְּחִלָּה, יִבְרַח מֵעֲזוֹר יָדוֹ בִּשְׁעַת כִּשְׁלוֹנוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the advisor who helped him at first runs away when he stumbles, as Harbonah did to Haman.

sources.quote: אַף חַרְבוֹנָה רָשָׁע — בְּאוֹתָהּ עֵצָה הָיָה, כֵּיוָן שֶׁרָאָה שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַיְּימָה עֲצָתוֹ, מִיָּד בָּרַח
sources.says: The Talmud says Harbonah was part of Haman's plot and fled once he saw it fail, and cites this verse.

sources.quote: מידו ברוח יברח - העניין יברח הונו מידו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means his wealth flees from his hand.

28:4.headline: Sodom made the traveler's foot forgotten
28:4.body: The Talmud and Rashi read "forgotten by the foot" as Sodom, whose people said their land was rich enough without visitors. So they set out to make the "law of the foot", the welcome of travelers, forgotten in their land.

sources.quote: בּוֹאוּ וּנְשַׁכַּח תּוֹרַת רֶגֶל מֵאַרְצֵנוּ
sources.says: The Talmud has the people of Sodom say, "Come, let us make the law of the foot forgotten from our land."

sources.quote: אֵלּוּ אַנְשֵׁי סְדוֹם, שֶׁשִּׁכְּחוּ תּוֹרַת רַגְלֵי אוֹרְחִים מֵאַרְצָם
sources.says: Rashi says these are the people of Sodom, who made the law of guests' feet forgotten.

28:4.headline: Dried up, or lifted up
28:4.body: Ibn Ezra reads דלו as "thinned out and dried up". Ralbag and Metzudat Zion read "raised up", as in Hezekiah's "my eyes are lifted (דלו) to the heights".

sources.quote: דלו - כמו דללו וחרבו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says דלו means thinned out and dried up.

sources.quote: דלו. גבהו וכמוהו דלו עיני למרום
sources.says: Ralbag says דלו means they rose up, as in Isaiah 38:14.

sources.quote: דלו. הורמו והוגבהו כמו דלו עיני למרום
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says דלו means raised high.

28:7.headline: The bird called "seer" because it sees so far
28:7.body: The Talmud says the איה is the bird the Torah calls ראה, "seer", because it sees farther than any other. It can stand in Babylon and spot a carcass in the land of Israel, yet even it has not seen this path.

sources.quote: רָאָה זוֹ אַיָּה, וְלָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמָהּ רָאָה? שֶׁרוֹאָה בְּיוֹתֵר
sources.says: The Talmud says the ראה is the איה, named for how far it sees.

sources.quote: עוֹמֶדֶת בְּבָבֶל וְרוֹאָה נְבֵלָה בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: The Talmud says it stands in Babylon and sees a carcass in the land of Israel.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁהִיא רוֹאָה יוֹתֵר מִשְּׁאָר עוֹפוֹת, וּלְכָךְ נִקְרְאָה רָאָה
sources.says: Rashi says it sees more than other birds, and so it is called ראה.

28:8.headline: A name of the lion, or simply pride
28:8.body: The Talmud lists שחץ and שחל among the six names of the lion. Ralbag and Metzudat Zion read בני שחץ as "the proud ones", the fiercest wild beasts.

sources.quote: שִׁשָּׁה שֵׁמוֹת יֵשׁ לַאֲרִי, אֵלּוּ הֵן: אֲרִי, כְּפִיר, לָבִיא, לַיִשׁ, שַׁחַל, שַׁחַץ
sources.says: The Talmud says the lion has six names, including שחל and שחץ.

sources.quote: בני שחץ. בני גאוה ותוקף והם פריצי החיות
sources.says: Ralbag says בני שחץ are the proud and strong, the wild beasts.

sources.quote: שחץ. ענין גאוה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שחץ means pride.

28:11.headline: The depths of rivers, or weeping
28:11.body: Metzudat Zion reads מבכי as the depths, like נבכי ים, "the springs of the sea". Rashi hears בכי, "weeping": the lower waters wept at creation, and another version says Israel wept for water in the desert.

sources.quote: מבכי. ענין עומק המים וכן נבכי ים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מבכי means the depth of the waters.

sources.quote: בִּבְרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם, כְּשֶׁבָּכוּ מַיִם הַתַּחְתּוֹנִים
sources.says: Rashi says this was at the creation of the world, when the lower waters wept.

sources.quote: מִפְּנֵי בְּכִיָּתָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהָיוּ בוֹכִין ״לֵאמֹר מַה נִּשְׁתֶּה״
sources.says: Another version of Rashi reads it as Israel's weeping when they asked what they would drink.

28:11.headline: Hidden riverbeds, or a hidden window in the sky
28:11.body: Ibn Ezra reads it plainly: what lay hidden under the rivers comes to light when they dry. Rashi, following Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer, says תעלומה is a window in the sky through which the sun comes out each season.

sources.quote: מה שהיה בתעלומות הנהרות יראו, כאשר ייבשו המים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says what was hidden in the rivers will be seen when the water dries up.

sources.quote: חַלּוֹן יֵשׁ בָּרָקִיעַ וּשְׁמוֹ תַּעֲלוּמָה, מִשָּׁם תּוֹלְדוֹת הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ לִתְקוּפָתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says there is a window in the sky named תעלומה, from which the sun comes out for its seasons.

28:13.headline: Wisdom is not found in those who pamper their lives
28:13.body: "The land of the living" sounds like this world. Rashi and the Talmud read it as people who live at ease: Torah is found only in one who wears himself out over it.

sources.quote: לֹא תִּמָּצֵא תּוֹרָה בְּמִי שֶׁמְּחַיֶּה עַצְמוֹ עָלֶיהָ
sources.says: The Talmud says Torah is not found in one who keeps himself comfortable over it.

sources.quote: בְּמִי שֶׁמְּחַיֶּה, אֶלָּא בְּמִי שֶׁמֵּמִית עַצְמוֹ עָלֶיהָ בִּיגִיעָה וּבְרָעָבוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says wisdom is found not in one who pampers himself but in one who toils and goes hungry for it.

28:15.headline: Gold so fine that other gold shops close
28:15.body: Rashi says that when this fine gold goes on sale, every other gold shop closes. Metzudat Zion says it is gold shut in the furnace to burn off the dross.

sources.quote: זֶהוּ זָהָב טוֹב, שֶׁבְּשָׁעָה שֶׁנִּפְתָּח, כָּל חֲנֻיּוֹת שֶׁל זָהָב נִסְגָּרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says this is fine gold: when it is opened for sale, all the gold shops close.

sources.quote: סגור. זהב טוב הנסגר בכור הצורף להסיר הסיג
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is fine gold shut in the smelter's furnace to remove the dross.

28:17.headline: Glass beside gold: easy to lose, but it can be mended
28:17.body: Glass appears only here, set next to gold. In the Talmud, Rabbi Meir says Torah is easy to lose like glass, but Rabbi Akiva taught that broken glass can be mended, and so can a scholar who goes astray.

sources.quote: אֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁקָּשִׁין לִקְנוֹתָן כִּכְלֵי זָהָב וּכְלֵי פָז, וְנוֹחִין לְאַבְּדָן כִּכְלֵי זְכוּכִית
sources.says: Rabbi Meir says words of Torah are hard to acquire like gold and easy to lose like glass.

sources.quote: מָה כְּלֵי זָהָב וּכְלֵי זְכוּכִית, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּשְׁבְּרוּ — יֵשׁ לָהֶם תַּקָּנָה, אַף תַּלְמִיד חָכָם, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁסָּרַח — יֵשׁ לוֹ תַּקָּנָה
sources.says: Rabbi Akiva's teaching says broken gold and glass can be repaired, and so can a scholar who sinned.

sources.quote: וזכוכית. היא זכוכית לבנה היקרה מזהב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is white glass, more precious than gold.

28:21.headline: Hidden from the birds, or from the angels
28:21.body: Ramban reads "the fliers of the sky" as birds that fly far into the heavens. Rashi reads them as angels: even they cannot find where wisdom lies.

sources.quote: גם מן העופות המעופפים למרחוק ברקיע השמים
sources.says: Ramban says wisdom is hidden even from birds that fly far up in the sky.

sources.quote: וּמֵעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם. מַלְאָכִים הַמְעוֹפְפִים
sources.says: Rashi says the fliers of the sky are the flying angels.

28:22.headline: The dead, or those who wear themselves out for wisdom
28:22.body: Ibn Ezra reads אבדון and מות as the dead, and the Targum as the house of destruction and the angel of death. Rashi reads them as people who wear themselves out over Torah, and they report that it lasts in whoever toils for it.

sources.quote: אבדון ומות - הם המתים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אבדון and מות are the dead.

sources.quote: בֵּי אַבְדָנָא וּמַלְאָךְ מוֹתָא
sources.says: The Targum renders them as the house of destruction and the angel of death.

sources.quote: הַמְּאַבְּדִין וּמְמִיתִין עַצְמָן עָלֶיהָ אָמְרוּ: בְּאָזְנֵינוּ שָׁמַעְנוּ שִׁמְעָהּ, שֶׁהַמִּיגֵּעַ בָּהּ, מִתְקַיֶּמֶת בּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says those who wear themselves out over wisdom report that it stays with whoever toils in it.

28:26.headline: Each thunderclap gets its own path
28:26.body: Readers differ on חזיז: Metzudat Zion says a cloud, Ralbag says lightning. Rashi says God made a separate path for each thunderclap, so that two never burst through one opening and destroy the world.

sources.quote: לחזיז. כן יקרא הענן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חזיז is a name for a cloud.

sources.quote: לחזיז קולות. לברק אשר הוא סבה לקולות והרעמים
sources.says: Ralbag says חזיז is the lightning that causes the thunder.

sources.quote: וּבַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ דֶּרֶךְ לְכָל הַחֲזִיזִים, שֶׁלֹּא יֵצְאוּ שְׁנֵי קוֹלוֹת דֶּרֶךְ נֶקֶב אֶחָד, פֶּן יַחֲרִיב אֶת הָעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says God made a path for each thunderclap so that two sounds would not come out of one opening and destroy the world.

29:2.headline: "Months of old": the sages hear the months in the womb
29:2.body: Rashi reads ירחי קדם as Job's earlier days of greatness. The Talmud notices that the verse counts months, not years, and says the only time counted in months is pregnancy, when a person is better off than ever again.

sources.quote: כְּיָמִים קַדְמוֹנִים, שֶׁהָיִיתִי בִּגְדֻלָּתִי
sources.says: Rashi says it means the earlier days when Job was great.

sources.quote: וְאֵיזֶהוּ יָמִים שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶם יְרָחִים וְאֵין בָּהֶם שָׁנִים? הֱוֵי אוֹמֵר: אֵלּוּ יַרְחֵי לֵידָה
sources.says: The Talmud asks which days are counted in months and not years, and answers: the months of pregnancy.

sources.quote: וּלְוַאי שֶׁהָיִיתִי כְּאוֹתָן הַיָּמִים שֶׁהָיִיתִי בִּמְעֵי אִמִּי
sources.says: The midrash has Job wish he were back in the days when he was in his mother's womb.

29:3.headline: The lamp over Job's head: success, or the light of the womb
29:3.body: Rashi reads God's lamp as light and joy in Job's good years, and Malbim as wisdom shining on him. The Talmud reads it as a lamp that burns over an unborn child's head, by which it sees from one end of the world to the other.

sources.quote: בְּהִלּוֹ נֵרוֹ. לְשׁוֹן אוֹר וְשִׂמְחָה
sources.says: Rashi says it speaks of light and joy.

sources.quote: וממשיל זה כנר אלוה שהיה מאיר על ראשו להשפיע עליו חכמה ודעת
sources.says: Malbim says the lamp stands for God shining wisdom and knowledge on Job.

sources.quote: וְנֵר דָּלוּק לוֹ עַל רֹאשׁוֹ, וְצוֹפֶה וּמַבִּיט מִסּוֹף הָעוֹלָם וְעַד סוֹפוֹ
sources.says: The Talmud says a lamp burns over the unborn child's head and it looks from one end of the world to the other.

29:4.headline: Job's early days: youth, sowing season, or days of battle
29:4.body: Rashi reads חרפי from Aramaic as "my early days". Ralbag ties it to חורף, winter, when sowing begins, and Ibn Ezra reports a reading from חרף, to taunt an enemy in battle.

sources.quote: בִּימֵי קַדְמוּתִי, לָשׁוֹן אֲרַמִּי הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says it means my early days, from an Aramaic word.

sources.quote: חרפי. נערותי והוא מענין חורף כי אז יחל זמן הזריעה
sources.says: Ralbag says it means my youth, from חורף, the season when sowing begins.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים: שהוא מן: בחרפם בפלשתים שערכו מלחמה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a view that it comes from taunting the Philistines in battle.

29:4.headline: God's secret in Job's tent: counsel, foundation, or prophecy
29:4.body: Rashi reads סוד as the worthy people who gathered in Job's tent to be grounded in God's words. Metzudat Zion reads it as counsel, perhaps from יסוד, a foundation, while Ramban says God's secrets were known in Job's tent, almost like prophecy.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁהָיוּ כְּשֵׁרֵי הַדּוֹר בָּאִים לְאָהֳלִי לְהִוָּסֵד בְּדִבְרֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says the worthy people of the generation came to Job's tent to be grounded in God's words.

sources.quote: בסוד. ענין עצה על כי נעשה בסוד, או שהעצה למעשה היא כיסוד לבנין
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means counsel, because it is made in secret, or because counsel is like the foundation of a building.

sources.quote: אמר כי היה סוד אלוה נודע באהלו, וכאלו היה מתנבא בכל הבאות
sources.says: Ramban says God's secret was known in Job's tent, as if he prophesied what was coming.

29:6.headline: Steps washed in butter, not in anger
29:6.body: חמה usually means anger or heat. Rashi and Ibn Ezra say it is חמאה, butter, with the א left out, as בית שן is spelled בית שאן elsewhere: Job had so much that his paths were washed in butter.

sources.quote: בְּחֵמָה. כְּמוֹ בְּחֶמְאָה
sources.says: Rashi says it means "in butter".

sources.quote: בחמה - חסר אל"ף והוא בחמאה, כמו בית שן ובמקום אחר בית שאן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is missing an א and means butter, like the two spellings of Beit She'an.

sources.quote: והוא מדרך גוזמא והפלגה
sources.says: Metzudat David says this is a deliberate exaggeration.

29:7.headline: The city gate, or a raised seat above it
29:7.body: קרת is a rare word for a city, and Metzudat Zion reads it that way. Rashi and Malbim read it as תקרה, a high platform at the gate where the elders sat, with the chief above all the people.

sources.quote: עלי קרת. אצל הקריה והעיר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means by the town and city.

sources.quote: קָרֶת. תִּקְרָה גְּבוֹהָה מוּכֶנֶת כְּכִסֵּא, לָשֶׁבֶת לְזִקְנֵי הָעִיר
sources.says: Rashi says it is a high platform set up like a seat for the city elders.

sources.quote: בשער ישבו הזקנים והראש ישב על תקרה הגבוהה של השער מעל כל העם
sources.says: Malbim says the elders sat at the gate and the head sat on its high platform above everyone.

29:14.headline: Job wore justice, and justice wore Job
29:14.body: Job says "I put on righteousness and it put me on". Rashi reads: I chased righteousness and it came to me, while Malbim says Job became its garment, since anyone who wanted to act justly learned by watching him.

sources.quote: רָדַפְתִּי אַחֲרֵי הַצֶּדֶק וְהוּא נִמְצָא לִי
sources.says: Rashi says Job pursued righteousness and it came to him.

sources.quote: אני לובש הצדק והצדק לובש אותי, ר"ל כל הרוצה לעשות צדק ילמד ממני
sources.says: Malbim says Job wears righteousness and righteousness wears him: whoever wants to do right learns from him.

29:18.headline: Days as many as the sand, or like the bird that never dies
29:18.body: Ramban and Metzudat David read חול as sand: Job hoped for days as many as the sand. Rashi and the midrash read it as a bird called חול, which did not eat from the tree of knowledge, so it never dies and renews itself every thousand years.

sources.quote: אחר שארבה ימים כחול הים
sources.says: Ramban says Job thought he would live days as many as the sand of the sea.

sources.quote: עוֹף וּשְׁמוֹ חוֹל. וְלֹא נִקְנְסָה עָלָיו מִיתָה, שֶׁלֹּא טָעַם מֵעֵץ הַדַּעַת
sources.says: Rashi says חול is a bird that was never sentenced to death because it did not eat from the tree of knowledge.

sources.quote: חוץ מעוף אחד ושמו חול. שלא שמע לאכול
sources.says: The midrash says Eve fed the fruit to every creature except one bird named חול, which refused.

sources.quote: שאמרו חז"ל שחי לעולם ושכל אלף שנה ישרף בקינו וישוב לחיות
sources.says: Malbim says the sages taught that it lives forever, burning in its nest every thousand years and coming back to life.

29:19.headline: Dew on Job's branches, or dew at harvest time
29:19.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read קציר here as branches, as in Job 14:9: dew rests on Job's boughs. The Sifrei reads it as harvest, and cites it for a blessing where plowing and harvest seasons run together.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ ״וְעָשָׂה קָצִיר״ (איוב יד:ט) – וְהֵן יוֹנְקוֹת עֲנָפִים רַכִּים שֶׁל אִילָן
sources.says: Rashi says קציר here means the soft young branches of a tree, as in Job 14:9.

sources.quote: בקצירי. בענפי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means "on my branches".

sources.quote: שֶׁיְּהֵא חוֹרֵשׁ בִּשְׁעַת קָצִיר וְקוֹצֵר בִּשְׁעַת חָרִישׁ, וְכֵן אִיּוֹב אוֹמֵר
sources.says: The Sifrei describes a blessing where a man plows at harvest time and harvests at plowing time, and cites this verse.

29:20.headline: Job's bow: renewed in strength, or passed from hand to hand
29:20.body: Ibn Ezra lists several readings of תחליף, among them passing the bow from hand to hand, and shooting arrows without missing. Ramban reads it as renewed strength, as in Isaiah 40:31, "those who hope in God will renew their strength".

sources.quote: יש אומרים: כי אחליפנו מיד אל יד ולא תסור ממני. ויש אומרים: תחלוף, כמו: כל בני חלוף שהייתי מורה בה חצי ולא אחטיא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some say Job passed the bow from hand to hand, and others that he shot arrows with it and never missed.

sources.quote: תחליף ידו כח ועצמה, מלשון וקוי ה' יחליפו כח
sources.says: Ramban says Job's hand would gain new strength, as in "those who hope in God will renew their strength".

sources.quote: וְקַשְׁתִּי. וְאֵיתָנִי תַּחֲלִיף תָּמִיד לְטוֹבָה
sources.says: Rashi says the bow stands for Job's strength, which kept renewing for the good.

29:22.headline: Job's words drip like dew, or speak like prophecy
29:22.body: נטף means to drip. Rashi says it is also a word for prophecy, as in Amos 7:16, so Job's words were like prophecy, while Ibn Ezra reads them as falling like dew.

sources.quote: תִּטֹּף מִלָּתִי. לְשׁוֹן נְבוּאָה
sources.says: Rashi says the word is a term for prophecy.

sources.quote: ועלימו תטוף - תזל כטל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means Job's words flowed down like dew.

sources.quote: ואולי כולם מן נטפי מים
sources.says: Ramban suggests that every use, prophecy included, comes from drops of water.

29:25.headline: The one who comforts, or the mourner who is comforted
29:25.body: Job sat at the head "as one who comforts mourners". The Talmud uses the verse to show that a mourner sits at the head, and answers that the written letters can also be read "is comforted".

sources.quote: מִנַּיִן לָאָבֵל שֶׁמֵּיסֵב בָּרֹאשׁ
sources.says: The Talmud asks how we know a mourner sits at the head, and cites this verse.

sources.quote: יְנַחֵם אֲחֵרִים מַשְׁמַע! אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: ״יִנָּחֵם״ כְּתִיב
sources.says: The Talmud objects that ינחם means comforting others, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that it is written so it can be read "is comforted".

3:2.headline: Nobody had spoken, so whom is Job answering?
3:2.body: ויען usually means "he answered", but no one has spoken yet. Rashi says it means he cried out loud. Ibn Ezra suggests his friends asked what was wrong after seven silent days.

sources.quote: וַיַּעַן. וַיִּצְעַק, שֶׁכָּל עֲנִיָּה הָאֲמוּרָה בַּתּוֹרָה אֵינָהּ אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן הֲרָמַת קוֹל
sources.says: Rashi says ויען means he cried out, since this word in Scripture means raising the voice.

sources.quote: או שאלוהו חבריו אחר מלאת שבעת ימים, מה לך? אז ענה להם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says perhaps his friends asked him after seven days what was wrong, and he answered.

3:3.headline: The night that spoke: the sages name an angel Night
3:3.body: The verse says "the night said". Rashi explains that the speaker is simply left out. He also cites the sages: the angel in charge of conception is named לילה, Night.

sources.quote: זֶה אֶחָד מִן הַמְּקוֹמוֹת שֶׁחִסֵּר הַמִּקְרָא אֶת דְּבָרָיו
sources.says: Rashi says this is one of the places where Scripture leaves out who is speaking.

sources.quote: מַלְאָךְ הַמְמֻנֶּה עַל הַהֵרָיוֹן, ׳לַיְלָה׳ שְׁמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages that the angel over conception is named Night.

sources.quote: וּמַלְאֲכָא דִי מְמַנֵי עַל עַבּוּר
sources.says: The Targum adds the angel appointed over conception.

3:3.headline: Conceived or born: which night does Job curse?
3:3.body: Rashi reads הרה as conception, the night Job's father made his mother pregnant. Ibn Ezra reads it as birth. Ramban notes the sages' reading: Job curses both the day he was born and the night he was conceived.

sources.quote: הוֹרָה גָבֶר. שֶׁעִיבֵּר אָבִי אֶת אִמִּי
sources.says: Rashi says it means my father made my mother pregnant.

sources.quote: והורה - כמו: יולד, וכמוהו: ותהר את מרים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says הרה here means was born.

sources.quote: וכן אמרו רבותינו ז"ל איוב מקלל יום לידתו וליל עבורו
sources.says: Ramban cites the sages that Job curses the day of his birth and the night of his conception.

3:5.headline: Let darkness stain that day, or claim it as kin
3:5.body: גאל can mean to defile or to redeem. Rashi reads it as staining, like the "defiled bread" of Malachi 1:7. Ralbag also offers the other sense: darkness as its גואל, its next of kin, living with it always.

sources.quote: וְהוּא לְשׁוֹן לִכְלוּךְ
sources.says: Rashi says the word means soiling.

sources.quote: או יהיה הרצון בו שיהיו גואלין וקרוביו חשך וצלמות בדרך שישכנו עמו תמיד
sources.says: Ralbag says it may mean that darkness and deep shadow are its kin and live with it always.

sources.quote: ויש אומר: שהוא מן גאל ועניינו שיפדוהו וימשכוהו לנפשם והוא רחוק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a reading of redeeming and taking it for themselves, and calls it far-fetched.

3:5.headline: A cloud can "dwell" on a day, says Maimonides
3:5.body: שכן usually means a living being dwells in a place. Maimonides cites this verse to show the word stretches further: a cloud is not alive, and a day is a span of time, not a place.

sources.quote: ואין ספק שהעננה אינה בעל חיים, והיום אינו גוף כלל, אלא הוא פרק זמן
sources.says: Maimonides says the cloud is not a living thing and the day is not a body at all, only a span of time.

3:6.headline: Let that night not rejoice, or not be counted?
3:6.body: יחד can come from joy or from oneness. Rashi gives both: let the night not rejoice among the days of the year, as Jethro rejoiced (Exodus 18:9), or not be joined to them. Ibn Ezra prefers joy.

sources.quote: אַל יִחַדְּ. אַל יִשְׂמַח, כְּמוֹ ״וַיִּחַדְּ יִתְרוֹ״
sources.says: Rashi says it means let it not rejoice, as in Exodus 18:9.

sources.quote: פֵּרוּשׁ אַחֵר: אַל יִתְאַחֵד
sources.says: Rashi also says it may mean let it not be joined.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני: שהוא אל ישמח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the right reading is let it not rejoice.

3:7.headline: Which joyful song should that night never hear?
3:7.body: רננה is a ringing cry. Ramban takes it as the noise of people out together at night. He also mentions a view that it is the angels' song. The Targum makes it the song of the wild rooster praising God.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים כי שירת מלאכי מעלה למקום היא רננה
sources.says: Ramban reports a view that רננה is the song of the angels to God.

sources.quote: לָא תֵעוּל רְנָנָא דְתַרְנְגוֹל בְּרָא לִמְקַלָסָא בֵיהּ
sources.says: The Targum says the song of the wild rooster will not come to praise in it.

3:16.headline: Grubby little children, or babies still in the womb?
3:16.body: Rashi says small children are called עוללים because they are all play and dirt. The midrash learns from this verse that עוללים also means babies in the womb, who "never saw light".

sources.quote: וּלְכָךְ קוֹרֵא אוֹתָם עוֹלְלִים, שֶׁכֻּלָּם שְׂחוֹק וְלִכְלוּךְ
sources.says: Rashi says children are called עוללים because they are all play and dirt.

sources.quote: עוֹלְלִים, אֵלּוּ שֶׁבִּמְעֵי אִמָּן, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: אוֹ כְנֵפֶל טָמוּן
sources.says: The midrash says עוללים are those in their mother's womb, citing this verse.

3:26.headline: The last trouble to arrive was the news about his children
3:26.body: Job lists three kinds of rest he lost, then "trouble came". The Targum matches each to a messenger from chapter 1: the oxen and donkeys, the fire, the camels. The final trouble is the news of his children.

sources.quote: לָא שָׁלַיָית מִבְּסוֹרְתָּא דְתוֹרֵי וְאַתְנָן
sources.says: The Targum says Job had no ease from the news about the oxen and donkeys.

sources.quote: וַאֲתָא רוּגְזָא עַל בְּסוֹרְתָּא דִי בָנַיָא
sources.says: The Targum says the trouble came with the news about his children.

30:2.headline: Old age is called כלח, as if recalling youthful moisture
30:2.body: Rashi says the rare word כלח means old age. Ramban hears לח, moist, inside it: old age is named for the fresh strength a person had when young.

sources.quote: עָלֵימוֹ אָבַד כָּלַח. זִקְנָה
sources.says: Rashi says כלח means old age.

sources.quote: יקרא כלח, כאילו היה לח בימי נעוריו
sources.says: Ramban says old age is called כלח as if the person had been moist in his youth.

30:3.headline: אמש: the dark of night, or just yesterday?
30:3.body: אמש usually means last night or yesterday. Metzudat Zion says here it means the darkness where these outcasts hide, while Ramban keeps the time sense: the recent past.

sources.quote: אמש. ר״ל חושך בחשכת הלילה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אמש here means the darkness of night.

sources.quote: הזמן הקרוב שעבר יקרא אותו אמש
sources.says: Ramban says the verse calls the recent past אמש.

30:4.headline: A bush, or idle chatter? The Talmud hears both
30:4.body: Rashi says שיח is a bush, as in Genesis 21:15. The Talmud hears שיחה, idle talk: whoever drops Torah study for chatter is fed coals of the broom plant named in this verse.

sources.quote: שִׂיחַ. אִילָן, כְּמוֹ ״אַחַד הַשִּׂיחִים״
sources.says: Rashi says שיח means a tree or bush, as in Genesis 21:15.

sources.quote: כׇּל הַפּוֹסֵק מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְעוֹסֵק בְּדִבְרֵי שִׂיחָה
sources.says: The Talmud reads the verse as about one who stops Torah study for idle talk, and says he is fed coals of broom.

30:4.headline: Broom roots: their bread, or their only warmth?
30:4.body: לחמם usually means "their bread". Ralbag offers a second reading, "to warm them": people sleeping in the open need the roots to make a fire.

sources.quote: או יהיה לחמם מקור ותהיה הלמד משמשת ויהיה עניינו לחמם עצמם
sources.says: Ralbag says the word may mean to warm themselves, since they stay in cold places without shelter.

30:11.headline: An unstrung bow, or untied ropes?
30:11.body: Rashi says יתרי is the string of Job's bow, which God has loosened, so his strength is gone. Ramban, following the Targum, says it is the cord Job once used to bind the wicked, and now they have untied it.

sources.quote: כִּי יִתְרִי פִּתַּח. יֶתֶר קַשְׁתִּי פִּתַּח
sources.says: Rashi says יתרי is the string of Job's bow, which has been loosened.

sources.quote: ואמר כי היתר אשר אסר בו את הרשעים
sources.says: Ramban, citing the Targum, says it is the cord Job bound the wicked with, and calls this the right reading.

30:12.headline: פרחח: a boy just budding, like a blossom or chick
30:12.body: The word comes from פרח, to bud. Metzudat Zion says it is a youth whose beard is just starting to grow, and Ramban compares אפרוחים, baby birds.

sources.quote: ענינו מי שהתחיל לצמוח ולהפריח שער זקנו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says פרחח is one whose beard has just begun to grow.

sources.quote: והוא כנוי לנער אשר יוציא עתה פרח, וכן יקראו קטני העופות אפרוחים
sources.says: Ramban says it is a name for a boy just putting out his first growth, like young birds called אפרוחים.

30:15.headline: "My noble one": Job's soul, or his generosity?
30:15.body: Metzudat Zion says the soul is called נדיבה, the noble one, as in Psalms 51:14. Ramban also allows the plain sense: Job was a generous lord, and that standing is what was chased away.

sources.quote: נדיבתי. כן תקרא הנפש על כי היא בעלת הנדיבות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the soul is called נדיבה because it is generous.

sources.quote: או נדיבתו ממש, כי נדיב עמים היה
sources.says: Ramban says it may mean his soul, or his actual generosity, since he was a noble among peoples.

30:17.headline: My veins, or my pursuers? Arabic and Hebrew pull apart
30:17.body: Rashi, citing Dunash, says ערק is the Arabic word for a sinew: Job's veins never rest at night. Ramban prefers the Hebrew sense "to flee" from verse 3: the men who chase Job do not lie down to sleep.

sources.quote: ׳גִּיד׳ בִּלְשׁוֹן עֲרָבִי ׳עוֹרֶק׳; כָּךְ פֵּירֵשׁ דּוּנַשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says, following Dunash, that עורק is Arabic for a sinew, and also gives a second reading, my pursuers.

sources.quote: רק יש לפרש כפשוטו מן העורקים ציה
sources.says: Ramban says it should be read plainly, from the word for fleeing in verse 3, as the people who chase him.

30:19.headline: Taught to sit in the mud, or thrown into it?
30:19.body: הרני can come from "to teach" or "to throw". Rashi first says the boils taught Job to sit as if in clay, and Metzudat Zion reads it as "threw me", as in Exodus 15:4.

sources.quote: הוֹרָנִי יְלַמְּדֵנִי הַשְּׁחִין הַזֶּה לֵישֵׁב כְּמוֹ בַחֹמֶר
sources.says: Rashi says the boils taught Job to sit as in clay, and offers a second reading, threw me.

sources.quote: הורני. השליך אותי כמו ירה בים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says הרני means threw me, as in cast into the sea.

30:19.headline: Like Abraham, yet judged like the builders of Babel
30:19.body: A midrash cited by Rashi hears two other verses here: Abraham called himself "dust and ashes", and the Babel builders used חמר, mortar. Job says he was as righteous as Abraham, yet was judged like them.

sources.quote: אֲנִי נִמְשַׁלְתִּי לְאַבְרָהָם בְּצִדְקָתִי שֶׁקָּרָא עַצְמוֹ ״עָפָר וָאֵפֶר״
sources.says: Rashi cites Tanchuma: Job was like Abraham, who called himself dust and ashes, but was judged like the generation of the tower.

sources.quote: וְאִמְתִיל לְאַבְרָהָם דְאִדְמֵי לַעֲפַר וּקְטַם
sources.says: A second Targum reading says Job was compared to Abraham, who likened himself to dust and ashes.

30:22.headline: Melted by weakness, or did Job's wisdom melt away?
30:22.body: The word is written תשוה and read תושיה. Rashi reads it as weakness that melts Job down, while Ramban says it is all Job's wisdom and knowledge that melt away.

sources.quote: חַלָּשׁוּת וְתַשּׁוּת כֹּחַ הָיָה מְמוֹגְגֵנִי
sources.says: Rashi says weakness and loss of strength were melting him.

sources.quote: יאמר כי תתמוגג ותאבד ממנו כל חכמה ודעת
sources.says: Ramban says all wisdom and knowledge melt and are lost from him.

30:24.headline: שוע: comfort, a cry for help, or wealth?
30:24.body: Rashi hears comfort: a nation God strikes is consoled by seeing another already struck, and he also reads it as prayer. Ibn Ezra reads it as generosity, that is, money, which cannot help in the grave.

sources.quote: הָיָה מְשַׁעֲשְׁעָן תַּנְחוּמִין בְּמִקְצָת
sources.says: Rashi says God would give them some comfort, and also reads שוע as prayer.

sources.quote: לא יועיל השוע לנפשות, והוא הנדיבות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שוע is generosity, meaning wealth, which does not help at the time of ruin.

30:29.headline: Ostriches: wailing all day, or the silent mourners?
30:29.body: Rashi says jackals and ostriches both cry all their days. Ramban says jackals wail but ostriches make no sound even when struck, so Job mourns both ways, with crying and with silence.

sources.quote: תַּנִּים וּבְנוֹת יַעֲנָה עֲסוּקִים בִּבְכִי כָּל יְמֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says jackals and ostriches spend all their days weeping.

sources.quote: ובנות יענה לא ישאו קולם ולא יצעקו כלל
sources.says: Ramban says ostriches never raise their voice, and silence is a way of mourning.

31:7.headline: A stain, or anything at all, stuck to his hands
31:7.body: Rashi reads מאום as מום, a stain, and notes the alef is written but not read. Ibn Ezra reads it as מאומה, "anything". Metzudat Zion and Ralbag give both readings.

sources.quote: מָאוּם. הוּא מוּם, דְּבַר שֶׁמֶץ. וְאָלֶ״ף זוֹ כְּתוּבָה וְלֹא קְרִיָא
sources.says: Rashi says מאום is a blemish or stain, and the alef is written but not pronounced.

sources.quote: מאום - כמו מאומה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like מאומה, anything.

sources.quote: מאום. כמו מום או הוא מל׳ מאומה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is like מום, or comes from מאומה.

sources.quote: מאום. כמו מום בלא אלף או יהיה כמו מאומה
sources.says: Ralbag says it is מום without the alef, or like מאומה.

31:10.headline: His wife grinding for another: at the mill, or in bed
31:10.body: Ralbag and Metzudat David read it plainly: poverty will force his wife to grind grain for others. Rashi says the sages read "grinding" as a word for intercourse, as with Samson grinding in prison. Ibn Ezra and Ramban explain the image of two millstones.

sources.quote: תטחן לאחר אשתי. הוא מענין טחינה ברחים
sources.says: Ralbag says it means grinding at a mill.

sources.quote: תטחן אשתי תבואה ברחיים של יד לצורך אחר
sources.says: Metzudat David says his wife will grind grain with a hand mill for someone else.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן תַּשְׁמִישׁ, כְּמוֹ ״וַיְהִי טוֹחֵן בְּבֵית הָאֲסוּרִין״
sources.says: Rashi says the sages read it as a word for intercourse, like Samson grinding in prison.

sources.quote: תטחן - דמה המשכב לשני טוחנות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the verse compares lying together to two millstones.

sources.quote: שבטחינה הרכב על הרחים התחתונה
sources.says: Ramban says the word was used this way because in grinding the upper stone moves on the lower one.

31:12.headline: One root means both to take root and to uproot
31:12.body: Job says the fire of sin תשרש all his crops. Rashi says this vowel pattern means "uproot", while תַּשְׁרֵשׁ, with other vowels, means "take root". Ralbag also reads it as uproot.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁהוּא מְדַבֵּר בִּלְשׁוֹן עִקּוּר, אוֹמֵר תְּשָׁרֵשׁ; וּבִלְשׁוֹן שֹׁרֶשׁ אוֹמֵר ״תַּשְׁרֵשׁ״
sources.says: Rashi says one form of the verb means uprooting and another means taking root.

sources.quote: תשרש. תעקר
sources.says: Ralbag says תשרש means it uproots.

31:18.headline: Who grew up with whom: Job and the orphan
31:18.body: Rashi reads גדלני as "raised me": doing right raised Job like a father from his youth. Ibn Ezra and Ralbag read it as "grew up with me": the orphan grew up in Job's house as with a father.

sources.quote: הַכִּשָּׁרוֹן הַזֶּה כְּאָב הַמְגַדְּלֵנִי
sources.says: Rashi says this good way raised him like a father.

sources.quote: מנעורי גדלני כאב - גדל היתום עמי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the orphan grew up with Job.

sources.quote: גדלני. גדל עמי
sources.says: Ralbag says גדלני means grew up with me.

31:24.headline: Trust is named after the loins, where the kidneys sit
31:24.body: Here כסלי means "my trust". Rashi explains why: the kidneys sit on the כסלים, the loins, and the kidneys give counsel. So thought and hope are called כסל.

sources.quote: וְעַל יְדֵי שֶׁכְּלָיוֹת עַל הַכְּסָלִים הֵם (ויקרא ג:ד), וְהַכְּלָיוֹת יוֹעֲצוֹת (תהלים טז:ז), נִקְרֵאת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה ׳כֶּסֶל׳
sources.says: Rashi says thought is called כסל because the kidneys sit on the loins and the kidneys give counsel.

sources.quote: כסלי. ענין בטחון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says כסלי means trust.

sources.quote: כסלי - משעני כמו: כי ה' יהיה בכסלך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means what he leans on, as in Proverbs 3:26.

31:32.headline: Doors open to the traveler, or open to the road
31:32.body: Metzudat Zion says ארח names both a traveler and the road itself. Ralbag reads it as the road: Job's doors faced the road so he could see guests coming. Rashi says the doors opened straight onto the main road.

sources.quote: לאורח. הוא שם משותף להאיש הבא מהדרך ולהדרך עצמו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word names both the traveler and the road.

sources.quote: לארח. לדרך כדי שאראה האורחים בבואם
sources.says: Ralbag says the doors opened to the road so Job could see guests coming.

sources.quote: אֶלָּא פְּתוּחִין לְאֵם דֶּרֶךְ, לָבוֹא כָּל הַבָּא
sources.says: Rashi says the doors opened onto the main road so anyone could come in.

31:34.headline: Did Job crush the crowd, or fear it?
31:34.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read אערוץ as "I crushed": Job once broke great crowds, and now lowly families frighten him. Ibn Ezra and Ramban read it as "I fear", as in "Him you shall hold in awe".

sources.quote: מִתְּחִלָּה הָיִיתִי מַכְנִיעַ הָמוֹן רַבָּה שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים
sources.says: Rashi says Job used to subdue a great crowd of wicked men.

sources.quote: אערוץ. אשבור כמו בערוץ נחלים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אערוץ means I break.

sources.quote: כי אערוץ - אפחד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אערוץ means I fear.

sources.quote: כמו את ה' אלהיכם אותו תעריצו. יאמר כי יירא מן המון בני אדם
sources.says: Ramban compares it to holding God in awe, and says it means fearing the crowd.

31:40.headline: A stinking weed, named like Isaiah's rotten grapes
31:40.body: Rashi ties באשה to באש, to stink, like the rotten grapes of Isaiah 5. Metzudat Zion says it looks like barley but is worse. Rashi adds a farming lesson from the sages: a field that grows these weeds is good for barley.

sources.quote: בָּאְשָׁה. (דָּבָר מַבְאִישׁ) כְּמוֹ ״בְּאוּשִׁים״
sources.says: Rashi says באשה is something that stinks, like the rotten grapes in Isaiah.

sources.quote: באשה. דומה הוא לשעורה וגרועה ממנה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it looks like barley but is worse.

sources.quote: שֶׁמַּעֲלָה בְּאוּשִׁים יָפֶה לְזוֹרְעָהּ שְׂעוֹרִים
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages: a field that grows these weeds is good for sowing barley.

sources.quote: באשה. הוא מין ממיני החוח מגזרת ויעש באושים
sources.says: Ralbag says it is a kind of thorn, from the same root as Isaiah's באושים.

31:40.headline: "Job's words are ended", yet he speaks again later
31:40.body: Metzudat David reads it plainly: Job has finished speaking. Rashi notes that Job speaks again later in the book. So he reads it as part of Job's oath: if I did not act rightly, let my words be ended.

sources.quote: נשלמו אמרי ולא אדבר עוד מעתה
sources.says: Metzudat David says Job means his words are complete and he will speak no more.

sources.quote: וְאַתְּ אוֹמֵר תַּמּוּ דִּבְרֵי אִיּוֹב? אֶלָּא כָּךְ אוֹמֵר אִיּוֹב: אִם לֹא עָשִׂיתִי כֵן, יִתַּמּוּ דִּבְרֵי אִיּוֹב
sources.says: Rashi asks how Job's words can be ended when he speaks again, and reads it as an oath: if I did not do so, let my words end.

32:1.headline: The Sabbath word here means the friends stopped talking
32:1.body: וישבתו comes from the same root as Shabbat, usually "rest". Maimonides uses this verse to show the root can mean "stop speaking", which helps him explain how God "rested" on the seventh day.

sources.quote: כי הפסקת הדיבור נקראת גם כן "שביתה", כמו שנאמר
sources.says: Maimonides says that stopping speech is also called שביתה, and quotes this verse as proof.

sources.quote: נחו ופסקו כמו שבת נוגש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means they rested and stopped.

32:2.headline: Sages hear a blessing in the name of Elihu's father
32:2.body: ברכאל sounds like "God blessed". In the Jerusalem Talmud, Rabbi Akiva says Elihu is Balaam, who came to curse Israel and blessed them, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says he is Isaac, the son God blessed.

sources.quote: בֶּן בַּרַכְאֵל. שֶׁבָּא לְקַלֵּל אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבֵירְכָן
sources.says: Rabbi Akiva reads the name as pointing to Balaam, who came to curse Israel and blessed them.

sources.quote: אֶלָּא אֱלִיהוּא זֶה יִצְחָק. בֶּן בַּרַכְאֵל. בֶּן שֶׁבֵּירְכוֹ הָאֵל
sources.says: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says Elihu is Isaac, and the name means the son whom God blessed.

32:2.headline: Buzite: a family name, or a hint of contempt
32:2.body: Plainly, Elihu comes from Buz, a son of Abraham's brother Nahor. The sages in the Jerusalem Talmud also hear בוז, "contempt": one says Elihu's prophecy was despised, the other that he despised the temples of idols.

sources.quote: מבני נחור אחי אברהם
sources.says: Metzudat David says the Buzites descend from Nahor, Abraham's brother, through his son Buz.

sources.quote: הַבּוּזִי. שֶׁהָיְתָה נְבוּאָתוֹ בְזוּיָה
sources.says: Rabbi Akiva says the name means his prophecy was despised.

sources.quote: שֶׁבִּיזָּה כָל בָּתֵּי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
sources.says: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says it means he despised all the temples of idols.

32:2.headline: Is Ram Abraham, or an Israelite ancestor?
32:2.body: רם means "high". Rashi and the Targum say the family of Ram is Abraham's family. Ibn Ezra thinks it is more likely Ram the father of Amminadav, which would make Elihu an Israelite.

sources.quote: מִמִּשְׁפַּחַת רָם. אַבְרָהָם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר
sources.says: Rashi says Ram is Abraham, called the great man among the giants.

sources.quote: מִן גְנִיסַת אַבְרָהָם
sources.says: The Targum translates "from the family of Ram" as "from the family of Abraham".

sources.quote: והקרוב שהוא אבי עמינדב והוא מבני ישראל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Ram is most likely the father of Amminadav, an Israelite.

32:3.headline: The scribes softened this verse to protect God's honor
32:3.body: The verse says the friends "condemned Job". Rashi says it is one of the verses the scribes reworded: it really means that by their silence they condemned God. Ibn Ezra reports this view but says it is beyond him.

sources.quote: זֶה אֶחָד מִן הַמִּקְרָאוֹת שֶׁתִּקְּנוּ סוֹפְרִים אֶת לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב
sources.says: Rashi says this is one of the verses where the scribes changed the wording.

sources.quote: וַיַּרְשִׁיעוּ כְּלַפֵּי הַמָּקוֹם בִּשְׁתִיקוֹתָם
sources.says: Rashi says the verse should have read that they condemned God by their silence.

sources.quote: הוא תיקון סופרים והוא כנוי אל המקום
sources.says: Metzudat David agrees it is a scribal correction standing in for God.

sources.quote: והאומרים כן ידעו מה שנעלם ממני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says those who call it a scribal correction know something hidden from him.

32:15.headline: Their words left them, or nothing worth passing on
32:15.body: העתיקו usually means "moved" something. Rashi reads it as their words left them, and Ibn Ezra also brings a view that they said nothing anyone would copy down.

sources.quote: הֶעְתִּיקוּ. סָרוּ מֵהֶן מִלִּין
sources.says: Rashi says the words departed from them.

sources.quote: והעניין שלא דברו עד שיעתיק אדם דבריהם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra brings a view that they did not speak words a person would pass on, and also the reading that their words moved away.

sources.quote: כמו ויעתק משם ההרה, נעקרו המלים מהם
sources.says: Malbim compares it to moving camp and says the words were uprooted from them.

32:16.headline: Here "they stood" means they fell silent
32:16.body: עמדו usually means "they stood". Maimonides uses this verse to show it can also mean "they stopped", and the Talmud uses it to rule that people must be silent once the Torah scroll is opened.

sources.quote: ויש לו משמעות של הימנעות והפסקה
sources.says: Maimonides says standing can also mean holding back and stopping, and cites this verse.

sources.quote: וְאֵין עֲמִידָה אֶלָּא שְׁתִיקָה
sources.says: The Talmud says standing here means silence, and learns from it that one may not talk while the Torah is read.

sources.quote: עמדו. שתקו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion explains the word as "they were silent".

32:19.headline: Wineskins, in a word that usually names a ghost
32:19.body: אוב usually names the spirit a medium raises. Here it means wineskins, a use Metzudat Zion says appears nowhere else, and Ibn Ezra ties the two senses together.

sources.quote: כאובות. כנאדות ואין לו דומה במקרא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means wineskins and has no match elsewhere in Scripture.

sources.quote: נוֹדוֹת עֲשׂוּיִין כְּקוֹמַת אָדָם, גְּבוֹהִים
sources.says: Rashi says they are tall skins, made the height of a man.

sources.quote: ורובי המפרשים אמרו: שהם נאדות, וזה נכון כי אל תפנו אל האובות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra agrees they are wineskins and links them to the warning not to turn to the ovot.

32:21.headline: Elihu refuses to soften words with polite substitutes
32:21.body: אכנה comes from כינוי, a respectful substitute name. Rashi links it back to verse 3, where the scribes softened the wording for God's honor: Elihu says he will not do that for anyone.

sources.quote: זֶהוּ ׳כִּנּוּי׳, שֶׁמְּשַׁנֶּה אֶת הַדִּבּוּר בִּשְׁבִיל כְּבוֹדוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says a כינוי means changing your words for someone's honor, as in verse 3.

sources.quote: אכנה. מל׳ כנוי שאינו שם העצמי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from a substitute name that is not the person's real name.

sources.quote: בלה"ק בא רק על שם הכבוד שנותן לחבירו
sources.says: Malbim says in Hebrew the word means only a title of honor given to someone.

33:7.headline: My pressure, or my hand: Elihu answers Job's plea
33:7.body: Rashi reads אכפי as "my pressure", as in Proverbs 16:26. Ralbag reads it as כפי, "my hand", with an extra alef. Then Elihu is answering Job, who begged God to take His hand away (13:21).

sources.quote: וְאַכְפִּי. כְּפִיָּתִי, כְּמוֹ ״אָכַף עָלָיו פִּיהוּ״
sources.says: Rashi says אכפי means my pressing, as in Proverbs 16:26.

sources.quote: ואכפי. כמו וכפי והרצון בו כמו ידי ומכתי והוא כנגד מה שאמר איוב כפך מעלי הרחק
sources.says: Ralbag says it means my hand, in answer to Job's words "take Your hand away from me".

sources.quote: ואחרים אמרו כי האל"ף נוסף, והוא וכפי עליך לא יכבד, ויענה זה לאיוב שאמר כפך מעלי הרחק
sources.says: Ramban reports others who say the alef is extra and the word means my hand, answering Job.

33:9.headline: Scrubbed clean, or with his sins covered
