33:9.body: Rashi reads חף as "clean and scrubbed", like the sages' word for washing the hair or scouring dishes. Ramban reads it as "covered": Job claims his sin is covered over. Ibn Ezra lists both, and also "wrapped in righteousness".

sources.quote: חַף. טָהוֹר וּמְשֻׁפְשָׁף
sources.says: Rashi says חף means pure and scrubbed, as the sages use the word for washing the head and scouring vessels.

sources.quote: חף. נגרד ומנוקה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means scraped and cleaned.

sources.quote: חף אנכי, כסוי חטאה, וכן וראש לו חפוי
sources.says: Ramban says it means one whose sin is covered, like a covered head.

sources.quote: ואחרים אומרים: שהוא חפוף בצדק כענין צדק לבשתי וילבשני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a reading that Job is wrapped in righteousness, beside the covering reading and the plain "clean".

33:10.headline: Excuses to find fault, perhaps תואנה with letters swapped
33:10.body: Elihu quotes Job: God finds תנואות against me. Rashi reads it as pretexts, like תואנה, the excuse Samson looked for. Metzudat Zion suggests it is that very word with its letters turned around.

sources.quote: תְּנוּאוֹת. עֲלִילוֹת, לְשׁוֹן ״תּוֹאֲנָה״
sources.says: Rashi says תנואות means pretexts, from the word תואנה.

sources.quote: ויתכן שהוא הפוך מן תואנה הוא מבקש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it may be תואנה turned around.

sources.quote: הן תנואות - כמו: וידעתם את תנואתי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares it to the same word in Numbers 14:34.

33:17.headline: God covers a man's pride, or covers his body
33:17.body: Rashi, Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra read גוה as גאוה, pride: God humbles a person. Ralbag also offers "body", and Ramban reads it that way. Ibn Ezra adds that pride lives in the eye, so God "covers" it.

sources.quote: גֵּוָה. כְּמוֹ גַּאֲוָה
sources.says: Rashi says גוה is like גאוה, pride.

sources.quote: וגוה. וגוף או ירצה בו וגאוה
sources.says: Ralbag says it means body, or else pride.

sources.quote: וגויתו מן הגבר יכסנה
sources.says: Ramban reads it as his body, which God covers.

sources.quote: ויכסה הפך יראה, כי עיקר הגאוה ראיית העין
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says "cover" is the opposite of "see", because pride starts in what the eye sees.

33:21.headline: His bones crushed, out of joint, or sticking out
33:21.body: Metzudat Zion reads ושפו as "crushed", as in the snake's curse in Genesis 3:15. Rashi reads it as "out of joint". Ralbag and Ramban read it as "stick up": with the flesh gone, the bones stand out like a bare hilltop.

sources.quote: ושפו. ענין כתיתה כמו הוא ישופך ראש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means crushing, as in Genesis 3:15.

sources.quote: וְשֻׁפּוּ עַצְמוֹתָיו. מִתְנַתְּקִין מִמְּקוֹמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says his bones come loose from their place.

sources.quote: ושפו. וגבהו
sources.says: Ralbag says it means they rose up.

sources.quote: ושפו, מן הר נשפה, על שפיים, עניינם מקום גבוה
sources.says: Ramban says it comes from "a bare hill", meaning a high place: the bones stick out.

33:25.headline: A rare word built from two: moist and spreading
33:25.body: Metzudat Zion says רטפש joins two words: רטוב, moist, and פש, to spread. Rashi rejects reading it from רפש, mud, with an extra tet. Ramban reports that the Aramaic translation reads it as flesh grown fine, like a small boy's.

sources.quote: רטפש. הוא מלה מורכבת מן רטוב ומן פש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רטפש is built from רטוב and פש.

sources.quote: וְהַפּוֹתְרוֹ בִּלְשׁוֹן ׳רֶפֶשׁ׳, וְאוֹמֵר הַטֵּי״ת נִתּוֹסְפָה בּוֹ, כְּמוֹ ״נִצְטַדָּק״ (בראשית מד:טז) – טוֹעֶה הוּא מְאֹד
sources.says: Rashi says anyone who reads it from רפש with an added tet is badly mistaken.

sources.quote: והתרגום אמר איתקליש בשריה, שחזר בשרו דק מנער קטן
sources.says: Ramban reports the Aramaic translation: the flesh became fine like a small boy's.

sources.quote: וכן: רטפש. ועניינו רך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says רטפש also has no partner in Scripture and means soft.

33:27.headline: He looks at people, walks among them, or lines them up
33:27.body: Ralbag and Ramban read ישר as "look": the healed man looks at others and confesses. Metzudat Zion reads it as "walk". Rashi says he gathers rows of people, and Ibn Ezra says "go around", like a city wall, a שור.

sources.quote: ישור. הוא מענין הבט' והשגחה
sources.says: Ralbag says ישר means looking.

sources.quote: ישור על אנשים, יביט על האנשים
sources.says: Ramban says he looks at the people.

sources.quote: ישור. יצעד וילך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means he steps and walks.

sources.quote: יַעֲשֶׂה שׁוּרוֹת שֶׁל אֲנָשִׁים
sources.says: Rashi says he makes rows of people and confesses before his Maker.

sources.quote: על כן נקראת החומה שור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means going around, which is why a wall is called שור.

34:6.headline: Job calls his judge a liar, or his hope fails
34:6.body: כזב means a lie, but also a spring that runs dry. Rashi reads Job as calling his judge a liar, while Metzudat Zion reads "I am cut off" from justice and Ramban reads "my hope failed".

sources.quote: אֲכַזִּיב שׁוֹפְטִי, שֶׁלֹּא דָנַנִּי אֱמֶת
sources.says: Rashi says Job accuses his judge of lying, since he did not judge him truly.

sources.quote: אכזב. ענין הפסקה כמו אשר לא יכזבו מימיו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means stopping, like a spring whose waters do not fail.

sources.quote: כי תוחלתי נכזבה במשפטי
sources.says: Ramban says Job means his hope for justice was let down.

34:9.headline: When a man pleases God, or runs with him
34:9.body: ברצתו can come from רצון, "favor", or from רוץ, "run". Ibn Ezra reads "when he does God's will", while Malbim allows "running with God", and one version of the Targum also reads "in his running".

sources.quote: ברצותו - כאשר יעשה רצון אלהים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means when a person does God's will.

sources.quote: ברצות, מענין רצון, או מענין הליכה וריצה
sources.says: Malbim says it comes either from "will" or from walking and running.

sources.quote: בְּמִרְהֲטֵיהּ עִם אֱלָהָא
sources.says: One version of the Targum translates "in his running with God".

34:16.headline: Not "understanding" but a command: understand!
34:16.body: בינה usually means "understanding", a noun. Rashi says here it is a command, "understand!", and that this is why it is stressed on its first syllable, unlike the noun.

sources.quote: בִּינָה זוֹ אֵינָהּ שֵׁם דָּבָר, אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן צִוּוּי
sources.says: Rashi says this בינה is not a noun but a command, with the stress on the ב.

34:17.headline: Can a hater of justice rule, or be healed?
34:17.body: חבש means to bind: a jailer binds prisoners, and a healer binds wounds. Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra read "rule", from the jailer, while a midrash reads "heal": one who hates justice has no cure for his wound.

sources.quote: ענין ממשלה ע״ש שהוא חובש במאסר את המחוייב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means ruling, because a ruler locks up the guilty.

sources.quote: יחבוש - ימשול כדרך יעצור יורש עצר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra also reads it as "rule".

sources.quote: ואין חבושה אלא רפואה שנאמר ומחבש לעצבותם
sources.says: The midrash says חבישה means healing, so one who hates justice has no cure.

34:20.headline: "At midnight" recalls the night Egypt's firstborn died
34:20.body: Elihu says people die suddenly at midnight. Rashi and the midrash hear the plague of the firstborn in Egypt, which struck at midnight, and the Targum names both Sodom and Egypt.

sources.quote: וַחֲצוֹת לָיְלָה. כְּמוֹ שֶׁעָשָׂה לְמִצְרַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says it is like what God did to Egypt.

sources.quote: וּפַלְגוּת לֵילְיָא מִתְרַגְפִין מִצְרָאֵי
sources.says: The Targum says the Egyptians were shaken at midnight, and the people of Sodom died in an instant.

sources.quote: אָמַר אֱלִיהוּא (איוב לד, כ): רֶגַע יָמֻתוּ וַחֲצוֹת לָיְלָה
sources.says: The midrash reads Elihu's words into the night of the plague, when all Egypt began to cry out.

34:24.headline: God crushes the mighty, or the mighty did evil
34:24.body: ירע here means "he shatters", as in "break them with a rod of iron". The midrash also hears רע, "evil": the generation of the Flood did evil beyond measure, and God put Noah's sons in their place.

sources.quote: יָרֹעַ. יְרוֹצֵץ
sources.says: Rashi says it means "he will crush".

sources.quote: ירוע. ירוצץ כמו תרועם בשבט ברזל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means crushing, like breaking with a rod of iron.

sources.quote: הֵרֵעוּ אַנְשֵׁי דוֹר הַמַּבּוּל בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם הָרָעִים
sources.says: The midrash reads it as the people of the Flood doing evil, with Noah's sons set in their place.

34:26.headline: God struck them down, or waited till their measure filled
34:26.body: ספק can mean to strike, as in clapping the hands. Metzudat Zion reads it that way, while a midrash reads it as "their fill": the wicked do not fall until their measure of sin is full.

sources.quote: ספקם. ענין הכאה כמו ויספוק את כפיו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means striking, like Balak striking his hands together.

sources.quote: אין הרשע נופל עד שתתמלא סאתו שנאמר (איוב לד כו) תחת רשעים ספקם
sources.says: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa says the wicked do not fall until their measure is full, citing this verse.

sources.quote: סְפָקָם. לְאַנְשֵׁי סְדוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says God struck the people of Sodom.

34:29.headline: Not "who can condemn" but "who can stir up trouble"
34:29.body: ירשע usually means "condemn". Metzudat Zion, Ramban and Ibn Ezra read it here as "shake" or "disturb", the opposite of God giving quiet, as in Saul who "troubled" his enemies wherever he turned.

sources.quote: ירשיע. יחריד ויבלבל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means to frighten and throw into confusion.

sources.quote: ירשיע, כמו ירעיש
sources.says: Ramban says it means "make tremble".

sources.quote: והעניין הפך ישקיט
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word means to shake, the opposite of "give quiet" in the same verse.

34:31.headline: I will not destroy, or I will not take a pledge
34:31.body: חבל can mean "destroy" or "take a pledge" from a debtor. Ramban gives both, and the midrash has God say about Sodom, "I do not take a pledge from them", as in the law of the pledged cloak.

sources.quote: לא אחבול, מן והבל את מעשה ידיך, או מן לא יחבול רחים
sources.says: Ramban says it is either "destroy" or "take a pledge", as in the law against taking a millstone.

sources.quote: לֹא אֶחְבֹּל, אֵינִי מְמַשְׁכְּנָם
sources.says: The midrash reads it as God saying he does not take pledges from the people of Sodom.

sources.quote: אחבול. אשחית
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means "I will destroy".

34:36.headline: "My father", or "I wish"?
34:36.body: אבי usually means "my father". Rashi reads Elihu calling God "my Father", and also brings a reading "my wish", from אבה, "want", which the Targum and Metzudat Zion follow.

sources.quote: אַתָּה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אָב לַכֹּל
sources.says: Rashi says Elihu addresses God as Father of all, then brings Menachem's reading "my wish".

sources.quote: אבי. ענין תאוה ורצון כמו לא אבה יבמי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means desire, from "he did not want".

sources.quote: והקרוב אלי: שיאמר אבי למקום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra knows the "my wish" reading but prefers "my Father", said to God.

sources.quote: צָבֵינָא דְיִתְבְּחַר אִיוֹב
sources.says: The Targum translates "I wish that Job be tested".

34:37.headline: Job claps, piles on words, or spreads doubt
34:37.body: The commentators disagree on ישפוק. Ralbag says Job claps his hands in protest, Rashi and Metzudat Zion say he speaks more than enough, and Ramban reads ספק as the Sages use it, "doubt": Job casts doubt on faith in God.

sources.quote: יספוק כפיו ויתרעם
sources.says: Ralbag says Job claps his hands and complains.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן רוֹב דְּבָרִים וַהֲרָמַת קוֹל
sources.says: Rashi says it means many words and a raised voice.

sources.quote: די הספוק ור״ל הרבה מאד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means "his fill", that is, very much.

sources.quote: ולדעתי יספוק זה מן הלשון הידוע בדברי חכמינו ז"ל, ספק חשכה ספק אינה חשיכה
sources.says: Ramban reads it from the Sages' word for doubt: Job raises doubts about faith in God.

35:2.headline: Job is accused of claiming to be more righteous than God
35:2.body: מאל could mean "from God". Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Ralbag read it as "more than God". Elihu says Job claimed his righteousness was greater than God's.

sources.quote: אֲשֶׁר אָמַרְתָּ צִדְקִי מִשֶּׁל הַבּוֹרֵא
sources.says: Rashi says Job claimed his righteousness was greater than the Creator's.

sources.quote: צדקי מאל. שאני צדיק יותר מאל
sources.says: Ralbag says it means: I am more righteous than God.

sources.quote: יותר הוא צדקי מצדק אל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means: my righteousness is greater than God's.

35:9.headline: The oppressed, or the oppressors?
35:9.body: עשוקים looks like "the oppressed". Rashi reads it as the oppressors, who make people cry out. Ralbag and Metzudat David read it as the oppressed, whose oppressors make them cry out.

sources.quote: מֵרֹב עֲשׁוּקִים. שֶׁהֵם עוֹשְׁקִים
sources.says: Rashi says the עשוקים here are the ones who oppress.

sources.quote: שימצאו רוב עשוקים יזעיקו אותם עושקיהם
sources.says: Ralbag says many are oppressed, and their oppressors make them cry out.

35:10.headline: Songs in the night, or cutting down the wicked by night?
35:10.body: זמרות usually means songs. Rashi reads it as pruning, as in "do not prune your vineyard": God cuts off the wicked at night, as He did to Egypt. Ralbag and the Targum keep the songs of praise.

sources.quote: נוֹתֵן זְמִירוֹת. כְּמוֹ ״כַּרְמְךָ לֹא תִזְמֹר״
sources.says: Rashi says the word is like "do not prune your vineyard" in Leviticus 25:4.

sources.quote: שֶׁמַּכְרִית אֶת הָרְשָׁעִים בַּלַּיְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says God cuts off the wicked at night.

sources.quote: זמירות. דברי שבח
sources.says: Ralbag says זמירות are words of praise.

sources.quote: דִמְסַדְרִין אַנְגְלֵי מְרוֹמָא קֳדָמוֹי תּוּשְׁבְּחָן בְּלֵילְיָא
sources.says: The Targum says the angels on high set out praises before God at night.

35:11.headline: "He teaches us", with a missing letter
35:11.body: מלפנו means "He teaches us". The commentators say it is missing an א: it is מאלפנו, from the word Elihu used in "I will teach you wisdom". God taught people more than the animals.

sources.quote: מלפנו - חסר אל"ף והוא מן: ואאלפך חכמה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is missing an א and comes from "I will teach you wisdom" (Job 33:33).

sources.quote: מלפנו. כמו מאלפנו באל״ף והוא ענין למוד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is like מאלפנו with an א, meaning teaching.

sources.quote: מְלַמְּדֵנוּ חָכְמָה יוֹתֵר מִבְּהֵמוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says God teaches us more wisdom than the animals.

35:15.headline: God's אף: His anger, or His face?
35:15.body: אף usually means anger, and the Targum reads it so. Metzudat Zion reads it as face, as in "by the sweat of your face". Then the verse says God turned His face away.

sources.quote: אפו. פניו כמו בזעת אפיך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אפו means His face, as in Genesis 3:19.

sources.quote: לזה הסר פניו והסתירו
sources.says: Metzudat David says God turned His face away and hid it.

sources.quote: כְּאִלוּ לָא הֲוָה אַסְעַר רוּגְזֵיהּ
sources.says: The Targum translates: as if His anger had not raged.

36:1.headline: Elihu's fourth speech is an extra
36:1.body: Rashi cites Rabbi Moshe HaDarshan: Elihu gave three answers, one for each of Job's three friends. This fourth one is an addition, so the verse says ויסף, "he added".

sources.quote: רָאִיתִי בְּטַעֲמֵי רַבִּי מֹשֶׁה הַדַּרְשָׁן, שֶׁלְּפִיכָךְ אָמַר שְׁלֹשָׁה מַעֲנוֹת, כְּנֶגֶד שְׁלֹשֶׁת רֵיעֵי אִיּוֹב. וְזֶה רְבִיעִי, לְפִיכָךְ נִקְרָא תּוֹסֶפֶת
sources.says: Rashi cites Rabbi Moshe HaDarshan that Elihu's three answers match the three friends, and this fourth is called an addition.

sources.quote: כי לא בא עתה רק להוסיף דברים לחזק מאמריו הראשונים
sources.says: Metzudat David says Elihu now only adds words to strengthen what he said before.

36:2.headline: Wait for me a little, or crown me a little
36:2.body: Rashi says this whole line is Aramaic: "wait for me a little and I will tell you". Ibn Ezra offers another reading from כתר, "crown": give me a little honor and listen.

sources.quote: כֻּלּוֹ לְשׁוֹן אֲרַמִּי הוּא: הוֹחֵל לִי מְעַט וַאֲגִידְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says the whole phrase is Aramaic and means "wait for me a little and I will tell you".

sources.quote: ויתכן היות כתרו סבבו כי כתר ועטרה קרובים בעניין
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says כתר may mean to surround, close to the idea of a crown.

sources.quote: ויהיה פירושו: כתר לי שים לי כבוד מעט
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it could then mean "give me a little honor".

36:14.headline: Not holy ones: people given to harlotry
36:14.body: קדשים looks like "holy ones", but the Targum and Metzudat Zion read it as people given to harlotry, as in Deuteronomy 23:18. The wicked die young, a shameful death like theirs.

sources.quote: בקדשים. הם המזומנים למשכב הזנות כמו ולא יהיה קדש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says קדשים are those set aside for harlotry, as in Deuteronomy 23:18.

sources.quote: וְחַיַתְהוֹן הֵיךְ מָרֵי זָנוּ
sources.says: The Targum says their life ends like that of harlots.

sources.quote: ר״ל במיתה מנוולת כמותם ושוה להם
sources.says: Metzudat David says they die a disgraceful death like theirs.

36:16.headline: God lures Job, but away from death
36:16.body: הסית usually means to lure someone into sin, but the Talmud notes that here God lures a person away from death, out of Gehinnom. Ramban says it is called luring because it came against Job's will.

sources.quote: מִדַּת בָּשָׂר וָדָם אָדָם מֵסִית אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ מִדַּרְכֵי חַיִּים לְדַרְכֵי מִיתָה, וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מֵסִית אֶת הָאָדָם מִדַּרְכֵי מִיתָה לְדַרְכֵי חַיִּים
sources.says: The Talmud says people lure others from life to death, but God lures people from death to life.

sources.quote: הֲסִיתְךָ וְהִדִּיחֲךָ מִגֵּיהִנֹּם, שֶׁפִּיהָ צַר וְתַחְתֶּיהָ רָחָב
sources.says: Rashi says God drew Job away from Gehinnom, which is narrow at the mouth and wide below.

sources.quote: כי מפני שבא לו שלא כרצונו יקרא הסתה
sources.says: Ramban says it is called luring because it happened against Job's will.

36:18.headline: Piling up words against God, or having more than enough
36:18.body: Rashi and the Metzudot had this word spelled בשפק, and Rashi reads it as Job piling up words against God, as in Job 34:37. The Metzudot read it as בספק, "plenty": comfort can tempt a person to kick against God.

sources.quote: בְּשָׂפֶק זֶה אֲשֶׁר תִּשְׂפֹּק, וְתֶרֶב אֲמָרֶיךָ לָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi links the word to Job multiplying his words against God.

sources.quote: בשפק. כמו בספק בסמ״ך וענינו די הספיק והצורך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is spelled for בספק and means having enough of what one needs.

sources.quote: פן יסיתך יצרך לבעט במקום בעבור די ספוק צרכך
sources.says: Metzudat David says plenty might tempt Job to kick against God.

36:19.headline: Your wealth, or your cry for help
36:19.body: שוע can mean a rich noble or a cry for help. Ibn Ezra and Ralbag read "your wealth", while Ramban reads "your cry", asking whether God will accept it.

sources.quote: היערך שועך - הוא ההון ובעל ההון קרא שוע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שוע means wealth, and a wealthy man is called שוע.

sources.quote: שועך. עושרך והוא מענין ולא ניכר שוע לפני דל
sources.says: Ralbag says שועך means your wealth, as in Job 34:19.

sources.quote: היערך שועך, כמו שועתך
sources.says: Ramban says שועך means your cry for help.

36:19.headline: Gold, or trouble
36:19.body: Ralbag reads בצר as one word, "gold", as in Job 22:25. Rashi and Ramban read it as ב־צר, "in distress".

sources.quote: בצר. זהב מגזירת והיה שדי בצריך
sources.says: Ralbag says בצר means gold, as in Job 22:25.

sources.quote: לא בצר, בבוא עליך צר ומצוק
sources.says: Ramban reads it as distress coming upon Job.

sources.quote: שֶׁלֹּא תְּבוֹאֲךָ שׁוּם צָרָה
sources.says: Rashi reads it as no trouble coming to Job.

36:30.headline: Light that means rain
36:30.body: אור normally means light, but the Targum and Metzudat Zion read it as rain, linked to יורה, the early rain. Ramban cites Rabbi Yochanan that every "light" in Elihu's speech means rain, though Ibn Ezra prefers plain light.

sources.quote: הָא פְרַס עֲלוֹי מִטְרָא
sources.says: The Targum translates: He spread His rain over it.

sources.quote: אורו. ענינו המטר וכן כל אור האמור בענין והוא מלשון יורה ומלקוש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אור here means rain, from יורה, the early rain.

sources.quote: אמר ר' יוחנן כל אורה הנאמרה באליהוא בירידת הגשם הכתוב מדבר
sources.says: Ramban cites Rabbi Yochanan that every "light" in Elihu's words speaks of rain.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני: כי הן פרש עליו אורו כי הוא כמשמעו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he thinks the word means light in its plain sense.

36:32.headline: Clouds the size of a palm, or hands full of theft
36:32.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read כפים as clouds, from Elijah's "cloud as small as a man's palm". The Talmud reads it as hands: because of theft, the rain is held back.

sources.quote: כפים. כן יקראו העננים לפי שבתחלה נראה ככף היד כענין שנאמר עב קטנה ככף איש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says clouds are called כפים because at first they look like the palm of a hand.

sources.quote: עַל כַּפַּיִם. עַל הֶעָנָנִים
sources.says: Rashi says כפים means clouds.

sources.quote: אֵין הַגְּשָׁמִים נֶעֱצָרִין אֶלָּא בַּעֲוֹן גָּזֵל, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״עַל כַּפַּיִם כִּסָּה אוֹר״
sources.says: The Talmud says rain is held back only because of theft, reading כפים as hands.

36:33.headline: Its thunder, or a friend who prays
36:33.body: רעו can mean "its shout", from תרועה, and Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion hear thunder announcing the rain. The Talmud hears "his friend": when rain is held back, go to someone who knows how to whisper prayers.

sources.quote: רעו - כמו תרועתו והוא הרעם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says רעו means its shout, the thunder.

sources.quote: רעו. מלשון תרועה והוא קול הרעם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רעו comes from תרועה and is the sound of thunder.

sources.quote: יֵלְכוּ אֵצֶל מִי שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ לִלְחוֹשׁ, דִּכְתִיב: ״יַגִּיד עָלָיו רֵעוֹ״
sources.says: The Talmud reads רעו as a fellow who knows how to whisper prayers.

37:1.headline: The heart leaps like a locust
37:1.body: ויתר is a rare verb for leaping. Rashi and the midrash compare it to locusts that "leap upon the earth" (Leviticus 11:21). Elihu's heart jumps from its place in fear.

sources.quote: וְיִתַּר. וְיִקְפֹּץ, כְּמוֹ ״לְנַתֵּר בָּהֶם עַל הָאָרֶץ״
sources.says: Rashi says ויתר means it leaps, as in Leviticus 11:21.

sources.quote: מַהוּ וְיִתַּר, וְקָפַץ
sources.says: The midrash asks what ויתר means and answers: it leapt.

37:2.headline: The rumble from His mouth: thunder, or Torah?
37:2.body: Ralbag says הגה here is a sound, the thunder. The midrash reads הגה as Torah study, and learns that God teaches new law in the heavenly court every day.

sources.quote: והגה. הוא שם מענין הגייה והרצון בו וקול והוא הרעם
sources.says: Ralbag says הגה means a sound, the thunder.

sources.quote: אֵין כָּל יוֹם וָיוֹם שֶׁאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְחַדֵּשׁ הֲלָכָה בְּבֵית דִּין שֶׁל מַעְלָה
sources.says: The midrash says God renews law in the heavenly court every day.

sources.quote: וְאֵין הֶגֶה אֶלָּא תוֹרָה
sources.says: The midrash says הגה means Torah.

37:4.headline: The heel word here means holding back
37:4.body: עקב can mean a heel, trickery, or an end. Here it means God does not hold back the rain. Ramban suggests the ק stands for כ, making it עכב, to delay.

sources.quote: עקב לשון מניעה, כמו ולא יעקבם כי ישמע קולו
sources.says: Sekhel Tov lists the senses of עקב and says that here it means holding back.

sources.quote: בחלוף הוא הקו"ף לכ"ף, כאשר יתחלף במלת כובע וקובע
sources.says: Ramban says the ק may stand for כ, as in כובע and קובע, both meaning helmet.

37:6.headline: Snow told to fall on the earth, or to become it
37:6.body: הוא is a rare form of "be". Ibn Ezra reads it as "be on the earth": God tells the snow to fall. A midrash reads "become earth": the dry land was made from snow under God's throne. Maimonides found that saying astonishing.

sources.quote: כי לשלג יאמר - להיות בארץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God tells the snow to be on the earth.

sources.quote: מִשֶּׁלֶג שֶׁתַּחַת כִּסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד, לָקַח וְזָרַק עַל הַמַּיִם וְנִקְפְּאוּ הַמַּיִם וְנַעֲשָׂה עֲפַר הָאָרֶץ
sources.says: The midrash says God threw snow from under His throne onto the water, and it froze into the dust of the earth.

sources.quote: שמעולם לא ראיתי מופלאים מהם בדברי אף אחד מן ההולכים אחר תורת משה רבינו
sources.says: Maimonides says he never saw stranger words from anyone who follows the Torah of Moses.

37:7.headline: Rain seals people indoors, or each man signs his own record
37:7.body: Ralbag reads יחתום as "seals up": heavy rain shuts everyone inside. The midrash reads it as signing: at death a person's deeds are read out, and he signs that they are true.

sources.quote: יחתום. יסגור ויסתום עד שלא יוכל איש לצאת לחוץ מרוב המטר
sources.says: Ralbag says it means God shuts people in so no one can go out for all the rain.

sources.quote: אוֹמְרִים לוֹ: חֲתוֹם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (איוב לז ז): ״בְּיַד כָּל אָדָם יַחְתּוֹם
sources.says: The Sifrei says that after a person's deeds are listed before him, he is told to sign, from this verse.

sources.quote: הָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ חוֹתֵם כְּתַב יָדוֹ בְּיוֹם מוֹתוֹ עַל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁעָבַר
sources.says: Rashi says on the day of his death a person signs in his own hand for the sins he did.

37:9.headline: Cold from מזרים: a storehouse, the stars, or scattering winds?
37:9.body: מזרים appears only here. Rashi says it is the name of a storehouse of cold. Metzudat Zion reads it as מזלות, constellations, with ר for ל. Ralbag reads it as the north winds that scatter.

sources.quote: וּמִמְּזָרִים. אוֹצָר יֵשׁ וּשְׁמוֹ מְזָרִים
sources.says: Rashi says there is a storehouse named מזרים.

sources.quote: וממזרים. מזלות וכן התוציא מזרות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מזרים means constellations, as in Job 38:32.

sources.quote: שכבר יהיה קור חזק מן הרוחות המזרים ומפזרים האידים והם הרוחות הצפוניות
sources.says: Ralbag says the cold comes from the scattering winds, the north winds.

37:11.headline: The cloud of His light is a cloud of rain
37:11.body: אורו means "His light". Rashi reads it as "His rain". Midrash Lekach Tov uses this verse to show that water is sometimes called light.

sources.quote: עֲנַן אוֹרוֹ. עֲנַן מְטָרוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the cloud of His light means the cloud of His rain.

sources.quote: וכן מצינו בהרבה מקומות נקראו אור. שנא' ואורו על כנפות הארץ (איוב לז ג). ואומר יפיץ ענן אורו
sources.says: Lekach Tov says that in many places water is called light, citing this verse.

37:16.headline: Openings in the clouds, or the scales they are weighed on?
37:16.body: מפלשי appears only here. Rashi links it to an open alley, מבוי מפולש. Metzudat Zion reads it as מפרשי, spreadings. A midrash reads it as weight: even the force of the rain is measured.

sources.quote: מִפְלְשֵׂי עָב. גִּילּוּי עָב, לְשׁוֹן מָבוֹי מְפוּלָּשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says it means the opening of the cloud, like an open alley.

sources.quote: מפלשי. כמו מפרשי בחלוף הלמ״ד ברי״ש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is like מפרשי, with ל in place of ר.

sources.ref: Otzar Midrashim, Midrash on Psalms, Midrash on Psalm 118 3
sources.quote: מהו מפלשי עב, אפילו גבורות גשמים במשקל, ואין מפלש אלא משקל
sources.says: The midrash says even the power of the rain is by weight, since מפלש means weight.

37:18.headline: The sky is as hard as a metal mirror
37:18.body: ראי, a mirror, appears only here. Rashi says it is the mirror women look into. Mirrors were cast from metal, so the sky is pictured as hard and shining.

sources.quote: כִּרְאִי מוּצָק. כִּרְאִי שֶׁהַנָּשִׁים רוֹאוֹת בּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says ראי is the mirror women look into.

sources.quote: כראי מוצק. כמראה הנתך
sources.says: Ralbag says it is like a cast mirror.

37:18.headline: Why the skies are called שחקים
37:18.body: Ibn Ezra stops to explain the name. The upper air is called שחקים because it is fine, like spice ground thin (Exodus 30:36).

sources.quote: ונקראו כן בעבור היותם אויר דק והוא מן ושחקת ממנה הדק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are called שחקים because they are thin air, from Exodus 30:36.

37:20.headline: Revealed to God, or swallowed up for saying too much?
37:20.body: Rashi first reads יבלע as "revealed": whatever a person says reaches God at once. The sages read it as "swallowed up": one who tries to tell all of God's praise is uprooted from the world.

sources.quote: כִּי יְבֻלָּע. יְגֻלֶּה אֵלָיו מִיָּד
sources.says: Rashi says it means it is revealed to Him at once.

sources.quote: אם מבקש אדם לומר שבחו של הקב"ה יותר מדאי מתבלע מן העולם
sources.says: Rabbi Abahu says one who tries to say too much of God's praise is swallowed from the world.

37:22.headline: From the north, or from what is hidden away?
37:22.body: צפון means north, and also hidden. Metzudat Zion hears both: gold comes from the north, and is hidden. Rashi reads that good gold is stored away for those who come to God's commands.

sources.quote: מצפון. ענין טמון ונסתר ואחז בלשון מליצה נאותה על שזהב בא מפאת הצפון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מצפון means hidden, and the poet chose it because gold comes from the north.

sources.quote: נִצְפַּן הַזָּהָב הַטּוֹב לְאוֹתָן שֶׁיֵּאָתִיּוּ אֶת עַצְמָן לְמִצְווֹת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says the good gold is hidden away for those who bring themselves to God's commandments.

37:23.headline: Too great to reach, or never heavy-handed with us?
37:23.body: Ibn Ezra reads: we cannot find God, but His deeds show great power. Rashi and the midrash read: we never found God using great force on us. He asks only small offerings, like a handful of flour.

sources.quote: שדי לא מצאנוהו - נדע במעשיו שהוא שגיא כח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says we know from His deeds that God is great in power.

sources.quote: וְכַפָּרַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת שָׂם בְּדָבָר מוּעָט לְפִי הַיְּכֹלֶת
sources.says: Rashi says God set atonement in small things, as much as people can give.

sources.quote: אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּא בִּטְרָחוֹת עִם יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: The midrash says God does not come to Israel with heavy demands.

38:1.headline: Job complained of a storm; God answers him from one
38:1.body: In 9:17 Job said God crushes him בשערה, with a storm, and the Talmud says God answers from a storm to match. Rashi also hears שערות, hairs: God tells Job to count his hairs, since each has its own root, so how could He confuse Job with an enemy?

sources.quote: בִּסְעָרָה חֵרַף – דִּכְתִיב: ״אֲשֶׁר בִּשְׂעָרָה יְשׁוּפֵנִי״
sources.says: The Talmud says Job blasphemed with a storm, citing Job 9:17, and was answered from a storm.

sources.quote: מְנֵה שְׂעָרוֹת שֶׁלְּךָ, וַאֲשִׁיבְךָ דְּבָרִים כְּנֶגְדָּן
sources.says: Rashi reads God as saying: count your hairs, and I will answer you about them.

sources.quote: כָּל שֵׂעָר וְשֵׂעָר שֶׁבָּרֹאשׁ פִּלַּגְתִּי לוֹ תְּעָלָה
sources.says: Rashi says God made a separate groove for every hair, and that this is what "from the storm" means.

38:6.headline: The cornerstone God threw into the sea
38:6.body: Rashi and the Talmud say God threw a stone into the middle of the sea and founded the whole world on it. Ramban calls it the Foundation Stone the sages speak of, or a figure for the earth's center point.

sources.quote: יָרָה אֶבֶן פִּנָּתָהּ. בְּאֶמְצַע הַיָּם, וּמִשָּׁם נִשְׁתַּת כָּל הָעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says the cornerstone was thrown into the middle of the sea, and the whole world was founded from there.

sources.quote: אֶבֶן יָרָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בַּיָּם, מִמֶּנּוּ נִשְׁתַּת הָעוֹלָם
sources.says: The Talmud says God threw a stone into the sea, and the world was founded from it.

sources.quote: אבן פנתה, משל לנקודת האמצעי
sources.says: Ramban says the cornerstone is a figure for the center point, and that the sages call it the Foundation Stone.

38:7.headline: Do the morning stars really sing?
38:7.body: Ibn Ezra says the stars sing by circling around the earth. Maimonides lists this verse among the sages' sources for his view that the heavens are living bodies that praise God.

sources.quote: ברן יחד - בעבור שיסובו סביבות נקודות הארץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they sing together in that they circle around the earth.

sources.quote: הרי גם הם אמרו במפורש שהשמים הם גופים חיים
sources.says: Maimonides cites this verse and concludes that the sages too held the heavens are living bodies.

38:10.headline: Trenches around the sea, or a decree over it?
38:10.body: Rashi reads it as breaking ground: God dug trenches around the sea to hold it in, as in Joshua 7:5. Ramban cites the Targum, which reads it as "I decreed", since שבר can mean to rule on something.

sources.quote: עָשִׂיתִי לוֹ שְׁבָרִים סָבִיב, לְעַכְּבוֹ בְּתוֹכָם
sources.says: Rashi says God made trenches around the sea to keep it inside them.

sources.quote: גזר ואשבור מלשון פסק וגזר דין
sources.says: Ramban says the Targum reads ואשבור as deciding and decreeing a judgment.

38:13.headline: The "wings" of the earth are its far edges
38:13.body: כנף first means a bird's wing, then the corner of a garment. Maimonides says it is borrowed here for the far ends of the earth, and Rashi pictures God gripping those corners like a cloak and shaking the wicked out.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 43
sources.quote: אחר כך הושאל לחלקים הנידחים ביותר של הארץ הנושבת ולקצותיה המרוחקים ממקומותינו
sources.says: Maimonides says כנף was borrowed for the most distant parts of the inhabited earth, citing this verse.

sources.quote: כְּאָדָם שֶׁאוֹחֵז בְּכַנְפֵי הַטַּלִּית וּמְנַעֲרָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says it is like a person who holds the corners of a cloak and shakes it out.

38:14.headline: Everyone is stamped from Adam's seal, yet no two match
38:14.body: Metzudat Zion says חותם here means a shape or form. The Talmud reads the verse as showing God's greatness: coins struck from one seal all match, but God stamps every person with Adam's seal and no two are alike.

sources.quote: חותם. צורה כמו חותם תכנית
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חותם means a form.

sources.quote: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא טוֹבֵעַ כׇּל אָדָם בְּחוֹתָמוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן וְאֵין אֶחָד מֵהֶן דּוֹמֶה לַחֲבֵירוֹ
sources.says: The Talmud says God stamps every person with the seal of the first man, and none is like another.

38:15.headline: The wicked lose daylight, or the hidden first light?
38:15.body: Ramban reads אורם as the morning light of the verses before. The Talmud reads it as the light made on the first day, by which a person could see across the whole world, which God hid once He saw the wicked generations.

sources.quote: וימנע מרשעים אורם, אור הבקר והשחר הנזכרים
sources.says: Ramban says their light is the morning and dawn light mentioned before.

sources.quote: אוֹר שֶׁבָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּיוֹם רִאשׁוֹן, אָדָם צוֹפֶה בּוֹ מִסּוֹף הָעוֹלָם וְעַד סוֹפוֹ
sources.says: The Talmud says the light of the first day let a person see from one end of the world to the other, and God hid it from the wicked.

38:28.headline: Drops of dew, a word with no match
38:28.body: Ramban follows the Targum, which renders אגלי as drops of dew, and says the word has no match. Rashi reads it as גלי טל with an extra א, or as אגני, basins of dew, with ל in place of נ.

sources.quote: והתרגום אמר: רסיסי טלא, בלא חבר, והוא הנכון
sources.says: Ramban says the Targum's drops of dew is right, and the word has no match.

sources.quote: לָשׁוֹן אַחֵר: אֶגְלֵי. כְּמוֹ אַגְנֵי טָל, כְּמִין אֲגָנוֹת
sources.says: Rashi offers that אגלי is like אגני, basins that hold the dew.

38:31.headline: Can you tie כימה's knots, or its sweet fruits?
38:31.body: Metzudat Zion reads מעדנות as knots and bonds, a sense also found in the Mishnah. Ralbag and Ibn Ezra read it as delights: the sweet fruits that this star group brings on.

sources.quote: מעדנות. ענין קשורים וכן וילך אליו אגג מעדנות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says מעדנות means bonds, as in 1 Samuel 15:32.

sources.quote: מעדנות. שם מיני תענוגים שימצאו בסבת כימה
sources.says: Ralbag says מעדנות are delights that come about because of כימה.

sources.quote: וכימה תקשר הפירות, שהם המעדנות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says כימה ties up the fruits, which are the delights.

38:36.headline: The kidneys are called טחות because fat coats them
38:36.body: Rashi says בטחות means the kidneys. Metzudat Zion and Ramban explain the name: they are טחות, plastered over, because fat covers them, as in Leviticus 14:42.

sources.quote: בַּטֻּחוֹת. אֵלּוּ הַכְּלָיוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says טחות are the kidneys.

sources.quote: בטוחות. בכליות ויקראו כן ע״ש שהם טוחות ומכסות בחלב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the kidneys are called this because they are coated and covered with fat.

sources.quote: ונקראו טוחות על שהם טוחות מן החלב אשר עליהם
sources.says: Ramban says they are called טוחות because they are coated by the fat on them.

38:36.headline: שכוי: the rooster, or the watchful heart?
38:36.body: The Talmud says that in a distant region people called a rooster שכוי, and reads the verse that way. Metzudat Zion says it is the heart, named for looking ahead, from the Aramaic word for watching.

sources.quote: וְלַתַּרְנְגוֹל שֶׂכְוִי
sources.says: The Talmud reports that in one region a rooster was called שכוי, and reads this verse as about the rooster.

sources.quote: לַשֶּׂכְוִי. זֶה תַּרְנְגוֹל; לְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים
sources.says: Rashi says שכוי is the rooster, and gives a second view that it is the heart.

sources.quote: לשכוי. הלב נקרא כן לפי שהוא צופה ומביט את הנולדות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the heart is called this because it looks out and foresees what will happen.

38:37.headline: Who counts the skies, or makes them shine like sapphire?
38:37.body: Ralbag reads יספר as counting, as in Psalms 22:18. Metzudat Zion and Ramban read it from ספיר, sapphire: God makes the skies bright and clear like the gem.

sources.quote: מי יספר. מענין מנין ומספר כמו אספר כל עצמותי
sources.says: Ralbag says יספר means counting.

sources.quote: יספר. מל׳ ספיר והוא שם אבן יקר הבהיר מאד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from ספיר, a very bright precious stone.

sources.quote: מי שם אותם כספירים בחכמתו
sources.says: Ramban says God set the skies like sapphires in His wisdom.

39:4.headline: The young grow strong here; they do not dream
39:4.body: The root חלם usually means to dream. Rashi says here it means to grow strong, and Ralbag links it to Isaiah 38:16, "heal me and let me live".

sources.quote: יַחְלְמוּ. יֶחֱזְקוּ
sources.says: Rashi says יחלמו means they grow strong.

sources.quote: מענין בריאות והוא מענין תחלימני והחייני
sources.says: Ralbag says the word is about health, as in Isaiah 38:16.

39:5.headline: Two names for the wild donkey: Hebrew and Aramaic
39:5.body: The verse names the wild donkey twice: פרא, and the rare ערוד. Metzudat Zion notes that the Aramaic translation of פרא is ערודא, so the second name is the Aramaic one.

sources.quote: ערוד. פרא למוד מדבר (שם ב) תרגומו כערודא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says that where Jeremiah 2:24 has פרא, the Aramaic translation has ערודא.

sources.quote: עָרוֹד. חֲמוֹר הַבָּר
sources.says: Rashi says ערוד is the wild donkey.

39:13.headline: A bird named for its song, or its joy
39:13.body: Rashi says רננים is a large bird, the one the sages call בר יוכני. Ibn Ezra guesses it is named for its sweet voice, and Metzudat David for the joy it takes in its beautiful wings.

sources.quote: כֵּן שֵׁם עוֹף גָּדוֹל רְנָנִים, וּלְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה קָרוּי בַּר יוֹכְנִי
sources.says: Rashi says רננים is a large bird, called בר יוכני in the language of the Mishnah.

sources.quote: שם עוף, אולי נקרא כן, בעבור נועם קולו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a bird, perhaps named for the sweetness of its voice.

sources.quote: ונקרא רננים ע״ש שתשמח ותרנן ביופי כנפיה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is called רננים because it rejoices and sings over the beauty of its wings.

39:15.headline: A foot crushes the eggs, as Gideon wrung out the fleece
39:15.body: Metzudat Zion says the word means to crush something until what is inside comes out. Ralbag links it to Judges 6:38, where Gideon wrung the water out of the fleece.

sources.quote: תזורה. ענין מעוך להוציא הבלוע
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means crushing to squeeze out what is inside.

sources.quote: תדרכה ותרמסה והוא מגזר' ויזר את הגיזה
sources.says: Ralbag says it means tread and trample, from the same root as wringing out the fleece.

39:16.headline: One word built from two: hard-hearted and forgetful
39:16.body: Metzudat Zion says הקשיח joins קשה, hard, and סח, put out of mind: the bird hardens her heart and forgets her young. Ibn Ezra notes the word appears only here and in Isaiah 63:17.

sources.quote: הוא מלה מורכבת מן קשה ומן סח ור״ל הקשה לבה וסחה מדעתה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says הקשיח is a word made of קשה and סח: she hardened her heart and put them out of her mind.

sources.quote: וכמהו תקשיח לבנו מיראתך ואין להם שלישי במקרא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the only other use is Isaiah 63:17, and there is no third in the Bible.

39:17.headline: "God made her forget", the root of Menashe's name
39:17.body: Metzudat Zion reads השה as "made her forget". Ibn Ezra ties it to Joseph's words when he named Menashe: "God has made me forget".

sources.quote: השה. השכיחה כמו אתם ישראל לא תנשני
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says השה means made her forget, as in Isaiah 44:21.

sources.quote: כי השה - מטעם: כי נשני אלהים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has the sense of כי נשני אלהים, God made me forget.

39:21.headline: Pawing the ground, or scouting the valley?
39:21.body: חפר usually means to dig, and Ralbag says the horse paws the valley floor. Rashi reads it as spying out, as in Deuteronomy 1:22, since horsemen lie in wait in valleys.

sources.quote: יחפרו רגליו בעמק כמנהג הסוסים
sources.says: Ralbag says the horse's feet dig in the valley, as horses do.

sources.quote: יַחְפְּרוּ בָעֵמֶק. כְּמוֹ ״וְיַחְפְּרוּ לָנוּ אֶת הָאָרֶץ״
sources.says: Rashi says it means to scout, as in Deuteronomy 1:22, because riders lie in ambush in valleys.

39:24.headline: The war horse swallows the ground, or pits it
39:24.body: Rashi first says יגמא means the horse makes pits, גומות, with its feet. Rashi and Ramban also read it as "swallows", as in Genesis 24:17: the horse runs so fast it seems to drink up the land.

sources.quote: עוֹשֶׂה גֻּמּוֹת בְּרַגְלָיו. עִנְיָן אַחֵר: יְגַמֶּא כְּמוֹ ״הַגְמִיאִינִי נָא״
sources.says: Rashi says the horse makes holes with its feet, or else the word means swallow, as in Genesis 24:17.

sources.quote: פירשוהו מן הגמיאיני נא, לשון משל, כי מרוב מרוצתו כאילו ישתה הארץ
sources.says: Ramban says it is a figure of speech: the horse runs so fast it is as if it drinks the land.

39:30.headline: Eaglets gulp blood, or crack ribs to get it?
39:30.body: Rashi hears the doubled sound, like saying על על, as gulping a lot. Ibn Ezra also offers עלעא, the rabbinic word for rib: the young break the ribs of the dead to get at the blood.

sources.quote: וְנִרְאֶה כְּבוֹלֵעַ הַרְבֵּה, כְּאוֹמֵר ״עַל עַל״
sources.says: Rashi says the young seem to swallow a great deal, as if saying על על.

sources.quote: או יהיה מגזרת עלעא בלשון רבנן. והטעם: ישברו צלעות החלל להוציא דם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word may come from the rabbinic עלעא, rib: they break the ribs of the slain to get the blood out.

4:2.headline: Tested once and worn out, or may we lift a word?
4:2.body: Rashi reads הנסה from testing: God tested you once, and you are already worn out? Ibn Ezra reads it as נשא, "to lift", with a samekh for a shin: if we raise a word to you, will you tire? Ralbag gives both and prefers testing.

sources.quote: בְּנִסָּיוֹן אֶחָד שֶׁנִּסְּךָ בּוֹרַאֲךָ וּבָא אֵלֶיךָ, אַתָּה נִלְאֶה
sources.says: Rashi says Eliphaz asks if Job is worn out by a single test from his Creator.

sources.quote: הנו"ן לשון רבים והסמ"ך מקום שי"ן והה"א מקום אל"ף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the samekh stands for a shin and the he for an alef, so the word is נשא, to lift.

sources.quote: או יהיה מענין נסיון והוא היותר נכון
sources.says: Ralbag gives the lifting reading, then says the testing reading is more correct.

4:6.headline: Was Job's piety his trust, or his foolishness?
4:6.body: Metzudat Zion, Ramban and Ibn Ezra read כסלתך as "your trust": your fear of God is what you lean on. Rashi reads it from כסילות, foolishness: Eliphaz says Job's piety came from folly, not from full understanding.

sources.quote: כסלתך. ענין בטחון ותקוה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says כסלתך means trust and hope.

sources.quote: כסלתך, כמו אם שמתי זהב כסלי, שהוא כמו מבטחי
sources.says: Ramban says it means what one trusts in, as in Job 31:24.

sources.quote: כסלתך - דבר שתשען עליו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is something you lean on.

sources.quote: כִּסְלָתֶךָ. הִיא (בבא מציעא נח.) מֵחֲמַת כְּסִילוּת הִיא, וְלֹא מִדַּעַת שְׁלֵימָה
sources.says: Rashi says Job's fear of God came from foolishness and not from full knowledge.

4:10.headline: Five words for lion in two verses
4:10.body: Verses 10 and 11 name the lion five ways: אריה, שחל, כפיר, ליש, לביא. Commentators stop to explain the pile-up. Rashi says the big, middle and small lions stand for kings, officers and servants. Metzudat Zion says all are names of the lion, some larger than others.

sources.quote: הָאֲרִי גָּדוֹל, וְהַשַּׁחַל בֵּינוֹנִי, וְהַכְּפִיר קָטָן; כֻּלָּם נִתָּעוּ. כְּלוֹמַר: הַמְּלָכִים וְהַשָּׂרִים וְהָעֲבָדִים
sources.says: Rashi says the lion is large, the שחל middle-sized and the כפיר small, standing for kings, officers and servants.

sources.quote: שחל. וכפירים ליש ולביא המה שמות הארי זכר ונקבה אלא שזה גדול מזה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says these are all names of the lion, male and female, one larger than another.

sources.quote: הם משל לאנשים הרעים אשר כל מגמתם להזיק לזולתם
sources.says: Ralbag says the lions are a picture of wicked people who aim to harm others.

4:11.headline: The lion is not losing its prey; it is perishing
4:11.body: Rashi says אובד here does not mean losing something. It means the lion itself goes to ruin, like "a lost sheep" in Psalms. Metzudat David says the mighty lion dies of hunger.

sources.quote: אוֹבֵד אֵינוֹ לְשׁוֹן אָדָם הָאוֹבֵד דָּבָר מִמֶּנּוּ, אֶלָּא הוּא עַצְמוֹ הוֹלֵךְ לְאִבּוּד
sources.says: Rashi says the word does not mean losing something but going to ruin oneself.

sources.quote: סופו אובד הוא מבלי מצוא טרף ומזון להחיות נפשו ומת ברעב
sources.says: Metzudat David says the lion perishes for lack of prey and dies of hunger.

4:12.headline: A prophecy that reached Eliphaz as if stolen
4:12.body: Commentators stop on this word because it says how Eliphaz heard from God. Rashi says the word came secretly, like something stolen, because a prophet outside Israel does not receive open revelation. Ralbag reads it as "hidden", and Ibn Ezra as "snatched".

sources.quote: כְּדָבָר גָּנוּב; לְפִי שֶׁאֵין רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ נִגְלֶה עַל נְבִיאֵי עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא
sources.says: Rashi says the prophecy came like a stolen thing, since the holy spirit is not revealed openly to prophets of the nations.

sources.quote: ויתייחס כאלו גנוב הוא מן הקדושה
sources.says: Metzudat David says the prophecy came as if stolen from holiness.

sources.quote: יגונב. ר"ל יעלם ויתכסה
sources.says: Ralbag says it means hidden and covered.

sources.quote: יגונב - מן גנב ועניינו נחטף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from stealing and means snatched.

4:12.headline: Only a little of the word, or not its best part
4:12.body: Metzudat Zion and Ralbag read שמץ as "a little". Ibn Ezra says all commentators read it that way from context. He thinks it means Eliphaz could not take in the best of it, as Moses saw God's back but not His face.

sources.quote: שמץ. ענין מעט ומשהו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שמץ means a little, a tiny amount.

sources.quote: כל המפרשים פירשו בו מעט לפי העניין
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says all commentators explained it as "a little" from the context.

sources.quote: כי לא יכלה אזני לקחת הטוב המעולה ממנו, כעניין פנים ואחור הנזכרים בפרשת כי תשא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the ear could not take in the best of it, like the face and back in Exodus 33.

4:15.headline: Hair standing stiff as nails
4:15.body: Rashi says תסמר describes hair standing on end. Metzudat Zion ties it to מסמר, a nail: the hair stiffened like a nail. Ramban cites Rav Hai Gaon for the same link to nails.

sources.quote: תְּסַמֵּר. הוּא לְשׁוֹן אָדָם שֶׁעָמְדוּ שַׂעֲרוֹתָיו
sources.says: Rashi says the word describes a person whose hair stood up.

sources.quote: תסמר. מל׳ מסמר ויתד ור״ל נתקשה כמסמר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from מסמר, a nail: the hair grew stiff like a nail.

sources.quote: פירשו בשם הגאון רבינו האי ז"ל כי הוא מלשון מסמרות נטועים, מרוב פחדו
sources.says: Ramban cites Rav Hai Gaon: the word comes from fixed nails, from great fear.

4:16.headline: A shape seen with the eyes, or an image in a dream
4:16.body: Maimonides says תמונה has three senses: a shape seen with the eyes, an image held in the mind, and a truth grasped by the intellect. Here, he says, it is the second: an image before Eliphaz's eyes while he slept.

sources.quote: ואילו "תמונה" היא מונח מסופק בעל שלוש משמעויות
sources.says: Maimonides says תמונה is a word with three meanings.

sources.quote: כלומר דמיון אל מול עיניי בשנתי
sources.says: Maimonides says that in this verse it means an image before the eyes in sleep.

sources.quote: תמונה. צורה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says תמונה means a form.

4:16.headline: A whisper, or a voice heard out of silence
4:16.body: Rashi gives two readings: a whispered voice, or a voice heard from the silence of angels singing softly. Ibn Ezra compares Elijah's "still small voice" and calls it a lower kind of prophecy. Maimonides lists it as prophecy where one hears speech but sees no form.

sources.quote: קוֹל שָׁמַעְתִּי מִדְּמָמָה, אֲבָל דְּמָמָה לֹא שָׁמַעְתִּי
sources.says: Rashi says in his second reading that Eliphaz heard a voice from the silence but did not hear the silence itself.

sources.quote: שמעתי קול נמוך מאד כאלו היתה מורכבת משתיקה וקול
sources.says: Metzudat David says it was a very low voice, as if made of silence and sound together.

sources.quote: דממה וקול - כמו: קול דממה דקה וזו דרך נבואה קטנה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares it to Elijah's still small voice and calls it a lesser form of prophecy.

sources.quote: ויש שהנביא אינו רואה אף צורה, אלא הוא שומע דיבור בלבד הקורא לו במראה הנבואה
sources.says: Maimonides says some prophets see no form at all and only hear speech, and gives Eliphaz as an example.

4:19.headline: Houses of clay: the homes people live in, or their bodies
4:19.body: Ibn Ezra first reads בתי חמר as the clay houses people live in. He prefers to read them as human bodies, whose base is dust. Metzudat David reads them as this lower world.

sources.quote: קל וחומר: הדרים בבתי חומר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra first reads it as those who live in clay houses.

sources.quote: ואף שוכני בתי חומר הם הגופות שיסודם בעפר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says his preferred reading is that these are the bodies, whose foundation is dust.

sources.quote: בני אדם השוכנים בבתי חומר ר״ל בעולם השפל
sources.says: Metzudat David says the clay houses mean the lower world where people live.

4:21.headline: Their best part is pulled up: wisdom, wealth, or a tent cord
4:21.body: Rashi reads יתרם as their pride and wisdom, pulled up like a tent peg. Ralbag reads it as the mind, which sets people above animals. Ibn Ezra mentions a tent cord and prefers wealth: at death people lose their money.

sources.quote: גַּאֲוָתָם וְחָכְמָתָם תִּתְבַּלַּע בְּגוּפָן (תהלים קז:כז), וְהִנֵּה נוֹסַעַת וְנִסַּחַת
sources.says: Rashi says their pride and wisdom are swallowed up and pulled away.

sources.quote: יתרונם אשר בם על שאר הב"ח והוא השכל
sources.says: Ralbag says it is their advantage over other living things, the mind.

sources.quote: ואחרים אמרו: כי הוא כמו: כי יתרי פתח - שיסע יתר אהלי. והקרוב אלי: שהוא כמו: יתרה עשה, שהוא ממון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a tent-cord reading and says the closest reading is wealth.

40:2.headline: Get the upper hand over God, or take a lesson
40:2.body: Rashi reads יסור as "to rule over": can a person get the upper hand over God? The Metzudot read it from מוסר, "discipline": the one who argued with God should now take the lesson.

sources.quote: הַאִם שַׁדַּי – אָדָם יִשְׂתָּרֵר
sources.says: Rashi asks whether a person can rule over God.

sources.quote: יסור. מל׳ מוסר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says יסור comes from מוסר, discipline.

sources.quote: האם אתה הרב עם שדי קבל מוסר מדבריו
sources.says: Metzudat David says the one who quarrels with God should accept His rebuke.

40:15.headline: A plural for beasts, or the name of one giant creature
40:15.body: בהמות looks like the plural of בהמה, "animal", and Ramban says it could mean all great beasts. But the sages held it is the name of one unique creature, and Rashi adds that it is kept ready for the future.

sources.quote: בהמות שם כלל לכל בהמה וחיה גדולה, ולויתן לדגים העצומים, רק רבותינו ז"ל קבלו ענין בהמות ולויתן שהם יחידים ושמן כן
sources.says: Ramban says the word could be a general name for great beasts, but the sages received that Behemoth and Leviathan are single creatures with those names.

sources.quote: בהמות - שם בהמה גדולה אין ביישוב גדולה ממנה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the name of one huge animal, the largest on land.

sources.quote: בְּהֵמוֹת. מוּכָן לֶעָתִיד
sources.says: Rashi says Behemoth is kept ready for the time to come.

40:17.headline: Not "he wants" but "he stiffens" or "he swings fast"
40:17.body: יחפץ usually means "he wants", but Rashi reads it like יחפז, "he stiffens", and Ralbag reads the צ as a ז, "he moves it fast". Ibn Ezra rejects the "want" reading with a pun: "I have no want for it."

sources.quote: יַחְפֹּץ. כְּמוֹ יַחְפֹּז
sources.says: Rashi reads יחפץ like יחפז and explains it as stiffening.

sources.quote: יניע זנבו בחפזה ובמהירות והנה הצד"י תמורת זי"ן כי הם ממוצא אחד
sources.says: Ralbag says he moves his tail quickly, with צ standing for ז because both are sounded in the same place.

sources.quote: והמפרשים הוציאוהו מגזרת חפץ ואין לי בו חפץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says others derived it from חפץ, "want", and jokes that he has no want for that reading.

40:17.headline: A word for fear that here means testicles
40:17.body: פחד usually means fear, but Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it here as testicles, from the Aramaic Targum's פחדין in Leviticus 21:20. Ramban says no other source for the word was found.

sources.quote: פַּחֲדָיו. בֵּיצָיו
sources.says: Rashi says פחדיו means his testicles.

sources.quote: פחדיו - תרגום: מרוח אשך פחדין והם הבצים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the Targum renders a Leviticus word for testicles as פחדין.

sources.quote: פחדיו, לא מצאו לו מוצא, רק מתרגום מרוח אשך
sources.says: Ramban says the only source found for the word is the Targum of Leviticus.

40:18.headline: Usually a riverbed, here it means strength
40:18.body: אפיק usually means a stream bed. Rashi and Ramban read it as "strong", from the same root as ויתאפק, "he held himself in": his bones are strong as bronze.

sources.quote: אֲפִיקֵי. חוֹזֶק
sources.says: Rashi says אפיקי means strength.

sources.quote: עצמיו אפיקי נחושה, חזקי נחושה, מלשון ומזיח אפיקים, אזור החזקים, וכל לשון התאפקות
sources.says: Ramban reads it as "strong as bronze" and ties it to התאפקות, holding oneself firm.

40:18.headline: A one-time word: a heavy iron load or an iron hammer
40:18.body: Ibn Ezra notes that כמטיל appears nowhere else, and Rashi reads it as a heavy load of iron. Ramban reads it as a great iron hammer, from ויטילו, "they hurled", in Jonah.

sources.quote: כמטיל ברזל - אין לו חבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner in the Bible.

sources.quote: כְּמַטִּיל. כְּמַשָּׂאוֹי שֶׁל בַּרְזֶל
sources.says: Rashi says it means a heavy load of iron.

sources.quote: מטיל ברזל הוא הפטיש הגדול שאדם נוטל על הסלע ויפוצץ אותו, מלשון ויטילו את יונה
sources.says: Ramban says it is the great hammer used to smash rock, from the verb in "they hurled Jonah".

40:20.headline: A thousand mountains grow his food every day
40:20.body: בול is יבול, "produce", with its first letter dropped. Rashi joins it to Psalms 50:10, "Behemoth on a thousand hills": a thousand mountains grow food for him, and he grazes them all each day.

sources.quote: בול. כמו יבול בחסרון פ״א הפעל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בול is יבול with its first root letter missing.

sources.quote: אֶלֶף הָרִים נָשְׂאוּ לוֹ יְבוּל וּבְכָל יוֹם רוֹעֶה אֶת כֻּלָּם
sources.says: Rashi says a thousand mountains yield produce for him and he grazes them all every day.

40:24.headline: With his eyes, or down to the river's springs
40:24.body: עין means both "eye" and "spring of water". Ibn Ezra reads "with his eyes", as if Behemoth thinks he can drink the Jordan, while Metzudat Zion reads "down to its springs".

sources.quote: כאילו יקח הירדן בעיניו, כי יחשוב שישתהו כולו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Behemoth eyes the Jordan as if he could drink all of it.

sources.quote: ועיניו הוא ענין מעין מים כמו עין המים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says עיניו here means springs of water.

sources.quote: את כל הירדן יקח אל פיו עד המעינות מקום נביעתו
sources.says: Metzudat David says he takes the whole Jordan into his mouth, down to the springs where it rises.

41:4.headline: "His branches": a righteous man's children, the beast's limbs, or boasts?
41:4.body: בד is a tree branch. Rashi says the branches are a righteous man's children, Metzudat Zion says they are the beast's limbs, and Ibn Ezra, as Ramban reports, reads them as a challenger's boasts.

sources.quote: בַּדָּיו. עֲנָפָיו, וְהֵם בָּנָיו
sources.says: Rashi says בדיו means branches, which are the righteous man's children.

sources.quote: בדיו. אבריו וכן יאכל בדי עורו (לעיל יח) והוא מושאל מבדי האילן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בדיו means limbs, a word borrowed from the branches of a tree.

sources.quote: לא אחריש מלספר בדיו וכזביו אם ינצחני
sources.says: Ramban reports Ibn Ezra's reading: God would not keep quiet about the challenger's boasts and lies.

41:4.headline: חין: the beast's grace, or a righteous man's plea?
41:4.body: Ralbag reads the odd word חין as חן, grace: the beauty of the beast's build. Rashi reads it as תחינה, the prayer of a righteous man, which God will repay.

sources.quote: וחין ערכו. כמו וחן ערכו והרצון בו ויופי סידורו
sources.says: Ralbag says חין is like חן, meaning the beauty of how the beast is put together.

sources.quote: וּתְחִנַּת סִדּוּרוֹ שֶׁל צַדִּיק אֲשַׁלֵּם שְׂכָרוֹ
sources.says: Rashi reads it as the plea of a righteous man, whose reward God will pay.

41:7.headline: The Leviathan's shields are scales, so it is a kosher fish
41:7.body: Rashi says the shields are the scales covering the beast. The Talmud uses this verse, with verse 22, to show the Leviathan has scales and fins, so it is a kosher fish.

sources.quote: הֵן קַשְׂקַשִּׂים שֶׁעָלָיו, הַמְּגִנִּין עָלָיו כְּמָגֵן
sources.says: Rashi says the shields are the scales on the beast, which protect it like a shield.

sources.quote: לִוְיָתָן דָּג טָהוֹר הוּא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״גַּאֲוָה אֲפִיקֵי מָגִנִּים״
sources.says: The Talmud says the Leviathan is a kosher fish, since these shields are its scales.

41:10.headline: The Leviathan sneezes light, and a sneeze is a good sign
41:10.body: Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra explain this rare word from the language of the sages, where it means sneezing. The Talmud cites this verse to show that a sneeze is a good sign for a sick person.

sources.quote: עטישותיו. לשון עטוש ידוע בדרז״ל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means sneezing, known from the sages' language.

sources.quote: ידוע מדברי רבותינו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is known from the words of the sages.

sources.quote: שִׁשָּׁה דְּבָרִים סִימָן יָפֶה לַחוֹלֶה, אֵלּוּ הֵן: עִטּוּשׁ
sources.says: The Talmud lists sneezing among six good signs for a sick person, citing this verse.

41:11.headline: Sparks that escape, or sparks born from his mouth?
41:11.body: The verb usually means to escape. Metzudat Zion says here the sparks are flung out, and Ralbag reads it as in Isaiah 66:7, "she gave birth": the sparks are born from the beast's mouth.

sources.quote: יתמלטו. יושלכו כמו אל מראיו יוטל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says יתמלטו means they are thrown out.

sources.quote: יצאו ויולדו ממנו מגזרת והמליטה זכר
sources.says: Ralbag says they come out and are born from him, from the same root as giving birth in Isaiah 66:7.

41:12.headline: אגמון: a boiling cauldron, or a steaming marsh?
41:12.body: Rashi and Ralbag say אגמון is a pot or big cauldron, giving off steam like the beast's nostrils. Ibn Ezra hears אגם, a pond, steaming as the air heats up.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן כְּלִי חֶרֶשׂ הוּא, כְּמוֹ דּוּד נָפוּחַ
sources.says: Rashi says, judging from context, that it is a clay pot, like a boiling kettle.

sources.quote: ואגמון. הוא דוד גדולה
sources.says: Ralbag says אגמון is a big cauldron.

sources.quote: ואגמון. אגם המים כאשר יתחמם האויר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a pond of water when the air heats up.

41:13.headline: His נפש is his breath, hot enough to light coals
41:13.body: נפש usually means soul or life, and Maimonides lists several meanings of the word. Ramban and Ibn Ezra say that here it is the breath blowing out of the beast's nose.

sources.quote: הרוח היוצא מן האף תקרא נפש
sources.says: Ramban says the air that comes out of the nose is called נפש.

sources.quote: נפשו - הרוח היוצא מאפו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says נפשו is the breath coming out of his nose.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 41
sources.quote: הוא שם נפש החי המשותפת לכל בעל תחושה
sources.says: Maimonides says נפש has several meanings, the first being the life shared by every creature that feels.

41:17.headline: Not sinning: the waves fall short before the beast
41:17.body: חטא usually means to sin, but Rashi and Metzudat Zion say here it means to fall short: the waves give way before the Leviathan. Ralbag reads it as "purge": the mighty are so afraid they lose control of their bowels.

sources.quote: יִתְחַטָּאוּ. לְשׁוֹן חִסָּרוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says יתחטאו means lacking, as in 1 Kings 1:21.

sources.quote: יתחטאו. ענין חסרון כמו קולע באבן אל השערה ולא יחטיא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means lacking, as in Judges 20:16, slinging at a hair and not missing.

sources.quote: ממשברי לב שישיגום בסבת הפחד יתנקו
sources.says: Ralbag says that from the heartbreak of fear they are cleaned out, that is, they relieve themselves.

41:21.headline: תותח: a fishing spear, or a wall-smashing stone thrower?
41:21.body: Ibn Ezra says the word has no match and is some kind of weapon. Ralbag reports a view that it is a spiked tool for catching fish, but prefers the great machine that hurls stones to break walls.

sources.quote: תותח - אין ריע לו, והטעם: כמו נשק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no match and means a weapon.

sources.quote: והנכון שתותח הוא הכלי הגדול שמשליכין בו האבנים הגדולות להפיל החומות
sources.says: Ralbag says the right reading is the large machine that throws big stones to knock down walls.

41:22.headline: חרוץ: a sharp threshing sledge, or a bed of gold?
41:22.body: Metzudat Zion reads חרוץ as something sharp and notched, like a threshing sledge. Rashi reads it as a kind of gold: the mud the beast lies on shines like a golden bed.

sources.quote: חרוץ. מל׳ חריצים וחדודים כמו למורג חרוץ
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חרוץ means notched and sharp, as in a threshing sledge in Isaiah 41:15.

sources.quote: זֶה טִיט רִפּוּדוֹ מַזְרִיחַ כְּזָהָב חָרוּץ
sources.says: Rashi says the mud he lies on shines like חרוץ, which is a kind of gold.

41:23.headline: The sea churns like a spice pot, and smells like one
41:23.body: Rashi says the beast stirs the sea the way spices are mixed into perfume. The Talmud says no creature could bear the Leviathan's smell, except that it puts its head into the Garden of Eden, and cites this verse.

sources.quote: כְּמִרְקַחַת רִקּוּחַ בְּשָׂמִים, שֶׁהִיא מְעוֹרָה וּמְעֹרֶבֶת
sources.says: Rashi says the sea is stirred like a blend of spices, which is all mixed together.

sources.quote: וְאִלְמָלֵא מַכְנִיס רֹאשׁוֹ לְגַן עֵדֶן – אֵין כׇּל בְּרִיָּה יְכוֹלָה לַעֲמוֹד בְּרֵיחוֹ
sources.says: The Talmud says that if it did not put its head into the Garden of Eden, no creature could stand its smell.

41:24.headline: Gray hair on the sea, or seventy years to recover?
41:24.body: Ibn Ezra says the beast's wake turns the deep white like gray hair. The Talmud reads שיבה as old age, which starts at seventy: the deep needs seventy years to regain its strength.

sources.quote: יחשוב תהום לשיבה, כי השיער לבן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the deep looks like white hair.

sources.quote: אֵין תְּהוֹם חוֹזֵר לְאֵיתָנוֹ עַד שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה
sources.says: The Talmud says the deep does not return to its strength for seventy years, since old age is no less than seventy.

sources.quote: לְשֵׂיבָה. לְחַלְשׁוּת שֶׁל זִקְנָה וְשֵׂיבָה
sources.says: Rashi says the deep is as weak as old age before him.

41:25.headline: No one rules him, or there is none like him?
41:25.body: Rashi reads משלו as ממשלתו, rule: no creature rules over him. Ramban reads it from משל, likeness: nothing on dry land compares to him in strength.

sources.quote: וּפִתְרוֹנוֹ: מֶמְשַׁלְתּוֹ – שֶׁאֵין בְּרִיָּה מוֹשֶׁלֶת עָלָיו
sources.says: Rashi says it means his rule: no creature rules over him.

sources.quote: יאמר כי אין ביבשה נמשל לו בחוזק ובתוקף
sources.says: Ramban says nothing on land is like him in strength and power.

42:2.headline: כל: "everything", or short for "You surely can"?
42:2.body: כל usually means "all". Metzudat Zion reads it as יכול with a letter dropped, so Job says "You surely can". Ibn Ezra weighs that, then prefers "You can do everything".

sources.quote: כל. כמו יכול והוא מל׳ יכולת ונפלה פ״א הפעל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says כל is like יכול, from the word for ability, with its first letter dropped.

sources.quote: כי כל תוכל - כמו: יכול תוכל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra first reads it as "You surely can".

sources.quote: והנכון כי כל דבר תוכל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the better reading is "You can do every thing".

42:3.headline: Job repeats God's words but swaps in a gentler verb
42:3.body: God had asked "who darkens counsel" (Job 38:2). Job quotes it back with מעלים, "hides", instead. Metzudat David says the two mean the same, but Job chose the more respectful word.

sources.quote: כי מעלים ומחשיך הוא אחד במובנם אלא שאחז ל׳ כבוד
sources.says: Metzudat David says "hides" and "darkens" mean the same, but Job used a language of respect.

sources.quote: אֲשֶׁר הֶעֱלִים וְכִסָּה עֲצָתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means one who hid and covered God's counsel.

42:5.headline: "Now my eye has seen You": what kind of seeing?
42:5.body: Job says he once only heard of God, and now his eye sees Him. Rashi says he saw God's presence. Maimonides says hearing is knowing God by tradition, and seeing is knowing Him for certain.

sources.quote: וְעַתָּה עֵינִי רָאֲתָה אֶת שְׁכִינָתְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says now my eye has seen Your presence.

sources.quote: ולא ידע את האלוה אלא כקבלה עיוורת
sources.says: Maimonides says that before this Job knew God only by blind tradition.

sources.quote: אך כאשר ידע את ה' ידיעה ודאית
sources.says: Maimonides says that Job then came to know God with certain knowledge.

sources.quote: כי איוב לא נתנבא קודם זה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra learns from this verse that Job had not been a prophet before.

42:6.headline: "I reject": but reject what? The verse does not say
42:6.body: אמאס, "I reject", has no object. Ibn Ezra says Job rejects his own words. Rashi says his life. The Targum says his wealth. Maimonides says all the things he used to want.

sources.quote: על כן אמאס - בכל דברי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Job rejects all his own words.

sources.quote: מוֹאֵס אֲנִי בְּחַיַּי
sources.says: Rashi says Job now rejects his life.

sources.quote: מַאֲסֵית עָתְרִי
sources.says: The Targum translates: I reject my wealth.

sources.quote: על כן אמאס כל אשר הייתי מתאוה
sources.says: Maimonides reads it as: I reject everything I used to desire.

42:6.headline: ונחמתי: Job is comforted, or Job regrets?
42:6.body: ונחמתי can mean "I am comforted" or "I regret". Metzudat David and Maimonides read comfort: Job is at peace with sitting in the ashes. Ibn Ezra reads it as Job admitting he was wrong.

sources.quote: עתה יש לי תנחומין רב על הצער שהייתי בו לשבת בתוך עפר ואפר
sources.says: Metzudat David says Job now has great comfort for the pain of sitting in dust and ashes.

sources.quote: וניחמתי על היותי בתוך עפר ואפר
sources.says: Maimonides reads it as: I am comforted for being in dust and ashes.

sources.quote: הטעם שהודה ואמר: ונחמתי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the reason God praised Job is that he admitted he was wrong and said ונחמתי.

42:8.headline: Would God really do something shameful to the friends?
42:8.body: God says He will not do נבלה, a shameful thing, to the friends. Ibn Ezra says God would never do anything shameful. The point is that punishing God's defenders would look shameful to people.

sources.quote: וחלילה שיעשה השם נבלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God forbid that God should do something shameful.

sources.quote: רק בעבור שהיו חברי איוב מצדיקי השם, אם השם יביא עליהם רע יאמרו תועי רוח הנה זה דבר נבלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the friends defended God, so if God harmed them, confused people would call it shameful.

sources.quote: נבלה. דבר כעור וגנות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says נבלה means an ugly and disgraceful thing.

42:10.headline: God brought Job back from a kind of captivity
42:10.body: שבות can mean a captive state or a fortune restored. Ibn Ezra says Job had been a captive in the Satan's hands, and God freed him. The Targum calls it Job's exile.

sources.quote: שהיה נשבה ביד השטן, הוציאו מרשותו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Job was a captive in the Satan's hand, and God took him out of its power.

sources.quote: אֲתִיב יַת גַלְוַת אִיוֹב
sources.says: The Targum translates: He brought back Job's exile.

sources.quote: שבות. מלשון השבה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שבות comes from the word for bringing back.

42:11.headline: A rare gift: a coin, or a small lamb?
42:11.body: קשיטה appears only three times in the Bible. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it is a coin, as when Jacob paid a hundred קשיטה for land. Ibn Ezra says it is a small lamb.

sources.quote: קשיטה. שם מטבע מעה וכן במאה קשיטה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the name of a coin, as in Genesis 33.

sources.quote: קְשִׂיטָה. מָעָה
sources.says: Rashi says קשיטה is a coin.

sources.quote: קשיטה - כבשה קטנה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says קשיטה is a small lamb.

5:3.headline: Eliphaz cursed the fool's home, or spelled out its end
5:3.body: ואקוב can mean "I cursed", the word Balaam uses when asked to curse Israel. Ibn Ezra and the Targum read it that way, while Malbim reads it as "I named" the fool's fate, as in "name your wages".

sources.quote: ואקב - קללתי, כמו: מה אקב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means "I cursed", like Balaam's "how can I curse".

sources.quote: וְלַטְטֵית מְדוֹרֵיהּ
sources.says: The Targum translates "I cursed his dwelling".

sources.quote: ר"ל פרשתי ענשו של זה וסופו, כמו נקבה שכרך עלי
sources.says: Malbim says it means "I spelled out" his punishment and end, as in "name your wages".

5:5.headline: Taken from among thorns, or by men with shields
5:5.body: צנים usually means thorns, and Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra read it that way: the hungry pick his crop out of the thorns. Ramban points out that the Targum hears צנה, a shield, and pictures soldiers carrying the crop off.

sources.quote: המ״ם נוספת וענינו קוצים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the מ is added and the word means thorns.

sources.quote: ויקחו הרעבים הקצים, מבין החוחים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the hungry take the crop from among the thorns.

sources.quote: פתר צנים מן ונושא הצנה לפניו
sources.says: Ramban says the Targum read צנים from צנה, a shield, as in "the shield bearer went before him".

sources.quote: וּפוּלְמוֹסִין בְּמָנֵי זְיָנָא יַדְבְּרוּנֵיהּ
sources.says: The Targum translates that armies with weapons will carry it off.

5:5.headline: Thirsty men, a hard stone, or long-haired robbers?
5:5.body: צמים appears only twice in the Tanach, and the commentators guess widely. Metzudat Zion reads "thirsty ones", Ibn Ezra reports a view from Arabic that it is a hard stone, and Ralbag reads it as wild men who grow their hair in braids.

sources.quote: צמים. כמו צמאים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the same as "thirsty ones".

sources.quote: ויש אומר: כי צמים - האבן התקיפה בלשון ישמעאל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra brings the thirsty reading, then a view that in Arabic it means a hard stone.

sources.quote: וקראו צמים לפי שמנהג הפריצים שיהיו מגדלי צמה
sources.says: Ralbag says it means lawless men, called this because they grow their hair in braids.

5:7.headline: Sparks flying up, birds, or demons?
5:7.body: רשף can mean a flame or spark. Metzudat Zion reads sparks that rise, Ramban reads birds, and Rashi reads angels and spirits, while the Talmud says they are demons that stay away from someone who says the Shema at bedtime.

sources.quote: רשף. גחלת אש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רשף is a burning coal, so its "children" are sparks.

sources.quote: ובני רשף, בני העוף
sources.says: Ramban says the phrase means birds, and also gives the sparks reading.

sources.quote: שֶׁהֵם מַלְאָכִים וְרוּחוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says they are angels and spirits, unlike man who is born to trouble.

sources.quote: וְאֵין ״רֶשֶׁף״ אֶלָּא מַזִּיקִין
sources.says: The Talmud says רשף means harmful spirits, which keep away from one who says the Shema in bed.

5:8.headline: Bring my words to God, or hand him my life
5:8.body: דברתי looks like "my words", and Rashi reads it as Eliphaz's prayer. Ramban and Malbim read it as "my leading", from words for steering rafts and leading sheep: Eliphaz would hand the running of his life to God.

sources.quote: וְאִלּוּ הָיִיתִי שָׂם, דִּבְרָתִי בְּבַקָּשָׁה
sources.says: Rashi says Eliphaz would put his words to God as a request.

sources.quote: דברתי, הנהגתי, כמו דוברות בים
sources.says: Ramban says it means "my conduct", like rafts steered at sea.

sources.quote: דברתי. מלשון הנהגה, כמו ורעו כבשים כדברם
sources.says: Malbim says it means leading, as sheep graze where they are led.

5:10.headline: Rain for the Land of Israel, water sent elsewhere
5:10.body: The verse says God "gives" rain on the land and "sends" water on the outlying places. Rashi, the Targum and the Talmud read "the land" as the Land of Israel, which God waters himself, and the outlying places as the rest of the world, watered through a messenger.

sources.quote: עַל יְדֵי שָׁלִיחַ, לִשְׁאָר אֲרָצוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the water on the outlying places goes to other lands, through a messenger.

sources.quote: אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל מַשְׁקֶה אוֹתָהּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ, וְכׇל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ עַל יְדֵי שָׁלִיחַ
sources.says: The Talmud says God waters the Land of Israel himself and the rest of the world through a messenger, citing this verse.

sources.quote: עַל אַפֵּי אַרְעָא דְיִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: The Targum translates "on the face of the Land of Israel".

5:12.headline: A word for success that the sages read as Torah
5:12.body: Ramban derives תושיה from יש, "there is", so it means a plan that actually comes to be. Ralbag says it means a fixed order, which is why the Torah is called תושיה, and Tractate Kallah plays on it as the Torah that wears down (מתשת) a person's strength.

sources.quote: כי תושיה נגזר מן יש
sources.says: Ramban says the word comes from יש, "there is".

sources.quote: ורבי משה פירש: שהוא מן יש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means wisdom, and cites Rabbi Moshe who derives it from יש.

sources.quote: ולזה נקרא התורה תושיה
sources.says: Ralbag says the word means law and order, and that is why the Torah is called תושיה.

sources.quote: ולמה נקראה תושיה שמתשת כחו של אדם
sources.says: Tractate Kallah says the Torah is called תושיה because it wears down a person's strength.

5:21.headline: A tongue like a whip, or gossip that roams
5:21.body: שוט can mean "whip" or "roam". Ibn Ezra says slander is like a whip, while Metzudat Zion and Ralbag picture slander roaming the land and you staying hidden from it.

sources.quote: כי הלשון הרע הוא כמו שוט
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says slander is like a whip, and also suggests "tongue" may mean a nation.

sources.quote: ענין ההליכה אנה ואנה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means going back and forth.

sources.quote: כאשר תשוטט לשון הרע בארץ
sources.says: Ralbag says it means when slander roams the land, you will not be mentioned.

5:23.headline: Stones of the field, or a strange wild creature
5:23.body: Plainly, Eliphaz says you will not trip on the field's stones, as Ibn Ezra explains. Rashi says אבני השדה is a kind of man-like creature, and the Jerusalem Talmud describes a mountain creature that lives by its navel.

sources.quote: כאילו ברית כרתה עם האבנים שלא תנזק בהן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is as if you made a pact with the stones so they will not hurt you.

sources.quote: אַבְנֵי הַשָּׂדֶה. מִין אָדָם הֵן
sources.says: Rashi says the "stones of the field" are a kind of man.

sources.quote: אַבְנֵי הַשָּׂדֶה חַיָּה. יַיסִי עַרְקִיי בַּר נַשׁ דְּטוּר הוּא
sources.says: The Jerusalem Talmud says it is an animal, a mountain man that lives from its navel.

5:26.headline: Coming to the grave ripe, or at sixty
5:26.body: Rashi says nothing else in Scripture explains בכלח, so he reads it from context as grain fully ripe. The Talmud counts its letters as sixty, and Ramban splits it into two words, "as if moist": still fresh in old age.

sources.quote: אֵין סֶמֶךְ בַּמִּקְרָא לְהָבִין מְלִיצָתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says there is no support in Scripture for the word, reads it as fully ripened grain, and cites the Sages' count of sixty.

sources.quote: ״בְּכֶלַח״ בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא שִׁיתִּין הָווּ
sources.says: Mar Zutra says the letters of בכלח add up to sixty, so dying at sixty is a natural death.

sources.quote: מלה מורכבת כאומר תבא לקבר בכאלו לח
sources.says: Ramban says it is two words joined, meaning you die old as if still young and moist.

sources.quote: בכלח - אין לו חבר כי אם שנים בספר הזה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has a match only in this book, and means dying at a full old age.

6:4.headline: Not anger but poison on the arrows
6:4.body: חמה usually means anger or heat. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as venom, as in "the venom of serpents", since Persian archers dipped their arrows in snake poison.

sources.quote: חֲמָתָם. אֶרֶס שֶׁלָּהֶם. דֶּרֶךְ פַּרְסִיִּים לָתֵת אֶרֶס שֶׁל נָחָשׁ בְּחִצֵּיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says חמתם is their poison, as Persians put snake venom on their arrows.

sources.quote: חמתם. ארסם כמו חמת תנינים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חמתם means their venom, as in Deuteronomy 32:33.

6:9.headline: Finish me off, or make me rich
6:9.body: Rashi reads ויבצעני as "finish me" and Ramban as "cut me to pieces": Job asks God to end his life. The Targum hears בצע, "gain", and ends the verse with "let Him open His hand and make me rich".

sources.quote: וִיבַצְּעֵנִי. וִיכַלֵּנִי
sources.says: Rashi says ויבצעני means "and finish me".

sources.quote: ויבצעני, יחתוך אותי לחתיכות
sources.says: Ramban says it means "cut me into pieces".

sources.quote: וּשְׁרֵי אֱלָהָא לִמְמַסְכֵּן יָתִי יַתִּיר יְדֵיהּ וִיעַתִּיר יָתִי
sources.says: The Targum speaks of God making Job poor, and of God opening His hand to make Job rich.
